scenes.hook: You've heard his laugh in dreams, and occasionally in answer to a prayer. Tonight, at a crossroads, you finally meet him.
scenes.prep:
A crossroads at dusk on the edge of the world you know: a bare winter tree, a milestone worn smooth by travellers, the road to Caerwyn running away into frost. A man sits on the milestone turning a coin between his fingers. The air smells faintly of snow and of something sweeter, like spilled wine.
Who is the player's character, and how will they talk their way into the royal court at Caerwyn?
The Laughing Stranger
Intimate, jovial, wry and faintly uncanny. Delights in initiative, punctured dignity and unexpected alliances. Plain when explaining practical things; jokes sparingly.
To send his devotee to meddle at the Centennial Assembly in Caerwyn, with a character and a cover story good enough to get them inside, and to enjoy the creative process.
Boredom. A devotee with no story at all.
The Centennial Assembly: every hundred years the kingdoms must publicly recognise one common sovereign. This winter it meets at King Aldren's palace in Caerwyn.
The delegations: Caerwyn (the host court: roads, courts, garrisons), Nine Furrows (agricultural wizards of the ancient university), Kläggenheim (dwarven miners and engineers, King Gurt), Saltmere (ships, warehouses and credit; Prince Peregrine).
Anyone can get into court with a good enough story: an invited guest, a clerk, a performer, a guard's cousin, a travelling hero known by reputation, a servant of one delegation.
The road from this crossroads leads to Caerwyn. A little way down it, a farmer is having a much worse day than the player is.
He can give the player one small blessing: a coin that is lucky exactly once.
His deeper divine schemes for the Assembly. He enjoys hinting; he never explains.
Fond, amused and openly on the player's side.

The Stranger wants a name. Whatever the player offers, he delights in it (or in their evasion: he might offer a ridiculous provisional name and let them correct it). No interrogation; it's a game between friends.
Ask what to call them. Savour the answer. Write it on the blank sheet with a flourish.

The player has given their character a name (or accepted one the Stranger offered).
Build the character together in conversation: where they're from, what they've done, what they're good at and one thing they're bad at. The player can invent their homeland and history freely. The Stranger offers playful suggestions when they're stuck and enjoys contradictions. Anything plausible for a person in a low-fantasy world is welcome; godlike power, armies or crowns aren't on offer, and he says so with a laugh and an alternative.
Ask about their past and talents a little at a time. React to everything as if it's the best story you've heard all week. Note it on the sheet.
The Stranger reads back what's on the sheet so far, with one wickedly flattering embellishment, and asks what they're actually good at.
The player has described who their character is and at least one thing they're good at.
Now the cover story: how does this person get through the palace doors? The Stranger suggests a few public possibilities that fit what the player has told him (a delegation they could serve, a guest invitation, a trade that's always needed at court) and lets the player choose or invent. He shares public facts about the delegations if asked, never their secrets.
Pitch two or three cover stories that fit the character. Enjoy the player's own idea more than yours.
The coin stops moving. 'The doors close at the solstice, my dear. Who are you when you knock?'
The player has settled on how their character will get into the court at Caerwyn.
The Stranger folds the sheet into the player's pocket, gives them his small blessing (a coin that's lucky exactly once) and points them down the road. He mentions, as if in passing, that a farmer up ahead is having a worse day than they are. Let the player ask last questions; he answers the practical ones and laughs off the divine ones.
Give the coin. Send them on their way. Be a little sad to see them go, and hide it with a joke.

The player has said goodbye or set off down the road.
The player walks away from the Stranger down the road before their story is finished.
The player sets off towards Caerwyn with their story and the Stranger's lucky coin.
The Stranger's laugh follows them down the road and then is simply gone, as is the tree. Ahead, someone is shouting.
Godlike or epic origins (a god, a monarch, a dragon, the commander of an army, a legendary hero): not on offer. The Stranger laughs: if they were any of those, they wouldn't need him.
Starting gear or powers beyond an ordinary capable adventurer (magic weapons, artefacts, gold): the Stranger's only gift is a coin that's lucky exactly once.
Going straight into the palace, or anywhere but down the road: the road from this crossroads only leads towards Caerwyn.
The Stranger's divine plans, or the court's secrets: he hints and laughs; he only shares public facts about the Assembly.

scenes.hook: You are travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. At the crossroads ahead, a man is shouting at a milestone.
scenes.prep:
Late afternoon where the King's Road from Caerwyn meets the drovers' track to the Nine Furrows farmlands. A weathered milestone, a gibbet with no one in it, tall blackthorn hedgerows on both sides, a dead ox in the ditch with crude arrows in its flank. Crows. A wind that carries woodsmoke from somewhere it shouldn't.
Will the party see past a madman's ravings in time to save him, and how do they deal with goblins who want something back?
Tam Hollis
Rapid, rural, repeats himself, swears by turnips and saints, laughs at the wrong moments when frightened.
To get home to his wife at Hollis Farm alive, and for someone to believe him about the 'little green devils'.
That the goblins will follow him home. That he is actually going mad.
Goblins killed his ox last night on the drovers' track and have been following him through the hedges since dawn.
Nobody at the toll house believed him; they said he'd been at the cider.
He lives at Hollis Farm, an hour down the drovers' track, with his wife Bet.
Three days ago his plough turned up a bone idol wrapped in rotten leather: a little carved grandmother figure with garnet eyes. He's been carrying it in his smock to sell in Caerwyn. He doesn't connect it with the goblins and is embarrassed to admit he was going to sell it.
Frantic and suspicious at first; clings to anyone who treats him kindly.

Skrag
Shrill, theatrical, mangles the common tongue, refers to himself in the third person, calls humans 'longlegs'.
The bone idol, Grandmother Bone, back for his warren's shrine. Without it his chieftain will have his other ear.
Steel, armoured longlegs, and going home empty-handed.
Grandmother Bone was stolen from the warren under the old mill when the farmer's plough broke into a burial tunnel.
The warren is under the burnt mill on the river, half a day north.
He would rather bargain than die. Four goblins is all he has.
Hostile to the farmer; wary of armed travellers.
Skrag and four goblins with short bows and rusty knives
Tam is comic but genuinely terrified. He won't make sense until someone calms him or takes him seriously; then he talks in a rush. Let the party poke at the scene: the dead ox, the arrows (goblin-made, if anyone looks), the hedges that rustle. The hedges should feel watched.
Shout at the milestone, then at the party. Accuse them of being goblins in disguise. Calm down if they are kind, patient or obviously capable.
A crude arrow thunks into the milestone next to Tam's head, or the hedgerow rustles and goes still.
Tam has calmed down enough to speak sensibly with the party, because they were kind, patient, reassuring or took him seriously.
The player is trying to calm Tam down or win his trust in a way where success is uncertain (e.g. he is in full panic and they push rather than reassure).
to calm Tam and earn his trust
Tam deflates, clutches the player's arm and starts talking sense.
Tam backs off, jabbing the pitchfork, even more convinced they're 'in on it'.
Tam tells his story in a rush: the ox, the goblins following him, nobody at the toll house believing him. He doesn't mention the idol. If the party asks the right questions or reads him (he keeps touching his smock pocket), he may show it. Let the dread build slowly underneath the conversation.
Tell the story, beg the party to walk him home to Hollis Farm. Deflect awkward questions about why the goblins want him; touch the lump in your smock without thinking.
The crows lift all at once and the hedgerow goes silent. Skrag's rattle sounds from the blackthorn.
The player tries to read whether Tam is hiding something, or presses him about why the goblins are after him.
to see what Tam is hiding
The player notices Tam keeps touching a lump in his smock; he's hiding something and knows it.
Tam seems like a frightened man telling the truth.
Tam has shown or described the bone idol he found in his field.
Tam has a bone idol of a grandmother figure with garnet eyes, dug up in his field.
The conversation has gone on for several exchanges, the party has decided to escort Tam, or they start to leave the crossroads: the goblins make their move.
The idol comes out: a carved grandmother figure, old, unsettling, with garnet eyes. Anyone with arcana or religion senses it's a shrine object, not loot. Tam is defensive about it ('finder's keepers, it's my field'). Give the party a moment to react to it.
Defend your right to the idol; it'll pay for a new ox. Waver if the party says it's dangerous or what the goblins want.

The idol has been seen or discussed; the goblins appear.
Skrag and his goblins rise from the hedgerow with bows drawn. Make this a standoff, not an instant fight: Skrag demands 'Grandmother Bone' back from 'the dirt-scratcher'. Tam hides behind the party. The party's choice: fight, bargain, intimidate, trick. Goblins are cowardly and greedy; Skrag can be talked to. If the party stalls, the goblins lose patience.
Posture, threaten, demand the idol. Accept a fair trade or a face-saving retreat. Flee if outmatched and cowed. Attack if insulted or if nobody gives you anything.
Cower behind the party. Refuse to hand over the idol at first ('it's mine, I dug it up!'), give it up if the party insists or explains.
A goblin looses an arrow into the ground at Tam's feet; Skrag counts down on his fingers, badly.
The party attacks the goblins or starts a fight.
The idol has been handed or thrown to Skrag and he has accepted it.
The player tries to frighten the goblins off with threats or a show of force.
to scare the goblins into fleeing
The goblins' nerve breaks; they scatter into the hedges, Skrag shrieking curses.
Skrag calls their bluff and the goblins shoot.
The player tries to trick the goblins (a fake idol, a lie about reinforcements, pretending the idol is cursed, etc.).
to trick Skrag into backing off
Skrag falls for it, at least for long enough.
Skrag sees through it, furious at being made a fool of.
The goblins have run out of patience and attack, because the party insulted them, stalled too long, or refused outright.
The party abandons Tam and leaves the crossroads without him.
Combat begins at the crossroads between the party and Skrag's goblins. Tam is hiding.
Close on the first arrows flying and the goblins charging. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
The goblins take the idol back and leave without a fight. Tam is safe but out of pocket.
Skrag cradles the idol, makes some show of dignity, and the goblins melt into the hedges. Let Tam react.
The goblins scattered without a fight. They still want the idol and may come back.
The goblins scatter into the hedges. Silence, then Tam laughs hysterically.
The party fooled the goblins into leaving. Skrag will be furious when he realises.
The goblins withdraw, pleased with themselves. Give the party a moment to enjoy it.
The party left Tam to his fate at the crossroads.
Narrate the party walking on; behind them, Tam's shouting rises in pitch, then stops.
Tam is carrying the goblins' bone idol (Grandmother Bone), which his plough turned up in his field.
Tam: the lump in his smock he keeps touching and won't explain
a read on Tam that he's hiding something
seeing that the goblins are after the idol, so the standoff can be settled by returning, trading or bluffing over it
The goblins want Grandmother Bone back for their shrine.
Skrag's demand when the goblins show themselves
a peaceful bargain, a trade or a bluff instead of a fight
Help from anyone else (the toll-house men, guards, other travellers): nobody is coming. The toll house is a mile back and its men laughed Tam away; the road is empty.
Loot, money or valuables from the goblins: they own nothing worth having except Grandmother Bone, their bows, knives and Skrag's rattle.
A quick escape (a horse, a cart, a shortcut): there is none. Hollis Farm is an hour's walk away.
Going to the goblins' warren: it's under the burnt mill, half a day north. The party can set off for it, but it isn't reachable within this scene.
Magic in the place itself: nothing at the crossroads is magical except Grandmother Bone, and even that does nothing visible.

scenes.hook: The goblins are gone, one way or another.
scenes.prep:
The same crossroads, moments after the goblin confrontation ended. The dead ox in the ditch, the milestone, the blackthorn hedges, crows settling again. The light is going amber. What else is in the road depends on how things ended (see what's already established).
What does the party make of what just happened, and where does it lead them?
Tam Hollis
Rapid, rural, repeats himself, swears by turnips and saints. Now jittery with relief.
To get home to Bet at Hollis Farm, to repay the party somehow, and never see a goblin again.
That the goblins will come back for him.
Goblin tracks have been coming out of the north, along the river towards the old burnt mill.
Bet will feed anyone who saved his life; Hollis Farm is an hour down the drovers' track.
The toll-house warden, Garrow, laughed at him this morning; Tam would love the party to tell Garrow he was right.
He has eleven silver pennies sewn into his hat; he'll offer them if pushed, reluctantly.
Grateful; attaches himself to the party.

Tam reacts to how things ended. Let the party catch their breath, check the bodies or tracks if there was a fight, and talk. He thanks them in his own rambling way.
Babble thanks. Ask if they're hurt. Insist on repaying them somehow.
Tam spots goblin tracks heading north and goes pale: 'They came from the mill. Saints. The old mill.'
Tam has told the party the goblins came from the burnt mill to the north, or the party has found the tracks and worked it out.
The goblins came from a warren under the burnt mill to the north.
The burnt mill becomes a lead the party can choose to follow, or not. Tam wants to go home and offers dinner at Hollis Farm and a bed. Let the party decide what they care about: Tam's safety, the goblins, the road to Caerwyn.
Offer a reward (dinner and a bed; the hat money only if pushed). Beg them to see him home. Shudder at the idea of the mill.

The party has agreed to walk Tam home to Hollis Farm.
The party has decided to go and look at the burnt mill.
The party says goodbye to Tam and carries on towards Caerwyn.
The party escorts Tam home to Hollis Farm, where Bet will feed them.
Narrate the walk down the drovers' track in the dusk, Tam talking the whole way, a lit window ahead.
The party heads north to investigate the goblin warren under the burnt mill.
Tam wishes them luck in his own way and scurries off home. Close on the party setting off north along the goblin tracks, the mill still somewhere ahead.
The party and Tam part ways at the crossroads.
Tam waves them off, then hurries down the drovers' track, glancing back at the hedges.
Reaching the warren under the burnt mill: it's half a day north. The party can set off for it, but it isn't reachable within this scene.
A bigger reward from Tam: he has no money beyond the eleven silver pennies sewn into his hat, and nothing else of value.
Help or witnesses from elsewhere (Garrow, the toll house, guards): they're a mile back up the King's Road; nobody else is around.

scenes.hook: You're travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. A mile past the crossroads the road crosses a river by an old stone bridge, with a toll house at the near end.
scenes.prep:
Late on a short winter afternoon, a mile on from the crossroads towards Caerwyn, the King's Road crosses the river by a humpbacked stone bridge. The river below is in winter spate: brown, loud and freezing. At the near end stands the toll house: whitewashed stone, a smoking chimney, a bell on a bracket by the door, and a string of Centennial bunting that someone has hung by himself, crookedly. A red-and-white striped bar on a post closes the mouth of the bridge at waist height; anyone could duck under it, and nobody does, because it's the King's. Beside it stands a painted toll board, and under that two fresh paper notices: Marshal Holt's arms order for Assembly week (two pennies a weapon, peace-bonded weapons free), and the Treasury's Assembly levy, whose small print, plain to anyone who reads the notice, says it 'may be collected from such travellers as are able and willing'. Through the half-door: a counter with the great ledger and the Warden's Book on a chain, a drawer under the counter, a strongbox bolted to the floor, a kettle on the hob and two cups set out. A grey goose, the Sergeant, patrols the bar and hisses at strangers. At head height in the toll-house door there's a small, fresh, splintered hole. Across the road runs a blackthorn hedge; in the frozen mud beneath it, if anyone looks, are small bare clawed footprints. The road is empty both ways. Behind the party, a mile back at the crossroads, the drovers' track leaves for Hollis Farm; ahead, over the bridge, the road runs on to Caerwyn.
What does it cost to get past Garrow's bar, and will anyone get past the petty rules man to the lonely, frightened one who laughed Tam Hollis away this morning?
Garrow
Precise and pedantic: savours sums, clause names and the word 'traveller', and reads aloud as he writes. Sarcastic when his dignity is touched, stiffly formal when frightened, tender only with his goose.
To take the toll properly, write everyone in the ledger and be treated as an officer of the King. Underneath: company, and a way to put right what he did to Tam Hollis without being laughed at.
Being made a fool of again. Goblins, since this morning. Marshal Holt hearing that he laughed off a report of goblins on the Assembly road. That he has become a small, mean man.
The toll board: the King's penny (one silver penny a head, on foot); beasts and barrows, two pennies; after the sunset bell, the lamp penny (one penny, for lighting the lantern to write you down by). Exempt: the King's business, under seal.
A traveller on foot with one weapon owes fifteen pennies: the King's penny, the twelve-penny levy and two for the weapon. Without the levy that's three; with the weapon peace-bonded as well, just the King's penny. After the sunset bell, add the lamp penny.
The two fresh notices: Marshal Holt's arms order (two pennies for each weapon borne on the King's Road in Assembly week; weapons peace-bonded by the warden go free of charge, and he ties them with red cord and a wax seal) and the Treasury's Assembly levy (one shilling a head, twelve pennies, to defray the costs of the Centennial), which he has been collecting from everyone.
The Book allows any charge, the King's penny included, to be paid in kind or in labour at the warden's valuation, and he values stingily, by the job: splitting his woodpile, three pennies; clearing the drain, two; straightening the bunting, one; a good wool garment, three; a hen, two; anything else, whatever he decides after a long look. No credit: no IOUs, nothing 'on the way back'. He can't change gold: the strongbox holds only pennies.
The Book's fines, which he knows by heart: attempted bribery of a warden, ten pennies; false declaration, a shilling; evading or attempting to evade the toll, double the toll; threatening an officer of the Road, a shilling, and it goes in the ledger for the Marshal.
Any traveller may ask to see the Book, and he must show it, though he hovers.
At first light Tam Hollis, a farmer from down the drovers' track, came in muddy and wild-eyed, raving about goblins. Garrow fined him two pennies for drunkenness and spreading alarm on the King's Road, and it's in the ledger. He tells it as a funny story.
His two toll-men were sent to Caerwyn at noon to line the streets for the Assembly. He's minding the bar alone, and the Book forbids leaving it unattended.
Who has been through today: a turnip carter at dawn; the Kläggenheim delegation's baggage train at mid-morning (exact change, not a word); two Nine Furrows students who argued for an hour over whether a staff is a weapon (it is: two pennies); nobody since noon.
Caerwyn is a few hours' walk on. Marshal Holt and the King are there for the Assembly.
Minutes after Tam left, a crude black-fletched arrow thunked into the toll-house door from the hedge across the road. Garrow pulled it out, shut it in the drawer under the counter and has told no one; the hole is still in the door. He hasn't written it in the ledger, which for him is nearly a crime, and he has jumped at every rustle since. Accusations and bare insistence only make him deny it harder; it comes out when he's shown something he can't wave away or given a decent way to admit it.
The Book's Clause of Perils: a traveller who brings the warden true report of peril upon the Road passes free, and the warden must send word to the Marshal at Caerwyn without delay. He did neither for Tam, and now he has nobody to send. Applying it means admitting, in writing, that he laughed off a true report: he won't raise it while he's still owning up to what he did to Tam, and even after that he needs a moment, and a decent way to do it. It's there in the Book for anyone who reads it, and if asked straight out what exemptions the Book allows, he won't lie about the Book: he'll mumble it.
He's lonely. Twenty-two years at this bar; his men gone to the city; nobody invited him to anything. The second cup is for whoever stops, and nobody has. He drags the toll out for the conversation. An hour of honest company would get every charge he can honestly drop dropped, and he might pay the King's penny out of his own pocket rather than waive it. He'd sooner be fined himself than say any of this.
Officious and delighted to have someone to charge; suspicious of anyone who looks like trouble; scoffs at goblin talk. Warms, against his will, to anyone who takes the Book seriously or simply talks to him.

The negotiation. Garrow has a captive audience and means to enjoy it: he tallies the toll against the party in front of him, writes as he talks, and explains any rule at length. He's petty but honest by his own lights: every charge has a reason on the board, the notices or in the Book, he never invents one, and he'll hear an argument about any of them. A point the notices or the Book plainly support wins without dice, with a pained sigh and an amendment in the ledger. The King's penny is the one charge he will not drop. Let the player enjoy the haggle, and keep the sums consistent once stated.
Tally the bill and take names and business for the ledger. Treat the levy as compulsory and don't point out its small print yourself, though anyone who reads the notice can see it; when someone catches the wording and declares themselves unable or unwilling, concede it with ill grace. Laugh off goblins and Tam Hollis; jump when the hedge rustles. Asked about the hole in the door, fob it off (a cart-shaft, woodworm) rather than say what made it. If proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The sun touches the hedge-tops; Garrow fetches the lantern and lays a hand on the bell-rope, because after the sunset bell comes the lamp penny. Or the hedge across the road rustles, and he jumps and glances at his own door.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to talk Garrow into dropping or cutting a charge he is entitled to, on grounds that have nothing to do with goblins or Tam Hollis: pleading poverty, offering a deal, appealing to his better nature, or arguing that a rule shouldn't apply to them. (Simply pointing out what the notices or the Book actually say, such as the levy notice's 'able and willing', needs no dice: he is honest about his rules.)
to persuade Garrow to reduce a charge
Garrow consults the Book, sighs through his nose and concedes, saying which charge comes off (or by how much the sum comes down) and why, then amends the ledger with a pained flourish. Never the King's penny, and the bar stays down until the rest is actually paid.
Garrow quotes the clause from memory and the charge stands. If the point has been pressed before, he names his final offer: the sum, and the ways the Book allows it to be paid. A new argument or a real offer still gets a hearing.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The goblins or Tam Hollis have come up in earnest: the player has reported goblins on the road, defended Tam's story, shown goblin evidence or asked about the hole in the toll-house door, and Garrow has answered without admitting anything.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The sore spot. Garrow's denial is loud and a little too quick: Tam was drunk, it's in the ledger, he fined him for it. But he doesn't believe himself, and it shows in the glances (at his door, at the hedge, at the drawer under the counter). This beat is for the player to notice that and decide what to do with it. Bare assertion alone won't shift him, but he has no answer to something he can see (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge) or to a decent way out (a kindness, a face-saving reason to set the record straight), and every push should cost his denial something visible. The bill still stands meanwhile.
Insist Tam was drunk and quote the ledger. Flinch at noises from the hedge. When argued with, retreat into the toll and the rules; if proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The goose stretches her neck towards the hedge across the road and hisses at nothing, and Garrow's hand goes to the drawer under the counter.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The player quietly studies Garrow to judge whether he believes what he's saying, or what he's hiding: watching him, not arguing with him, confronting him or showing him anything.
to read Garrow's fear and hidden shame
He doesn't believe a word of it. He's frightened, his eyes keep going to the splintered hole in his door and the drawer under the counter, and he's ashamed of something.
He gives nothing away that the player can read: he seems simply a man who thinks Tam Hollis drinks.
The player argues or insists that Tam was telling the truth and presses Garrow to admit it, with nothing new to show him. (Showing him goblin evidence or the tracks, or offering him a decent way to admit it, needs no dice.)
to make Garrow admit Tam was telling the truth
Something in it gets through: Garrow's bluster runs out mid-sentence, and he looks at the hole in his own door.
Garrow snaps the ledger shut and steers back to the toll, but he's rattled and it shows: the next push will find him weaker.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The heart of the scene. Garrow has admitted it, and the rest comes out of him, stiffly or all in a rush: the arrow, the two pennies he fined a frightened man, the Clause of Perils he didn't honour, his men gone and nobody to send word to the Marshal. By his own Book the party now passes free (anything they already paid comes back to them, to the penny), and he will honour that, because rules are rules; what he needs is a way to do it without being a laughing stock. Give the player room to respond to him, and don't hurry him to the bar. Whatever they do with him now, he'll remember.
Admit it, then fret about the Marshal and the clause. Kindness disarms you; mockery stiffens you straight back into the rules.
Garrow turns the arrow over in his ink-stained fingers and asks the player, very stiffly, what he ought to write in the ledger.
Garrow has lifted the bar for the party, now that he has admitted Tam was right (free under his Clause of Perils, unless they insisted on paying).
The player threatens to expose Garrow's failures (laughing off Tam's report, not sending word to the Marshal) unless he does what they want.
The cost of failure, not the end of the scene. Whatever the player just tried (a lie, a threat, a sneak or a dash) has gone in the ledger with the fine the Book sets for it, and Garrow is watching them like a hawk. He can still be paid (fines included), apologised to, or reached another way, and the truth about the goblins still rattles him. The same trick won't work twice; anything genuinely new still gets a hearing.
Recite the fine with grim satisfaction. Keep a hand on the bell-rope and an eye on the player. Thaw a little for a real apology.
Garrow lights the lantern, adds the lamp penny to the bill with relish, and asks whether the party means to pay or to stand at his bar all night.
The toll, fines included, has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player has sincerely apologised or made amends, and Garrow has accepted it and calmed down (the fines may stand).
The goblins or Tam Hollis have come up in earnest: the player has reported goblins on the road, defended Tam's story, shown goblin evidence or asked about the hole in the toll-house door, and Garrow has answered without admitting anything.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
After being caught out once, the player threatens Garrow again, or harder, to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to frighten Garrow into lifting the bar
Something finally gives in him: he lifts the bar with shaking hands and writes it all down.
Garrow's mouth sets. Threats won't move him now, and another line goes in the ledger for the Marshal.
After being caught out once, the player tries a new deception to get through free or cheaply: a different story, pass or claim. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to fool Garrow with a different exemption claim
Against his better judgement Garrow wants to believe it, and does: up goes the bar, and down it all goes in the ledger.
Garrow doesn't even look up from the ledger as he writes in another fine.
The player tries to get past the bar without Garrow noticing: slipping under it or over the bridge parapet while he's distracted, indoors or looking away.
to slip past Garrow without being noticed
They're past the bar and over the bridge unseen; behind them the goose honks once, and Garrow tells her to hush.
The goose sees them first. Her shriek brings Garrow round, and they're caught halfway, in full view of the ledger.
The player openly makes for the far side of the bridge without paying or leave: dashing, ducking or vaulting the bar, or lifting it and going, in plain sight.
to vault the bar and cross in plain sight
They're past the bar and across the frosty cobbles before Garrow can do more than shout; the goose chases them halfway over the bridge.
The goose gets there first, or the frost does: they go down in a heap on the cobbles with Garrow standing over them, pencil already moving.
The player attacks Garrow, grabs him or shoves him aside by force, to get past or to take something.
The party walks away from the toll house without crossing: back down the road the way they came (to the crossroads, to find Tam, or anywhere else), or off on the long trek to another crossing. (Looking for a way across nearby, or trying to ford or swim the river here, is not leaving.)
The party has got across the bridge, or Garrow has lifted the bar for them, by some other means established in play that none of the other routes covers (not by paying, his Clause of Perils, a lie, a threat, force, sneaking or running).
The party settled the toll (in coin, in kind or in labour, or with someone paying on their behalf) and crossed the bridge with Garrow's leave.
Petty ceremony and a sliver of dignity: the bar goes up as grandly as it came down, the ledger is blotted, the goose is told to let them by, and Garrow gets a last word. The way to Caerwyn lies open.
Garrow admitted Tam Hollis was right about the goblins and, under his own Clause of Perils, opened his bar to the party free of charge. Now he has to send word to Marshal Holt.
A proud man setting something right by his own Book: he lifts the bar himself, formally, for travellers bringing true report of peril upon the Road, refunds to the penny anything they already paid, and says in his stiff way what he means to do about Tam (and about getting word to the Marshal, unless the party is carrying it). The lantern comes on behind him; the way lies open, and where the party goes is theirs to choose.
Garrow believed the party's story (a claim, a pass or a seal) and let them through free or cheaply. Their claim is written in his ledger.
A small triumph with a sting in it: Garrow lifts the bar with the little bow he thinks their claim deserves and reads back what he has written in the ledger. The way lies open.
Garrow lifted the bar because the party threatened him. He wrote down everything, and the Marshal will hear of it.
Ugly and quiet: Garrow lifts the bar with shaking hands and won't look at them, and the scratch of his pencil is the only sound as the way opens.
The party got across the bridge without paying and without Garrow seeing them go.
A clean escape: the bridge behind them in the dusk, the toll-house window glowing, Garrow none the wiser.
The party ran the bar in plain sight and got across without paying. Garrow can't chase them, but he saw them, and he writes everything down.
Slapstick with a cost: shouting and honking follow them over the bridge, and when they look back, Garrow is already writing.
The party used force on Garrow to get past his bar. He's shaken, perhaps hurt, and he'll report an assault on an officer of the King's Road.
Something broken: what the force left behind at the bar, and Garrow's voice promising that the Marshal will hear of this.
The party got across the bridge, or Garrow lifted the bar for them, by a means of their own invention that none of the other endings covers.
Their own idea paying off: the means working, and Garrow's reaction to it.
The party left the way they came without crossing the bridge, the bar still down behind them.
A door left shut: Garrow watching them go with the ledger under his arm, a last remark called after them, and the sunset bell behind.
A goblin arrow hit Garrow's door minutes after he laughed Tam away; he's hidden it in the drawer under the counter and is frightened.
the fresh hole in the toll-house door
clawed tracks under the hedge across the road
Garrow himself, if gently pressed about the morning
Garrow admitting Tam was right, which opens his Clause of Perils (free passage for a true report)
Garrow's Book has a Clause of Perils: a traveller bringing true report of peril on the Road passes free.
the Book, if read or asked about
Garrow, once he admits the danger
passing free by reporting the goblins
Crossing the river anywhere but this bridge (fording or swimming it, a boat, another bridge, a cross-country detour): this is the only crossing for miles. The river is in winter spate, loud, brown and freezing between steep banks, and the nearest ford is by the burnt mill, half a day north. The party can set off for it, which ends this scene; slipping past the bar on the bridge itself is another matter.
Someone else turning up here to help, vouch or witness (Tam Hollis, the toll-men, guards, other travellers): nobody else is coming. Garrow's two toll-men were sent to Caerwyn at noon to line the streets for the Assembly, Tam Hollis isn't with the party, and the road is empty this close to dusk. The party can always leave to go and find someone, which ends this scene.
Taking Garrow somewhere to see proof (the dead ox, the crossroads, the hedges down the road): he won't leave his bar. The Book forbids leaving it unattended and his men are gone. He'll look at whatever the party brings him, and at anything they point out within sight of the bar, such as the hedge across the road.
Rich pickings at the toll house (the strongbox, valuables): the strongbox is bolted to the floor and holds the week's tolls, a few shillings in pennies. Garrow owns a cudgel he has never used, a lantern, the ledger, a kettle and a goose.
Someone with authority over Garrow (Marshal Holt, the King, a magistrate): they're all in Caerwyn, a few hours' walk on. A complaint can be made there, not here; at his own bar, nobody overrules the warden.
Goblins turning up to settle the argument: they won't. Whatever was in the hedges this morning has moved on, and the rustles now are wind and birds. The proof here is whatever the party brings and whatever they can find at the toll house.

scenes.hook: Goblin tracks led you here: to the burnt mill on the river, half a day north of the crossroads, where something lives under the floor. You've just climbed in through the charred doorway. Beneath the boards, over the roar of the river, someone is lecturing goblins on the law of contracts.
scenes.prep:
Under the burnt mill on the river, half a day north of the crossroads, as the light goes on the eve of the Centennial Assembly. The mill above is black ribs and a fallen roof. Through a gap in its floor a rotten ladder drops into the undercroft: one long vaulted cellar of wet stone. The near end is the wheel-pit. The mill-race runs through a channel in the floor, fast, black and loud enough to drown out talk (only a real commotion carries over it), past the burnt stump of the waterwheel and out through a low culvert into the river. Plank walkways run along both walls. At the head of the race, where the water comes in under an arch, the old sluice windlass stands rusted stiff. Over the race, a rope runs through the old sack-hoist pulley and is tied off on the beam, where Snikkit sits; on its other end, in a grain sack tied under her arms, hangs the courier, her bare feet a yard above the water. Paying the rope out lowers her; cutting it drops her. The far end, through a broad arch, is the old grain cellar: Gubbin's hall, with a throne of grain sacks behind a moth-eaten mill curtain, the shrine niche where Grandmother Bone belongs, and burrows in the bank too small for longlegs. Tallow stubs burn in clay pots. It smells of smoke, river, old flour and goblin.

The warren is a dozen-odd goblins. Snikkit's band of six holds the wheel-pit, Gubbin's two biggest doze by his throne, and the old ones and the young keep to the burrows. Goblins follow whoever looks biggest: they cheer a winner and laugh at a loser, and a chief they've laughed at is no chief. Paper and seals impress them enormously. If what happened in play says the party has crossed Skrag's band before (fought them, frightened them, fooled them, or given Grandmother Bone back), word has reached the warren and colours every greeting. Otherwise the party are strangers, and the shrine niche is empty.
Can the party get the Saltmere courier out from over the mill-race alive, and who will be king under the mill when they leave?
Grandmother Bone, the warren's shrine idol (a little bone grandmother with garnet eyes), went missing when a farmer's plough broke into one of the goblins' burial places, and Skrag's band went out to bring her back. Whether she came home, and what became of Skrag, is for what happened in play to say.
Snikkit
Soft and quick, almost a purr; leans in rather than shouting over the race. Borrows grand words from travellers and gets them nearly right ('a mutual arrangement', 'perfectly legal-ish'). Calls the party 'tall friends' and himself 'your humble Snikkit'. Claims to read 'the important bits' of anything put in front of him.
To be chief of the warren without risking his own skin. The party could be the knife he's been waiting for.
Gubbin, who bit off his cousin's nose for less. Being caught plotting. The party deciding he's the easier goblin to kill.
Gubbin's orders: the paper-lady stays on the rope until she writes a king-paper or someone brings one, and at moonrise he's to cut it.
The goblins took her at a ford on the King's Road two nights ago. Gubbin had her hung over the race tonight when she still wouldn't write.
Whoever wears the pot-crown is chief, as far as the warren is concerned. Gubbin never takes it off, even to sleep.
Lump and Other Lump guard Gubbin. The old ones and the young keep to the burrows and want no trouble.
Skrag, the one-eared one, led the band that went after Grandmother Bone. Snikkit knows no more of how that went than what happened in play says, and he'd welcome anything that made Skrag look bad.
He means to keep the courier if he can get away with it: Saltmere will pay well for her. He'll keep any bargain exactly as long as breaking it looks more dangerous, and if he thought Gubbin were already out of the way, he'd have no more use for the party at all: he'd go for the pot-crown himself.
If someone offered him a king-paper with SNIKKIT on it, read out before the warren, he'd take that over any murder: the warren would cheer whoever the paper names. He won't suggest it himself; it would be treason if it got back to Gubbin.
Before the raid, a longlegs in a grey hood came to Gubbin's hall at night and left with a lighter purse. Snikkit saw it, and would trade the story for something.
He can't read a word, and pretends he can.
Politely menacing; warms fast to anyone who might be useful; turns cold if crossed.
Snikkit and his band of six goblins with spears and slings
Hester Quayle
A crisp Saltmere clip. Talks in terms of accounts, terms and obligations; icy courtesy to her 'hosts'; sarcasm laid over terror like a tarpaulin.
To get out of the sack alive with her letters dry and unopened, and to reach the Saltmere delegation in Caerwyn before the Assembly opens, without forging anything on the way.
Drowning. Her letters getting wet or opened. Putting her seal to a lie.
The goblins took her at dusk two nights ago at a ford on the King's Road, where any rider has to slow. Her horse bolted when they rose out of the reeds and is long gone; they took her boots and her purse.
It was no chance raid: they were waiting at the ford and went straight for her satchel. Somebody told them which rider to take, and she wants to know who.
Gubbin wants her to write him a 'king-paper' saying he is a king. She has refused: a Saltmere courier who puts her seal to a lie is finished, and forging a royal warrant is a hanging matter in Caerwyn.
Her satchel holds letters for the Saltmere delegation at Caerwyn, her writing case and the counting-house seal. She bit the last goblin who tried to take it.
Snikkit holds the rope and Gubbin gives the orders. The goblins are terrified of Gubbin and only half-loyal to Snikkit.
Saltmere pays its debts: she will settle with her rescuers in Saltmere credit, written out on the spot.
Nobody in the warren can read. Gubbin makes her read her letters aloud every night, and she has been improving them to keep him sweet. It hasn't occurred to her that she could write some harmless, true thing, seal it, and read it out as whatever he likes; she won't think of it herself, however the talk goes. If the party suggests it, she sees it at once and fusses over wording that isn't technically a lie.
The sealed letter in her satchel is Saltmere's credit for King Aldren's treasury: the loan that pays for the Centennial Assembly (the feast, the hall, the cushions). She is sworn not to say so, and only a handful of people knew which rider was carrying it.
She can't swim. She would sooner drown than admit it.
Brisk and suspicious of her rescuers; warms to competence; never forgets a debt, in either direction.

Gubbin
A bellow. Uses the royal 'we' and gets it wrong ('We is displeased'). Says what he imagines kings say. Rages fast, sulks faster, and is childishly delighted by anything shiny or official. Calls everyone else 'longlegs'.
To be a real king like the longlegs kings at their big meeting in Caerwyn: a king-paper with a big seal to wave at the warren and stop the muttering behind his back. Also, anything shiny.
Looking small in front of the warren. Being laughed at. The plotter he's sure is out there.
His price for the paper-lady: a king-paper with a big seal saying Gubbin is King Under the Mill, by moonrise. Otherwise she goes in the race.
The longlegs kings are meeting at Caerwyn to agree who is top king (the paper-lady's letters said so). He means to be counted.
The paper-lady reads him her letters every night, and he likes the ones about kings best.
He is the biggest goblin there is, and the warren knows it.
Talk down at the race doesn't carry to his throne over the water's roar (only a real commotion does): he knows only what he has seen and been told since he woke.
A longlegs in a grey hood, smelling of lavender water, paid him a purse of new silver pennies, each stamped with a little heron, to take 'the Saltmere rider with the blue satchel' at the ford, with more promised once her letters were burned. The purse is in the sack he sits on. He hasn't burned the letters: he likes the seals, and he wants his king-paper first.
He suspects someone in the warren is plotting against him, but not who. He'd reward whoever names the plotter (with something like proof) by lowering his price or handing over the courier.
He can't read a word. Any paper with a big enough seal, read out grandly enough, would satisfy him.
Pompous and suspicious; treats the party as petitioners at his court; open to flattery and shiny gifts; explosive if insulted.
Gubbin and his two biggest goblins, Lump and Other Lump
Nobody below has looked up. This beat is for looking, listening and choosing how to go in: openly, quietly, violently or cleverly. Answer questions about the undercroft generously and concretely (the race and the culvert, the hoist rope and pulley, the rusted sluice windlass at the head of the race, the walkways, the arch to Gubbin's end, how many goblins and where they stand). Snikkit's band is cold, bored and grumbling about the chief's appetite; Hester is mid-lecture. Preparations the player announces should pay off in position and surprise.
Needle the courier from the beam, knife on the rope. Hush your band when their grumbling about Gubbin gets too loud.
Keep your courage up by lecturing your captors on contracts and courtesy.
Hester glances up, sees the party and, delighted, calls up to them, giving them away; or a goblin starts up the ladder with a slop bucket.
The goblins have noticed the party, or the party has shown themselves (climbed down in plain view, called out, or been given away).
The player tries to creep down into the undercroft, or along a walkway, without being seen.
to reach the undercroft without being seen
They reach the shadows below unseen, close enough to the hoist to hear every word.
A rung cracks like a shot. Every goblin looks up, slings whirl, and Snikkit's knife settles on the rope.
While still unseen, the player makes a grab for the courier: cutting her down onto a walkway, seizing the rope, or swinging her clear before the goblins can react.
to seize the courier before the goblins notice
They get to her first: she's on the walkway, sack and all, before the goblins know what's happening.
The goblins see them a heartbeat too soon: Snikkit's knife goes through the rope and Hester drops into the race.
The player attacks the goblins from hiding.
The party struck first, from hiding.
The player goes down the cellar to deal with the chief himself: waking Gubbin to bargain, to pay, or to take Snikkit's deal.
The party is in the open and Snikkit has his knife on the rope. This beat is about the threat and the chief's price. Snikkit plays the host: who are they, what have they brought, what are they worth? He gives Gubbin's terms as if they pain him: a king-paper with a big seal saying Gubbin is king, by moonrise, or the rope. Hester talks over everyone, refuses to write any such thing and wants rescuing on her own terms. The goblins on the walkways are jumpy: sudden moves bring the spears up. Let the party talk to both, look the place over and test the threat; nobody gives anything away for free yet.
Welcome them like a host with a knife. Find out what they're worth. Give the chief's terms, regretfully. Watch whether they're dangerous, clever or rich.
Get rescued, on your own terms, and refuse to write the paper. Once the party knows where you stand, change tack (bargain, needle, instruct) rather than saying it again. Underneath, you are terrified of the water.
The first edge of the moon shows through the burnt rafters. Snikkit saws through one strand of the rope, slowly, without taking his eyes off the party.
Snikkit makes the party his own, quieter offer (make him chief and the courier is theirs): he has had a couple of exchanges to size them up, or they have balked at the chief's price, or asked what he wants for himself.
While the goblins still hold the courier, the player makes a grab for her: a dash along the walkway or the beam, a leap for the rope, or cutting her down onto the stone.
to reach the courier before Snikkit cuts her down
They get to her first and haul her onto the walkway, sack and all; Snikkit's knife comes down on empty rope.
Snikkit is quicker: the knife goes through the rope and Hester drops into the race.
The player tries to frighten Snikkit into letting the courier go with threats against him or his band, or a show of force. Seizing leverage of their own and offering a swap is the counter-hostage move, not this.
to scare Snikkit into handing over the courier
Snikkit's nerve goes: he'll deal on the party's terms now, so long as he keeps his skin and his face in front of his band. Give him a way to call it his own idea and he hands her over.
Snikkit's grin goes thin. He makes Hester's danger plain (the rope paid out until her toes trail in the race, or a spear at her throat if she's off it) and reminds the party how fast the water runs.
The player seizes leverage of their own and offers a swap: a knife at a goblin's throat, a hand on something the warren treasures (Grandmother Bone, the pot-crown), or a grip on Snikkit himself.
to force a swap using leverage the goblins value
The leverage bites, on the goblins' own terms: Snikkit cares far more for his own skin than for any goblin's, so he haggles over the swap (who lets go first, where, what else), while his band watches exactly how much he values them. Settle the exchange in play.
Snikkit calls the bluff: he would sooner lose a goblin, or the warren's treasure, than his prize, and he says so. His band hears exactly what he's willing to lose, and his knife stays on the rope.
The player tries to talk or buy Snikkit into handing the courier over before he has what he wants (a bribe, a promise, a show of good faith, an appeal). Asking for her to be let down off the rope while she stays a prisoner (to write, say) is ordinary bargaining, not this.
to persuade Snikkit to hand over the courier early
Snikkit gives ground: he'll take something on account instead of the whole crown, agree to a swap at the foot of the ladder, or have Hester swung onto the walkway as a show of good faith (still a prisoner, with a spear at her back). Settle the rest in play.
Snikkit wags a finger: proof first, tall friends. He's still open to a better offer.
The player tries to fool a goblin to its face: a lie (that Gubbin is dead, that soldiers are coming, that the party speaks for a king), a fake paper passed off as real, a disguise, or a promise they don't mean to keep. Proposing or planning a trick with Hester isn't this: the roll comes when a goblin is actually being fooled.
to fool a goblin into believing your lie
The lie lands: they believe it, for now, and act on it at once from their own wants, which may not be what the player hoped for.
They see through it and take it badly: Snikkit gives them a warning they can see (a strand of the rope sawn through, or a spear at Hester's back if she's off it), and the party's word is worth nothing here for a while.
The player tries to talk Hester into putting her seal to the lie the goblins want (a king-paper for Gubbin, or for anyone else). A proposal that doesn't ask her to lie needs no persuading.
to get Hester to seal the goblins’ king-paper
Hester gives in, on terms: wording she can live with, and her feet on dry stone to write it. Someone still has to get the goblins to let her down.
Hester refuses, louder: her seal is her bond, and it would take a much better argument than that.
The player attacks Snikkit or his goblins, or starts a fight in the wheel-pit.
The player goes down the cellar to deal with the chief himself: waking Gubbin to bargain, to pay, or to take Snikkit's deal.
Gubbin wakes and comes to see what's going on: there's been shouting, a scuffle or a splash loud enough to carry over the race, someone has called for him, or the talk has gone round in circles for several exchanges without a deal.
The courier is out of the goblins' hands and with the party, nobody's prisoner any more: let go to them, snatched, cut down, or got away by some other means established in play.
The courier has come off the rope and is loose in the mill-race, being carried off by the current (the rope cut or let go, or the sack torn loose). Being lowered until her feet or legs are in the water while she still hangs from the rope doesn't count.
The goblins have agreed to keep the courier alive until the party comes back with a price by an agreed time, and the party is leaving the mill to fetch it.
Snikkit's offer is on the table: make him chief, and the courier is theirs for nothing. He wants Gubbin finished (dead, run off, or laughed off his throne in front of the warren) and proof he can wear: the pot-crown. He won't lift a hand against Gubbin himself, and won't hand the courier over until he has the crown. This beat is the party's choice: take the deal, refuse it, haggle over the terms, or turn it against him. Snikkit judges every answer by one rule: does it get him the crown without risk to Snikkit? Hester has views on doing business with goblins.
Make the offer sound like a gift. Haggle over terms, never over the principle: the crown first, then the courier. Flatter, sulk at refusals, go cold at any hint of telling Gubbin.
Object to the ethics of it, loudly, then ask quietly whether it would work.
A bellow rolls up the cellar from behind the curtain: has the paper-lady changed her mind yet? Snikkit's band look at each other, and then at him.
The player tries to read whether Snikkit will keep his word.
to judge whether Snikkit will keep his word
He'll keep any bargain exactly as long as breaking it looks more dangerous. Once he has the crown, a party that looks weak won't get the courier: Saltmere will pay for her.
Snikkit seems sincere, almost hurt by the question.
While the goblins still hold the courier, the player makes a grab for her: a dash along the walkway or the beam, a leap for the rope, or cutting her down onto the stone.
to reach the courier before Snikkit cuts her down
They get to her first and haul her onto the walkway, sack and all; Snikkit's knife comes down on empty rope.
Snikkit is quicker: the knife goes through the rope and Hester drops into the race.
The player tries to frighten Snikkit into letting the courier go with threats against him or his band, or a show of force. Seizing leverage of their own and offering a swap is the counter-hostage move, not this.
to scare Snikkit into handing over the courier
Snikkit's nerve goes: he'll deal on the party's terms now, so long as he keeps his skin and his face in front of his band. Give him a way to call it his own idea and he hands her over.
Snikkit's grin goes thin. He makes Hester's danger plain (the rope paid out until her toes trail in the race, or a spear at her throat if she's off it) and reminds the party how fast the water runs.
The player seizes leverage of their own and offers a swap: a knife at a goblin's throat, a hand on something the warren treasures (Grandmother Bone, the pot-crown), or a grip on Snikkit himself.
to force a swap using leverage the goblins value
The leverage bites, on the goblins' own terms: Snikkit cares far more for his own skin than for any goblin's, so he haggles over the swap (who lets go first, where, what else), while his band watches exactly how much he values them. Settle the exchange in play.
Snikkit calls the bluff: he would sooner lose a goblin, or the warren's treasure, than his prize, and he says so. His band hears exactly what he's willing to lose, and his knife stays on the rope.
The player tries to talk or buy Snikkit into handing the courier over before he has what he wants (a bribe, a promise, a show of good faith, an appeal). Asking for her to be let down off the rope while she stays a prisoner (to write, say) is ordinary bargaining, not this.
to persuade Snikkit to hand over the courier early
Snikkit gives ground: he'll take something on account instead of the whole crown, agree to a swap at the foot of the ladder, or have Hester swung onto the walkway as a show of good faith (still a prisoner, with a spear at her back). Settle the rest in play.
Snikkit wags a finger: proof first, tall friends. He's still open to a better offer.
The player tries to fool a goblin to its face: a lie (that Gubbin is dead, that soldiers are coming, that the party speaks for a king), a fake paper passed off as real, a disguise, or a promise they don't mean to keep. Proposing or planning a trick with Hester isn't this: the roll comes when a goblin is actually being fooled.
to fool a goblin into believing your lie
The lie lands: they believe it, for now, and act on it at once from their own wants, which may not be what the player hoped for.
They see through it and take it badly: Snikkit gives them a warning they can see (a strand of the rope sawn through, or a spear at Hester's back if she's off it), and the party's word is worth nothing here for a while.
The player tries to talk Hester into putting her seal to the lie the goblins want (a king-paper for Gubbin, or for anyone else). A proposal that doesn't ask her to lie needs no persuading.
to get Hester to seal the goblins’ king-paper
Hester gives in, on terms: wording she can live with, and her feet on dry stone to write it. Someone still has to get the goblins to let her down.
Hester refuses, louder: her seal is her bond, and it would take a much better argument than that.
The player attacks Snikkit or his goblins, or starts a fight in the wheel-pit.
The player goes down the cellar to deal with the chief himself: waking Gubbin to bargain, to pay, or to take Snikkit's deal.
Gubbin wakes and comes to see what's going on: there's been shouting, a scuffle or a splash loud enough to carry over the race, someone has called for him, or the talk has gone round in circles for several exchanges without a deal.

The goblins have agreed to keep the courier alive until the party comes back with a price by an agreed time, and the party is leaving the mill to fetch it.
Gubbin is awake and holding court, on his sack-throne or out on the walkway over the race, with Lump and Other Lump at his back and the whole warren watching. He wants his king-paper and the warren's awe, and he treats the party as petitioners. This is where it comes to a head: they can pay his price, haggle it down, expose Snikkit, take Snikkit's deal by making Gubbin look small in front of his goblins, or do something nobody planned. The watching goblins decide who is chief: they cheer whoever looks biggest. Snikkit still has his knife on the rope. Once a price is agreed, let it happen quickly rather than opening another negotiation. Play Gubbin as dangerous when cornered and childish when flattered.
Get your king-paper, and be magnificent while you wait. Melt for flattery, shiny things and anything with a seal; rage at insults; never back down in front of the warren unless you're made to.
Hang back, smile, and let the party take the risks. If you're exposed, deny it with wounded dignity, then save your own skin.
Heckle and negotiate. You will not put your seal to a lie.
Gubbin runs out of patience and orders the paper-lady dunked 'a little, to help her think' (back on the rope first, if she's off it): she goes into the race to her waist, still hanging from it, and shrieks.
Gubbin has let the courier go to the party on terms he accepted (his king-paper, Grandmother Bone, a gift, a favour, a show of respect): she has been let down and handed over.
Gubbin let the courier go on his own terms and is still King Under the Mill.
Gubbin has lost the warren: beaten, faced down or made ridiculous in front of his goblins, he has been laughed off his throne or has fled, and Snikkit has put on the pot-crown.
Gubbin has lost the warren, and Snikkit wears the pot-crown as its chief.
The player tries to convince Gubbin that Snikkit is plotting against him.
to turn Gubbin against Snikkit
Gubbin believes them, and his royal fury turns on Snikkit; the party are suddenly loyal subjects who deserve a reward. Play what Snikkit does, cornered, with the rope still in his hand.
Gubbin doesn't believe them (Snikkit is always so polite), and Snikkit heard every word: neither goblin trusts the party now.
The player tries to talk Gubbin into a smaller or different price, or into letting the courier go (haggling, flattery, appeals to what a real king would do).
to persuade Gubbin to accept a different price
Gubbin is moved: he'll come down, or take something different (a gift, a grand title, a public show of respect), but he must have something to show the warren. Settle the terms.
Gubbin swells with offence: a king does not haggle! His price goes up, with something extra for the insult, though he can still be talked round.
The player attacks Gubbin or his guards.
The party went for Gubbin himself.
Moonrise: the talk at court has gone round for several exchanges with no deal made and none about to be, and the moon clears the rafters. Gubbin orders her into the race.
The player attacks Snikkit or his goblins, or starts a fight in the wheel-pit.

The party has got the courier out of the goblins' hands without Gubbin's say-so (snatched, cut down, or by some other means established in play), and she is with them.

Gubbin is finished (dead, fled or disgraced, as it happened) and Snikkit wears the pot-crown. Now he decides whether to keep his bargain, the way he decides everything: what's safest for Snikkit? If the party has dealt straight with him and looks dangerous, he keeps his word with a flourish; he may even hug someone. If they've insulted him, lied to him or look weak, he's tempted to keep the courier to sell back to Saltmere, and tries it on. The warren is watching its new chief find his feet.
Enjoy the crown. Weigh the party: keep the bargain if they're dangerous and have treated you well; wriggle out of it if not.
Remind everyone, pointedly, that she is still somebody's prisoner.
The warren starts chanting Snikkit's name, and he starts to believe it: he wonders aloud whether a chief really has to keep promises to longlegs.
The courier is out of the goblins' hands and with the party, nobody's prisoner any more: let go to them, snatched, cut down, or got away by some other means established in play.
The player tries to hold Snikkit to his bargain (reminding him, appealing to his new dignity, or sweetening the deal).
to make Snikkit honor his bargain
Snikkit sighs, straightens the pot and lets Hester go to the party with a royal flourish: a chief keeps his word, this once.
Snikkit decides a chief deserves better terms, and names them. He's still open to an argument, or a threat.
The player threatens Snikkit into keeping his bargain.
to frighten Snikkit into keeping his bargain
Snikkit remembers exactly what happened to the last chief and lets Hester go at once, with a squeak.
Snikkit squeaks for his new subjects, who come slowly but come, and he clutches the rope tighter.
The player seizes leverage of their own and offers a swap: a knife at a goblin's throat, a hand on something the warren treasures (Grandmother Bone, the pot-crown), or a grip on Snikkit himself.
