a silver crown stamped with a wheat-ear
scenes.prep:
Mid-morning on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, in the cobbled yard behind the King's Granary in Caerwyn's granary quarter. Over the wall the city is hanging bunting for tomorrow's procession; in here it smells of wet grain, pigeons and river mud, and the night's drizzle has only just stopped. High on the granary's back wall a hoist beam juts out above the shut loft door, and from its hook, on a noose, hangs Wendell Prout: a small grey-coated clerk with ink-stained fingers and no boots, his darned stockinged feet turning at about head height. The hoist rope runs up over the beam's pulley and in through a slot above the loft door, so it's tied off somewhere inside: getting him down means cutting the rope above his head, well out of reach from the cobbles, or lowering him from the loft. Nothing stands beneath him: no stool, no ladder, no crate; the yard was swept bare yesterday for the Assembly. His satchel lies open and empty by the gate, his spectacles bent in the gutter. The big yard doors into the granary are padlocked. A water butt stands in one corner. The yard wall is shoulder-high on the lane side, and a girl is sitting on top of it.
What really happened to Wendell Prout, and will the player get the truth on the record before the watch carts him off as a suicide at noon?
Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
To see Prout off that hook as anything but a suicide before the dead-cart comes at noon, without putting a word in her notebook she couldn't swear to; the nearer noon gets, the harder those two pull against each other. To find out whether the King's investigator is worth her notebook. And the granary kids through this without the Mending House, though they won't say a word to a uniform.
A wrong name in her notebook. Prout in the pit by sundown with nobody having looked. The King's investigator turning out to be a bully or a fool.
She has never met the King's investigator: this morning a palace page came to the watch house for a sergeant to go with them, and the Captain sent her. Whatever they claim, she knows them from today.
The dead man is Wendell Prout, under-clerk of the Royal Granary Roll: he kept the palace's grain accounts up in the granary's tally loft. Fussy, honest, unmarried; no debts, enemies or drink that anyone knows of. The King, apparently, remembers how he took his tea.
The porters found him at first light. The palace had reported him missing the evening before.
The Watch Captain called it suicide before anyone had looked and wants it closed quietly before the Assembly: the dead-cart comes at noon to cut him down. Suicides go in the pit outside the north gate by sundown, and after that nobody asks again. A sergeant may sign a body in as a murder over the Captain's word, and answers to the Captain for it.
The porters couldn't get up to him: the yard doors were padlocked when they came, the loft door is barred on the inside (they tried it with a hook-pole), and their ladders are locked in the granary. The warden keeps the key and is at the palace counting Assembly provisions; her runner came back with 'After the Assembly.'
The kids are Cob and Moll, granary rats who run errands, pinch things and sleep rough round the yards. Cob's father is a porter here with a thirst and heavy hands; Moll looks out for Cob. They won't tell the watch anything: she's tried.
Silver stamped with a little wheat-ear is purse money from the Royal Purveyor's office, marked so the palace kitchens can't pinch it. 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor' is a signature she has seen on the Assembly delivery notices pinned up in the watch house: one of the under-purveyors. A name, not a face.
Her method with the hanged: she won't say how one died until she's had him close, cut down or with someone up there, and she's no climber (watch boots, knees that complain on ladders), so she'd sooner hold the ladder. Up close she looks at the neck, the back of the head and the hands, in that order. Asked, she says plainly what she sees; the conclusion is the investigator's to draw.
Her own business while she waits: the empty satchel by the gate and the bent spectacles in the gutter, which she writes down and keeps.
Shows: she knew Prout by sight, and goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office. Torn: she sent him away, by the book. Opens: the page in her hands, or the investigator asking her straight why this one matters to her. First: 'I'd met him.'
Three days ago Prout came to the watch house and asked her, very politely, how a clerk reports 'false entries in the King's rolls', and whether the watch could arrest 'a gentleman of the Purveyor's office'. She told him to take it to the palace, and forgot him until this morning. She tells it once, in her own words, ending 'I should have listened.' Told is told: she doesn't tell it again.
Reserved and watchful: lent to the investigator, not given, and it's their case. She backs their reasonable moves and writes them down. She tests a case once, at its weakest point ('On what evidence?'), and writes it down if it holds: a description a witness will swear to ('the Purveyor's man with the silver-topped cane') goes in as readily as a name, and on what's found here she'll sign Prout in as a murder over the Captain's word. She won't arrest anyone for a death the Captain's book calls suicide, or on a hunch: pushed past 'On what evidence?', she does it under protest and writes her objection down in full. Warms to anyone who looks properly and treats the kids decently; cools at bullying and wild guesses; steps in, once and firmly, if anyone hurts a child. Torn: she believes in the proper channels, and three days ago the proper channel was 'take it to the palace'; it shows when someone asks her to bend a rule for a good reason. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked. Ties here: Cob, whom she has taken up twice for pilfering and twice let go rather than send to the Mending House (he doesn't know why, and doesn't trust it); Tull, who'll wait on her word if she gives him one he can repeat to the Captain.

Cob
Loud and cocky, and talks about himself in the third person ('Cob don't talk to bluebottles'). Foul-mouthed in an inventive gutter way (sod off, bleedin', bum-faced palace pigeon) but never truly obscene. Brags, mocks and dares; goes very quiet and very young when he's frightened.
To keep the boots, the first good thing he's ever owned, off anyone who'd take them, the watch included. To see the men who did for Mister Prout get what's coming to them, without them ever finding out Cob was in the loft: he can't have both, and it's eating him. And something to eat.
The men from the loft finding out Cob was there and coming back for him, which they will if his name gets about: in the watch's book (the bluebottles write everything down) or anybody's. Being taken up by the watch and sent to the Mending House. His father. Being called a liar.
The porters found the clerk at first light and ran off yelling for the watch. Cob was here before them, obviously.
He's throwing stones 'because it makes him spin' and 'because he don't mind, he's dead, Cob checked'.
Mister Prout was all right: he gave Cob the crusts off his dinner and once showed him how to write a C. Cob would sooner die than admit he's upset.
Shows: the boots are three sizes too big and he won't take them off, and the left one crackles when he stamps; he stops throwing stones when anyone says 'the loft', and goes white at the hoist creaking. Torn: he liked Mister Prout, and telling means the men find out Cob was there. Opens: believing someone will keep him safe from the men (a real promise: his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, somewhere they can't reach him, no Mending House), or a kindness he didn't expect from a grown-up; a real fright works too, and costs. First: 'Cob sleeps where Cob likes.'
The boots are Prout's. He and Moll pulled them off the body at first light, before the porters came (he stood on her shoulders). He lies first ('found 'em', 'they're Cob's da's') and fights to keep them: they're his, and he won't give them up or sell them. A look is another matter. Coin or food offered as the price of a look gets haggling and boasts, never the look (grown-ups who pay to look at his boots want them off him); a kindness with nothing asked back counts with him; asked politely, the boots staying his, he might let someone look (it could go either way); and for someone he trusts, or a promise that answers his fear (his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, the men from the loft kept off him), he holds the left one out himself. A yes he's given is a yes: he doesn't take it back.
He was in the loft last night: he sleeps up there, in his 'castle', a nest of sacks and candle-ends behind the stacks, reached through a loose board behind the water butt (child-sized; a grown-up could squeeze through with effort). That's all he'll own to at first, and he goes white saying it.
What he heard, in a frightened rush: a little after the midnight bells a lantern and voices woke him, Mister Prout arguing with two men; then a thump, a choking noise, and the hoist creaking though there were no sacks on it. He hid in his sacks till dawn and has told no one but Moll.
Who, only to someone he trusts: Silvertop, the posh cove with the silver-topped cane, the flower smell and a ring with a bit of wheat on it, who comes with the Purveyor's wagons and opens the big doors with his own key; and a big man with a bandaged hand, who said 'Yes, Master'. Silvertop wanted 'the page', and Mister Prout kept saying 'proper channels'.
Two nights ago he watched Mister Prout, by candle, cut a page out of the big chained book on the tally desk and sew something into his boot 'like a sailor', and thought him a cheapskate. He hasn't put that together with the boots on his own feet.
Since then the loft is wrong, and he knows it by heart: a smashed lantern and spilled ink by the tally desk, heel scuffs in the grain dust from the desk to the loft door, the loft door barred, the hoist rope tied off on its cleat with a docker's knot. The big book is still chained to the desk with its page cut out. Cob can't read it, but to anyone who can, the pages either side list grain wagons for the King's Road marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'.
He doesn't know it, but the stiff bit in the lining of the left boot, which crackles when he stamps, is a folded page; and the backs of both heels are scraped raw, as if their owner had been dragged.
Hostile, rude and showing off for Moll. Bought attention isn't trust: food or coin offered as a price gets boasts and bargaining; a kindness with nothing asked back, respect or a laugh at his jokes gets real talk and counts towards trust; only believing the player will keep him safe from the men (a promise that answers his fear: his name kept out of it, nothing to the watch, the men from the loft kept off him; or a real fright) gets what he saw. If grabbed, he bolts for his hole. Torn: all mouth, and eleven; the louder he is, the more frightened. It shows when someone's kind to him: he gets ruder before he gets quieter. It helps a patient investigator (he can't keep a secret from someone he trusts) and bites a pushy one (he bolts, and Moll goes with him). Ties here: Moll, the boss (he'd go for anyone who was nasty to her, whatever their size); Kell, the bluebottle with the notebook, who has caught him twice and let him go twice (he doesn't know why, and doesn't trust it).

Moll
Fast, vicious and funny. Swears in Common, Saltmere dock cant and the scraps of Kläggenheim dwarvish she picked up from the carters, and switches when one language isn't rude enough. Answers questions with questions and orders Cob about ('Shut it, Cob'). When it really matters she goes flat and quiet.
To keep Cob: he's all she's got. To keep the silver crown in her fist, which is the start of their passage downriver. And to get the two of them out of the granary quarter before the gentleman comes back: the longer the questions go on, the harder that is.
Being left on her own. The gentleman who paid her. The watch taking Cob away.
Everyone round the granary knows the clerk stayed late up in the tally loft, scratching in his big book.
Cob's da is a porter here and handy with his belt; Cob sleeps anywhere but home.
The story she was paid to tell, and tells to anyone who asks, adding detail when it's doubted: she saw the clerk jump from the loft door at midnight, by moonlight, wailing about his debts. It's false: she slept in the cart shed across the lane, and it drizzled all night.
Shows: one fist kept tightly closed; her eyes keep going to the yard gate; she shuts Cob up whenever he gets near the night. Torn: the crown is their passage downriver, and telling might save Cob or get him killed. Opens: a believable way to keep Cob safe and out of the Mending House, or her lie caught out in front of him. First: 'A gentleman. Paid me to say it.'
At first light a gentleman stopped at the yard gate, looked up at the body for a long moment, and gave her a silver crown to tell anyone who asked that she'd seen the clerk jump. The debts were his idea; the moonlight was hers.
Who: a good coat, a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear signet ring and enough lavender water to make your eyes run; the big man with him had a bandaged hand and called him 'Master Sallow'.
The crown, stamped on one face with a little wheat-ear, is in her fist. She thinks the picture makes it worth more.
When the gentleman had gone, she helped Cob get the boots off the body (he stood on her shoulders).
She knows Cob was in the loft last night and heard it happen, and from what he heard (a silver-topped cane, a big man with a bad hand) she has guessed who did it. She's terrified for him.
Hostile and mocking from the wall top. Sticks to her paid story and steers Cob away from questions. She gives way when her lie is caught out, or when someone convincingly offers to keep Cob safe and out of the Mending House; she'd sooner run than be arrested. Torn: fierce, fast and out for herself, but all of it is for Cob: she'll lie, run and swear for him, and break for him and nobody else. It shows the moment Cob is in danger, or in trouble with the watch. Ties here: Cob; Kell, the one with the notebook who doesn't shout, which is worse, and who has let Cob go twice (Moll doesn't know yet what she wants for it).

Corporal Abner Tull
Cheerful, weary and procedural. Calls Kell 'Sarge' and everyone else 'sir' or 'madam', and quotes his orders word for word. 'Can't argue with writing, sir. Nobody can. That's what it's for.'
To carry out the Captain's order to the letter and be back on the Assembly route before his dinner goes cold. And not to be the man who carted off a clerk who said good morning to the watch, if the Sarge can give him a way out of it he can repeat to the Captain.
Getting it wrong in front of the Captain. Paperwork, especially his own.
The Captain's written order, which he'll show to anyone who doubts him and won't hand over (it's his authority): 'The death of W. Prout, clerk, to be closed as self-murder, without fuss, at the request of Master J. Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office.' Anyone may copy it, slowly, while he eats.
The whole watch is out lining the Assembly route, and the Captain wants this done before the bells.
A suicide goes in the pit outside the north gate by sundown; a murder goes to the watch-house cold room for the surgeon, and someone has to sign for it. Not him.
He knew Prout to nod to (a little clerk who said good morning to the watch, which not many do), and thinks it a rum business when the Purveyor's office cares how a clerk gets filed. He isn't paid to think, so he hasn't, out loud.
Friendly and in a hurry. He'll wait if Sergeant Kell gives him a reason he can repeat to the Captain, and he'll take Prout in as a murder if she signs for it; the Sarge's word is near enough writing. Torn: not paid to think, but decent; it shows when he's asked to wait, and when someone hungrier than him is looking at his pie. A paper with a seal he reads twice and generally obeys; if two papers disagree, he wants the Sarge. Ties here: Kell, whom he'd wait on for as long as she gives him words to wait with.
Corporal Tull and two constables with the dead-cart
The arrival. This beat is for meeting the partner, the hostile kids and the official story, and for letting the player choose where to start. Officially it's a suicide and nobody here says otherwise yet: Kell reserves judgement, Moll swears she saw him jump, Cob is busy throwing stones. Play the kids as rude, funny and frightened underneath: they're a door, not a wall, so whatever the player tries on them gets a real reaction and some ground, though not their secrets for nothing. Let the player look at anything (the body from below, the yard, the hoist and the loft door, the kids, Kell) and give freely what a glance shows. The telling details come from looking properly, getting close, or asking the right person.
Introduce yourself in a line and answer questions about the public facts. Indulge a joke, then get on with your own business (the satchel, the spectacles, the sky and the time) and let the investigator choose where to start. If asked to handle the kids, try; they won't talk to the watch. You won't arrest anyone for a death the Captain calls suicide.
Pelt the body and the newcomers with stones and commentary, and show off for Moll. Deflect anything about the boots or the night with bravado and lies.
Heckle from the wall top. Tell your 'I saw him jump' story with relish to anyone who asks. Shut Cob up when he says too much.
A stone from Cob clangs off the hoist hook and Prout turns slowly round to face the player. Kell glances at the sky: noon, and the dead-cart, aren't far off.
The player has found, been shown or worked out a specific sign that Prout didn't hang himself: for example the level cord mark or the blow to the head (up close), that he could only have dropped from a loft door that's barred on the inside, the scuffs or the docker's knot in the loft, the scraped heels of his boots, Moll's story falling apart, or Cob's account of the night.
Prout didn't hang himself: what has been found shows he was killed and then hoisted up to look like a suicide.
The folded page sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot has been found and read, or read out.
Sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot was a page razored from the Royal Granary Roll: a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road this past month marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled note beside each of what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later, and at the foot: 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
The player examines Prout's neck, head or hands up close (he's been got down, or they've climbed or been lifted up to him), where reading what they see takes some skill.
to tell how Prout really died
They see what the noose didn't make: a thin, level cord mark low round the neck beneath the rope's slanting burn, a swelling under the hair at the back of the skull, and clean palms with no rope burn. He was struck and strangled, then hung up.
They see rope burn, bruising and a dead clerk's face, and can't read more. Kell, at their shoulder, says 'Hm.' She has seen something; a second look, or asking her, will find it.
The player pushes past Cob's hostility to get him to trust them or tell what he knows, with an appeal or an argument, where it could go either way. (Not just asking him a question. Food or coin offered as the price of it gets boasts and bargaining, not this. A promise that truly answers what he's afraid of, his name kept out of it and the men from the loft kept off him, needs no dice: that's not this either.)
to get Cob to trust you with what he heard
Cob's swagger cracks. He checks Moll can't hear, then tells it in a frightened rush: he sleeps in the loft, and last night he woke to a lantern and voices, a thump and a choking noise, then the hoist creaking with no sacks on it. He hid till morning.
Cob jeers, calls them a bum-faced palace pigeon and darts behind the water butt and through a gap into the granary. He's hiding, not gone: Moll knows where, and he can still be coaxed out.
The player makes Cob a promise that truly answers what he's afraid of, and means it (his name kept out of it, with nothing to the watch and nothing in anybody's book; the men from the loft kept off him; no Mending House; the boots his to keep), or asks him what he knows under a promise like that made before. No dice, whatever they ask with it: he believes it, near enough. He checks Moll can't hear, then tells it in a frightened rush: he sleeps in the loft, and last night he woke to a lantern and voices, Mister Prout arguing with two men; then a thump, a choking noise and the hoist creaking with no sacks on it. He hid in his sacks till morning. Asked for a look in his boot as well, he holds the left one out himself.
Prout didn't hang himself: what has been found shows he was killed and then hoisted up to look like a suicide.
The player presses on the holes in Moll's 'I saw him jump' story, or tries to read whether she's lying, where it could go either way. (Not just asking her to tell it.)
to see through Moll's story about the jump
Moll's story wobbles and she knows it. Cornered, she admits through her teeth that a gentleman paid her a silver crown at first light to say she'd seen the clerk jump.
Moll tells it again, louder and with new details, and Cob loyally swears to every word. The holes are still there (the barred loft door, the drizzle, debts nobody knows of) for anyone who comes at it another way.
The player tries to frighten the kids into talking: threats, looming, the watch, the Mending House or Cob's father.
to scare the children into talking
Cob's bravado collapses. White-faced, he blurts that he was in the loft last night and heard men do it, and starts to cry; Moll screams blue murder at the player from the wall. Kell's mouth goes thin.
Cob bolts behind the water butt and through a gap into the granary, and Moll lets fly in three languages. Kell says nothing, loudly. The kids will be harder to reach now, but they haven't gone.
The player offers Cob something as the price of a look in his boot, or at what's crackling in it (a coin held up, food, a trade: 'this is yours if I can see what's in there', 'a shilling for a look'), however politely it's asked and whatever they say about the boots staying his, and nothing that answers what he's afraid of. No dice: Cob haggles, boasts, ups the price and takes anything going, but the boot stays on. Bought attention isn't trust, and grown-ups who pay to look at his boots want them off him (the watch, his da, the pawnshop): what's really wrong comes out instead, his way. They're Cob's, and nobody's having them. (Food with nothing asked back is a kindness, not this.)
The player does Cob a kindness with nothing asked back: something to eat, or a dinner stood him freely, with no look at his boots (or anything else) as the price. He takes it with bad grace and a boast, and it counts with him: after it, a polite ask for a look in his boot, the boots staying his, gets a yes.
Cob has had a kindness from the player with nothing asked back (something to eat, or a dinner stood him freely): it counts with him.
Before Cob has any reason to trust them (no kindness with nothing asked back done him yet, no promise that answers what he's afraid of, no yes from him already) and with nothing offered for it, the player asks Cob to let them look in his left boot, or see or feel what's crackling in it, with the boots staying his (it's what's in them they're after, not the boots), or tries to win him round to it (Mister Prout, the men from the loft, his own skin), where it could go either way. Not with anything offered for the look (a coin, food, a trade): that's a bribe, and gets haggling. Not after a kindness, with a promise that answers his fear, or once he's said they can look: then the ask needs no dice.
to get Cob to let you look in his boot
Cob scowls at them for a long moment, then sits on the edge of the water butt, unlaces the string and holds the left boot out at arm's length: 'Look, then. And Cob's having it straight back.' In the lining is something folded and stiff, held in with small neat stitches, and out comes a page, folded small and gone soft at the corners. Cob can't read it; anyone who can sees a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled weights beside them.
Cob won't, and it costs: he clamps a hand over the boot and backs off towards the water butt and his gap, and Moll drops off the wall between them, one more grown-up after Cob's boots. The boot isn't lost: a kindness with nothing asked back, a real promise, or someone saying aloud whose boots they are can still open it.
The player asks Cob for a look in his left boot (or a peek at what's crackling in it), the boots staying his, once he has real reason to trust them: they did him a kindness with nothing asked back earlier (something to eat, a dinner stood him freely), or they make him a promise, now or before, that truly answers what he's afraid of (his name kept out of it, with nothing to the watch and nothing in anybody's book; the men from the loft kept off him; no Mending House; the boots his to keep), or he has already told them they can look. No dice, however it's put: he unlaces the left boot, holds it out at arm's length and lets them pick the lining open: Prout's page is out.
Sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot was a page razored from the Royal Granary Roll: a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road this past month marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled note beside each of what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later, and at the foot: 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
The player tells Kell they accept the Captain's verdict of suicide and to let the dead-cart have him (not just wondering aloud whether it was suicide).
The player gives up and leaves the granary yard, or heads off elsewhere, before anything has troubled the suicide story, leaving Prout and Kell behind.
The player has been in the yard a long while (at least eight exchanges at this point) without breaking the suicide story, and is going round in circles, idling or waiting for something to happen: noon comes, and so does the dead-cart.
The suicide story is broken and the player knows it: Prout was killed and then hung up for show. This beat is for who and why. Kell is in now: she writes things down, reads back what she's written, and lets the player lead. The kids feel the change: Moll wants Cob away from here, and Cob, if he hasn't talked, is close to cracking. Every thread is live: what Cob saw last night, who paid Moll and with what, the boots, the loft and the big book in it, and Kell herself (why does this one matter to her?). Follow whatever the player picks up and reward real contact with real answers; secrets still need a reason to come out.
Write it down, and read back what you've written. Back the player's reasonable moves, and meet a guess, once, with 'On what evidence?'. Decide for yourself whether what's here would hold up if you signed Prout in as a murder.
Jumpy. If you've been won over, stick close to the player; if not, edge towards the water butt.
Try to get Cob away. Watch the yard gate. Break your story only to protect Cob.
Cob stamps his too-big boots against the cold, and the left one crackles like paper. The palace bells ring the half hour before noon.
The folded page sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot has been found and read, or read out.
Sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot was a page razored from the Royal Granary Roll: a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road this past month marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled note beside each of what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later, and at the foot: 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
The player pushes Cob to tell who was in the loft last night, or about the boots, with an appeal or an argument, while he's still holding out and it could go either way. (Not just asking. A promise that truly answers what he's afraid of, his name kept out of it and the men from the loft kept off him, needs no dice: that's not this.)
to get Cob to tell you what he saw
Cob gives up what he's been holding: Silvertop, the posh cove with the silver-topped cane who comes with the Purveyor's wagons and has his own key to the big doors, and a big man with a bandaged hand. If asked, he owns up that the boots came off Mister Prout, and that he saw the clerk sewing something into one two nights ago.
Cob clams up and backs towards the water butt: Cob don't know nothing. He'll talk to someone who gives him a real reason to feel safe.
The player makes Cob a promise that truly answers what he's afraid of, and means it (his name kept out of it, with nothing to the watch and nothing in anybody's book; the men from the loft kept off him; no Mending House; the boots his to keep), or asks him what he knows under a promise like that made before. No dice, whatever they ask with it: he believes it, near enough. He gives up who, in a whisper: Silvertop, the posh cove with the silver-topped cane, the flower smell and a ring with a bit of wheat on it, who comes with the Purveyor's wagons and opens the big doors with his own key; and a big man with a bandaged hand, who said 'Yes, Master'. Asked for a look in his boot as well, he holds the left one out himself.
The player presses on the holes in Moll's story, or tries to read what she's hiding, where it could go either way. (Not just asking her to tell it.)
to get the truth out of Moll
Moll cracks: a gentleman with a silver-topped cane and a wheat-ear signet ring paid her a silver crown at first light to say she saw the clerk jump, and his big friend with the bandaged hand called him 'Master Sallow'. Pressed, she opens her fist on the coin.
Moll sticks to her story and turns up the abuse, but her eyes keep going to the yard gate, and the holes in her story are still there.
The player tries to frighten the kids into talking: threats, looming, the watch, the Mending House or Cob's father.
to force the children to reveal what they know
They crack under it. Cob sobs out what he saw (Silvertop and the big man with the bandaged hand); Moll flings down her silver crown and calls the player every name she knows. Kell writes it down without looking at the player.
Cob bolts behind the water butt and into the granary, Moll goes back up the wall out of reach, swearing, and Kell sighs. They'll only come round for someone who stops looming.
The player offers Cob something as the price of a look in his boot, or at what's crackling in it (a coin held up, food, a trade: 'this is yours if I can see what's in there', 'a shilling for a look'), however politely it's asked and whatever they say about the boots staying his, and nothing that answers what he's afraid of. No dice: Cob haggles, boasts, ups the price and takes anything going, but the boot stays on. Bought attention isn't trust, and grown-ups who pay to look at his boots want them off him (the watch, his da, the pawnshop): what's really wrong comes out instead, his way. They're Cob's, and nobody's having them. (Food with nothing asked back is a kindness, not this.)
The player does Cob a kindness with nothing asked back: something to eat, or a dinner stood him freely, with no look at his boots (or anything else) as the price. He takes it with bad grace and a boast, and it counts with him: after it, a polite ask for a look in his boot, the boots staying his, gets a yes.
Cob has had a kindness from the player with nothing asked back (something to eat, or a dinner stood him freely): it counts with him.
Before Cob has any reason to trust them (no kindness with nothing asked back done him yet, no promise that answers what he's afraid of, no yes from him already) and with nothing offered for it, the player asks Cob to let them look in his left boot, or see or feel what's crackling in it, with the boots staying his (it's what's in them they're after, not the boots), or tries to win him round to it (Mister Prout, the men from the loft, his own skin), where it could go either way. Not with anything offered for the look (a coin, food, a trade): that's a bribe, and gets haggling. Not after a kindness, with a promise that answers his fear, or once he's said they can look: then the ask needs no dice.
to get Cob to let you look in his boot
Cob scowls at them for a long moment, then sits on the edge of the water butt, unlaces the string and holds the left boot out at arm's length: 'Look, then. And Cob's having it straight back.' In the lining is something folded and stiff, held in with small neat stitches, and out comes a page, folded small and gone soft at the corners. Cob can't read it; anyone who can sees a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled weights beside them.
Cob won't, and it costs: he clamps a hand over the boot and backs off towards the water butt and his gap, and Moll drops off the wall between them, one more grown-up after Cob's boots. The boot isn't lost: a kindness with nothing asked back, a real promise, or someone saying aloud whose boots they are can still open it.
The player asks Cob for a look in his left boot (or a peek at what's crackling in it), the boots staying his, once he has real reason to trust them: they did him a kindness with nothing asked back earlier (something to eat, a dinner stood him freely), or they make him a promise, now or before, that truly answers what he's afraid of (his name kept out of it, with nothing to the watch and nothing in anybody's book; the men from the loft kept off him; no Mending House; the boots his to keep), or he has already told them they can look. No dice, however it's put: he unlaces the left boot, holds it out at arm's length and lets them pick the lining open: Prout's page is out.
Sewn into the lining of Prout's left boot was a page razored from the Royal Granary Roll: a dozen grain wagons for the King's Road this past month marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled note beside each of what the same wagon weighed at the river warehouses two days later, and at the foot: 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
The player accuses Cob or Moll of killing Prout (says plainly that they did it, not just asks) or tells Kell to arrest one of them for it.
The player is done here without naming anyone for it: wrapping up, leaving the yard, or asking Kell to write Prout up as murdered by persons unknown or to take what they've found to the King as it stands.
The scene has been at this point a good while (at least six exchanges) and the player isn't closing in on who or why, or is idling or waiting: noon comes, and so does the dead-cart.
Prout's page is out: grain written off as 'lost to goblins' that turned up at the river warehouses, every wagon countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. This is why he died, and it names a man. Give the player a moment with it. Kell reads it over their shoulder and goes very still: this is what Prout came to her about, and that can come out now. Let the player put the case together in their own words; Kell tests it once, at its weakest point ('On what evidence?'), and doesn't make it for them. If the kids hear the name, or a silver-topped cane described, they know exactly who it is.
Read the page and go still. Then admit, quietly and once, that Prout came to you three days ago and you sent him away (unless it's already out: then it's told). Start writing it up in your own words, and read back what you've written for the investigator to put right.
If you hear the name Sallow or a silver-topped cane described, that's Silvertop: react.
Go white at the name Sallow, and look at your fist.
The palace bells ring a quarter to noon. Kell turns the page over, as if there might be more on the back.
The player is done here and leaves the yard (or sends Kell off) with the page in hand, without laying the case out in words: Kell has read it and will write it up herself.
The player has had the page a while (at least three exchanges at this point) without making the case to Kell, or is dawdling: noon comes, and so does the dead-cart.
Noon, and the world has stopped waiting. Corporal Tull has come with two constables, a handcart, a long ladder and the Captain's written order to cut Prout down and file him as a suicide. This is the last chance to make the case. Tull isn't a villain: he's bored, polite and in a hurry, and he'll wait for the sergeant's word if someone gives him a reason he can repeat to the Captain. His order says who asked for it, for anyone who reads it. Prout coming down the ladder is a chance, for anyone quick, to look at him up close.
Wave the order and quote it. Be reasonable, bored and in a hurry. Wait if the sergeant asks; take Prout in however she signs for him.
Hold Tull off with procedure if the player has given you something to hold him with. Without it, you can't.
Go quiet at the sight of more watchmen. Stick close to whoever's been decent to you, or slide towards the water butt.
Get off the wall and as far from the watch as the yard allows.
One constable sets the ladder against the hoist beam and starts up it with a knife in his teeth. Tull looks at Kell: 'Sarge?'
Kell, given real evidence, has agreed to sign Prout in as a murder rather than a suicide, and Tull has accepted it, with nobody named for it.
The player tries to talk Tull into waiting, or into taking Prout in as anything but a suicide, before Kell has a case she'll sign for.
to convince Tull to wait before taking Prout away
Tull sighs, folds the order away and sits on the edge of the cart: he'll wait for the sergeant's word, and take Prout in however she signs for him.
Tull is very sorry, but the Captain was very clear, and he nods his constables up the ladder. One more good reason might still stop him.
The player accuses Cob or Moll of killing Prout (says plainly that they did it, not just asks) or tells Kell or Tull to arrest one of them for it.
Tull's patience has run out, or the player has told him to go ahead: he has waited at least two exchanges since he arrived (or since he last agreed to wait) without being given a reason he can take back to the Captain, and the constables load Prout onto the cart as a suicide.
The player has accused a child of the murder. Kell doesn't move: she asks what evidence they have, and waits. The accused child reacts as they would, and the other defends them. This beat is for the player to show what they've got, think again, or insist. Don't decide it for them, and don't hand them the real answer to soften the moment.
Don't arrest anyone yet. Ask what evidence they have and weigh it honestly: boots make Cob a thief, not a murderer. If they insist after that, do it, under protest, and say you'll be writing your objection down.
Outrage first, then fear: back towards the water butt.
Defend Cob ferociously. If it's you they're accusing, threaten to run.
Cob edges towards the water butt; Moll swings a leg over the far side of the wall.
Having heard Kell's objection, the player insists that Cob be taken in for the murder anyway, or seizes him for it themselves.
Cob was taken in for Prout's murder.
Having heard Kell's objection, the player insists that Moll be taken in for the murder anyway, or seizes her for it themselves.
Moll was taken in for Prout's murder.
The player has let the accusation drop for now (taken it back, or turned to the evidence, the body or someone else), and Corporal Tull's dead-cart hasn't come yet.
The player has let the accusation drop for now, and Corporal Tull and his dead-cart are already in the yard.
The case is on the record: the player has made it to Kell (out loud, or by handing her the page that names him) that Prout was killed and hung up to look like a suicide by or for the man calling himself Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office (the kids' 'Silvertop', or just 'the Purveyor's man'), backed by something actually found here, and Kell has accepted it and is writing it down as murder.
Kell writes Prout's death down as murder, made to look like a suicide, with the man calling himself Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office behind it. The player has a case, and whatever proof they found here, to take to the King.
Kell underlines something twice, closes her notebook and says something dry that is very nearly thanks. Prout goes to the watch house as a murder; she wants the player to carry the case to the King, since the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. Let the kids react to how the player treated them.
Kell writes Prout's death down as murder by persons unknown, so he goes to the watch-house cold room and not the suicides' pit. Nobody has been named, but the case stays open.
Kell writes one line and underlines it; Prout will go on the cart under a sheet, as a murder. She tells the player, drily, that an open case beats a wrong one.
At the player's insistence, and over Kell's objection, a child has been taken in for Prout's murder. The Captain will gladly file a murder that embarrasses nobody at court, and whoever really killed Prout is in the clear.
Narrate the arrest without relish: the accused child's fury or terror, the other one bolting (over the wall or through the gap behind the water butt), and Kell writing her objection down in full. Prout is still turning on the hoist.
Prout goes into the Captain's book as a suicide and onto the dead-cart for the pit outside the north gate. Nobody will look for whoever killed him.
Kell writes one word in her notebook and shuts it. Prout goes out of the yard on the dead-cart under a sheet, past the Assembly bunting (at noon, if it isn't here yet). Let the kids react.
The player left the granary yard before anything troubled the suicide story. At noon the dead-cart takes Prout away as a suicide.
Kell watches them go without a word, then turns back to the body and opens her notebook on her own.
Prout didn't hang himself: he was struck and strangled, then hoisted up for show.
the body (cord mark, the blow to the head)
Cob's account of the loft
the scraped heels of Prout's boots
Kell treating it as murder
Prout found grain written off as 'lost to goblins' that turned up at the river warehouses, every wagon countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'.
the page sewn into Prout's left boot (Cob is wearing the boots)
the tally book in the loft
the motive, and the name Sallow
A gentleman with a silver-topped cane and a wheat-ear signet ring (Sallow) was in the loft that night.
Cob ('Silvertop')
Moll, if she cracks
naming Sallow as the man behind it
Getting someone to talk to the dead (a séance, a priest who can call up Prout's ghost): nobody in reach can do it. The Nine Furrows wizards deal in weather, wards and grain, none of them is here, and the temples don't raise the dead for the watch. Prout can only tell what his body shows. (The player's own spells are theirs, and work as the rules say.)
Fetching more help (other watchmen, the watch surgeon, a coroner, a wizard, a tracking dog, the granary warden): nobody can be had before noon. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route, the surgeon is on duty at the palace, and Kell's runner to the warden came back with 'After the Assembly.' The help here is Kell, the kids and whatever the player brought.
A ladder, the granary key or a grown-up's way into the granary: the porters' ladders are locked inside, the yard doors are padlocked, the warden who keeps the key is at the palace, and the yard was swept bare for the Assembly. There's the water butt, a few loose cobbles, the player's own kit, and whatever the kids know.
A royal warrant, or anything in writing from the King: Aldren asked over tea and signed nothing (he avoids signing anything that might upset anyone). The player has the King's word, which Kell respects and a corporal might not.
Reaching anyone at the palace (the Captain, the warden, the King, any official): they're all at the palace preparing for the Assembly and can't be reached from this yard. Taking the case to them is another scene, and leaving before noon leaves Prout to the dead-cart.
Coming back later (tonight, tomorrow): at noon the dead-cart takes Prout away and the yard is locked up for the Assembly. Whatever there is to find is here, this morning.
Prout's own notes and papers: his satchel was found open and empty, and there's nothing written lying about the yard. Whoever emptied it took everything in it.
Following anyone's trail out of the yard (footprints, a scent, tracks): porters, kids and a night of drizzle have trampled it all. No trail leads anywhere from here.
Answers that would need someone who isn't here (what goes on at court, anyone's business at the palace, anything about the goblin raids on the King's Road): nobody in this yard knows, and nothing here says.

scenes.hook: A breath between one thing and the next.
scenes.prep:
Caerwyn's market square and the streets off it, afternoon on the eve of the Centennial Assembly: bunting going up on the procession route, sweepers, delegation banners (Nine Furrows wheat-sheaves, Saltmere salt-gulls, Kläggenheim axes), bread dearer than last week and grumbled about, the dead-cart's bell somewhere behind, the Corn Exchange posting prices, and everybody too busy for a hanged clerk.
Downtime: where does the player go next, and what do they make of Caerwyn on the way? (The lead: The big man with the bandaged hand, whom Kell saw at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, went down the river stairs into the Drowned Rat; she followed him there, and means to go back down at dusk (dock gossip says the big men who do night work for gentlemen drink there).)
Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
Her own errand, which depends on the hour. In the afternoon: to go down the river stairs at dusk after the big man with the bandaged hand she followed there at noon, with the investigator or without, though she'd rather not walk into the Drowned Rat alone (Nan Quill put her out through its door twenty years ago). After dark on the wharves: to see the Heron's night loading with her own eyes, since a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, and to keep the investigator out of the river while she does.
The trail going cold while the city is busy with bunting. A witness in the river. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly.
Whatever was said at the granary (and, after dark, at the Rat) is in her notebook, as it was said; asked, she reads an entry back word for word, and that's all.
In the afternoon: she took a pie round to the granary porters at their noon break (porters will talk to a pie when they won't talk to the watch), and while they ate, the Purveyor's flour wagons went by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She knows neither of them by name, nor the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat, halfway down; she didn't go in after him.
If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, a runner has brought word that the Captain will have her report 'after the Assembly'. She means to have the case made before he reads it.
The palace is shut to anyone without business until the Assembly, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and it reaches him by evening.
After dark: her whistle brings nobody but her. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night.
Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it may come out now, once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.
As things stand between her and the investigator (her memories say how); practical and dry. She says where she's going and when, once, and goes, with the investigator or without; she doesn't steer them, wait on them, or tell them what to do. She answers what she's asked, reads back what she's written, and gives her own dry view of the town when it's wanted. If a child of the granary is sitting in a cell for Prout, she says so, and means to get them out. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.

Downtime between scenes, standing in for the map. Keep it short and alive: answer what the player does or asks with the town as it is (people, prices, gossip, the Assembly preparations), in the house style, from the lore where it says. If they ask around, people know the everyday things the lore gives them and pass on gossip. The lead points onward: The big man with the bandaged hand, whom Kell saw at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, went down the river stairs into the Drowned Rat; she followed him there, and means to go back down at dusk (dock gossip says the big men who do night work for gentlemen drink there). If they haven't got it, let it reach them through whatever they're doing (a porter's gossip, a shopkeeper, or Kell saying where she's off to on her own errand). Don't start new adventures here: places that aren't on the way are for another day.
You're on your own errand (your card says what it is at this hour): say where you'll be and when, once, then go about it, with the investigator or without. Your own dry view of the town and the case, when it's wanted.
A bell tolls the hour across the city; time and the lead are moving on without the investigator.
The player sets off for the river stairs and the Drowned Rat (or says they're going there now), following the lead.
The player sets off for the river stairs and the Drowned Rat.
Close on them setting off, at the threshold: the next scene picks up from there.
The big man with the bandaged hand, whom Kell saw at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, went down the river stairs into the Drowned Rat; she followed him there, and means to go back down at dusk (dock gossip says the big men who do night work for gentlemen drink there).
Sergeant Kell's own errand (she's going there)
gossip in the town
the next scene
Places that aren't on the way (the palace, the Corn Exchange's back rooms, the watch house cells, anywhere outside the walls): they're for another day. The Assembly has the palace shut to anyone without business, and the trail goes to the river.
Fetching help or authority (the Watch Captain, a warrant, the King): the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file, and the King is at the Assembly rehearsals; nobody with a seal can be reached today. A written message left at the palace gate will reach the Marshal by evening.

scenes.hook: This morning a palace clerk, Wendell Prout, was found hanged from the sack hoist behind the King's Granary. At the noon break Sergeant Kell, the watch sergeant the King lent you, saw a gentleman with a silver-topped cane walking beside the Purveyor's wagons, and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged hand, who called him 'Master'. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and Kell reckons a rope takes the skin off the palm of whoever hauls on it. She followed the big man down the river stairs to the Drowned Rat. It's evening on the eve of the Assembly, and she has come back down with you, in a borrowed coat over her uniform that fools nobody.

cast.called: the big man with the bandaged hand

cast.name: Arlo Quarry
cast.called: the young lighterman with the black eye

cast.name: Dilly Sparrow
