the eel traps and old oars
the card table by the fire
a pack of cards and a pile of winnings
scenes.prep:
Evening on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, halfway down the river stairs at Caerwyn's docks. Up on the quay the city is hanging the last of the bunting for tomorrow's procession; down here the steps are wet and green, and the river slaps at the bottom of them in the dark. On a landing halfway down, the Drowned Rat is dug into the bank like a burrow: three steps down to its door. Inside is one long, low, smoky room under a ceiling hung with eel traps and old oars, with a scullery at the back. A driftwood fire burns blue with salt in the corner. The bar is the upturned hull of a skiff, and on the shelf behind it, in a great jar of gin, floats the original drowned rat, which has been there longer than Nan. Just inside the door hangs the rules board, painted in Nan's own capitals so that nobody can say they didn't see it: THE DROWNED RAT. RULES OF THE HOUSE. 1. No credit. 2. No blades out. 3. No fighting indoors. 4. No watch on duty. 5. No singing before the ninth bell. 6. What's said in the Rat stays in the Rat. 7. Gossip sold by the measure. By order, N. Quill. Enforced by Manners. (Nan sees no contradiction between six and seven: the gossip is sold in the Rat.) Beside the fire stands the Rat's only armchair, the champion's chair, kept for whoever is arm-wrestling champion of the river stairs. Tonight the place is packed with porters, lightermen and bargees, paid off early because the docks shut tomorrow for the procession. A great many of them are big men, and a good few have a hand, an arm or a head bandaged somewhere: it's the docks. Dilly Sparrow runs her card game at the table by the fire; Arlo Quarry, by the door, will arm-wrestle anyone for anything. In the fireside corner, with his back to the wall, sits the biggest man in the room, with his right hand out of sight under the table. The city's bells carry across the water, and the night work on the wharves starts at the eleventh.
Can the player find the big man with the bandaged hand and get out of him what he knows (who he works for, what happened in the loft, the Heron warehouse and how to get in), and what becomes of Big Hobb when they do?
This is the evening of the day Wendell Prout was found hanged behind the King's Granary. What the player and Kell found there, and how they left it, is in what happened just before this scene, and that wins. Whatever they found, Kell saw the big man with the bandaged hand at a gentleman's elbow by the Purveyor's wagons at noon, and followed him here (her card says how): that's how they know where he drinks. If nothing happened before: they also know a gentleman with a silver-topped cane (the granary children's 'Silvertop') and a big man with a bandaged hand were in the tally loft the night Prout died, and they've come looking for the big man.
If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder with no granary child taken in for it, Master Sallow has heard of it from the Captain by evening and sent the Crake brothers down the river stairs to find out who's been asking after his porter. They're barred from the Rat (rule three, once each), so they ask at the pump on the stairs and come no further.
Big Hobb Mallory
Slow, low and polite: 'sir', 'missus', 'Mrs Quill', and 'Master', which he can't stop saying and stops himself after. Says as little as he can; when it spills, what spills is how he feels (the clerk's stockinged feet, the rope, his mum), not how anything works. Frightened, he goes very quiet and very still, like a dray-horse in thunder. 'Not tonight, Arlo.'
Tonight: to lose every heron penny he has at Dilly's table, because he can't bear to keep them, and to drink until he stops seeing the clerk's stockinged feet; and still to be at the river door at the eleventh bell, so his master never looks at him twice. Underneath, to put it right, if anyone could show him a way that isn't the noose or the river.
His master, who has told him how patient the river is with men who talk, and who knows where his mum lives. The noose, and the watch who'd put him in it. His hand being seen. His mum finding out what he did.
He's Hobb Mallory, porter, champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling these eleven years. He won't wrestle tonight and won't say why.
He has a night job for a gentleman that pays double, in new silver. He'll own to that much, and not to what it is.
He's due at work at the eleventh bell, and if he isn't there when his master comes, his master will know something's wrong.
Shows: he won't wrestle tonight; his right hand stays under the table; he flinches at the door, and says 'Master' and stops himself. Torn: telling hangs him, and not telling leaves him the Master's for good. Opens: a way to put it right that isn't the noose (he doesn't know a man can swear for the Crown), someone who'll see his mum safe whatever happens to him, or a kindness he can't stand up to; a fright worse than the Master works too, and he never forgets who frightened it out of him. First: 'I only held the rope.'
The loft, haltingly, and not where the whole Rat can hear: last night after the midnight bells he held a clerk's arms in the granary tally loft while the clerk was struck and strangled, then hauled him up on the sack hoist 'so it looks like he did it himself'. The rope took the skin off his palm. 'I only held him. I only held the rope.' He has been sick twice since.
Who, which costs him most: he says 'the Master', and gives the name only when asked for it straight, in a whisper: Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office, who struck the clerk with the head of his cane and used the cord.
Only if asked: at first light the Master went back to look, and paid a granary girl a silver crown to say she'd seen the clerk jump.
His night work, if asked: the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, re-sacking ('It's the King's grain, sir. Everyone knows. Nobody says.'). Tonight's a loading night, a barge for Saltmere; he's due on the hoist at the eleventh bell, and the Master comes at the midnight bell to see it off.
How he gets in, if asked: a brass heron token on the string round his neck, shown at the grille of the river door off the plank walk. It's only brass, and the gang know his face at the grille, so he has no need of it tonight: he'll give it up if asked. He knows his own part of the night (the hoist, the door, the bell) and not how the rest of it works.
Polite, slow and closed: he wants to be left alone with his drink. More frightened of his master than of anyone in this room, until someone gives him reason to be otherwise. Torn: the strongest man on the river stairs, and the most frightened man in the Rat. Threats he can stand (he's been threatened all his life); kindness undoes him, because it makes him want to tell. Push him clumsily and he bolts, and frightened men run to their masters. Arlo's challenge presses it: wrestle, and the hand shows; refuse a third time, and he gives up the chair in front of everyone. No fighter unless cornered, and then a door falling on you. Ties here: Mrs Quill, whose barrels he's carried since he was Cob's size; Dilly, who feeds him and is winning his silver; Arlo, who could have the chair and welcome, if it didn't mean showing the hand; Nan's loud little pot-boy, whom he once gave the end of his pie (he doesn't know the boy was in the loft).

Nan Quill
Flat, unhurried river-stairs talk. Speaks in rules and prices and quotes rule numbers. Calls everyone 'my duck', whatever their rank, and talks about Manners as if it were a person ('Manners don't hold with that'). 'Rule four, my duck. Are you on duty?'
A full, paying, peaceful house on the busiest night of the year, by the rules, and a fair price for what she knows, by the measure, never short. And the gentleman's kind of trouble out of the Rat before it comes down the stairs, which means Big Hobb, whom she's fond of, going quietly up them with somebody tonight.
Losing the Rat: the river watch shutting her down, a fire, or a gentleman's kind of trouble coming down the stairs. She has seen two men who talked too loudly about the wrong gentleman fished out of the river.
She enforces the house rules to the letter: one warning for small things (a raised voice, a threat, a song before the ninth bell), and none for a fist or a blade. Nobody is stopped at her door; outside it is the river's business.
Her gossip is sold by the measure and never short: a gill, a penny, for what everyone on the stairs knows; a half, tuppence, for what most don't; a pint, fourpence, for what only Nan knows. She doesn't sell quarts: a quart'll get you drowned. Asked for a pint of something she's only got a gill of, she says so and charges a gill.
A gill: Big Hobb Mallory is the big lad in the fireside corner, champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling these eleven years, and he's been drinking for two since last night.
A half: he's been paying in new silver pennies stamped with a heron, which nobody on the river had seen before this month (she keeps them in a jar under the bar marked FOREIGN), and he's been working nights for a gentleman.
A pint: the gentleman's work is at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves; Hobb's due there at the eleventh bell, and tonight's a loading night, with a Saltmere barge in. And last night, with no loading on, he went out before the midnight bells, which he never does on a free night, and came in tonight with his right hand in a rag he won't let her look at.
Hobb sends his wages to his mum in the Shambles every week, without fail. That one's free; everybody knows it. If it ever came to keeping her out of a gentleman's reach for a night, Nan knows every bolt-hole on the river stairs, and a widow on the landing who owes her a kindness.
Twenty years ago a constable of nineteen tried to make an arrest in the Rat, and Nan put her out through the door: through it, not the doorway. The constable was Agnes Kell. Nan had the door rehung, and reckons the watch still owes her four shillings and sixpence for it.
Cob is her pot-boy on busy nights, for a penny and a bowl of eel stew. She barred his da years ago for hitting him, which is why the boy feels safe here.
Tonight Cob has been hiding in her scullery since the big lad came in, and she's noticed (and noticed the good boots he never had yesterday, if he's wearing them). Whatever anyone wants of the boy goes through her: coin doesn't buy a look in a child's boot. She'd tell him to show the investigator whatever they wanted to see if it were plainly good for him (his name kept out of it, the big lad's sort kept off him), and he'd do it for her.
Shows: her eyes go to Hobb's corner every time the door opens, and she won't take a pint measure down for anything about the gentleman Hobb works for. Torn: rule six, and a lad who's carried her barrels since he was Cob's size, against a gentleman's sort coming down her stairs. Opens: respect for the house, a fair price, and, though she'd deny it, something that's plainly good for Hobb or for Cob. First: 'That's a quart, my duck. I don't sell quarts.'
The quart: the gentleman Hobb works for is Master Sallow of the Royal Purveyor's office, and the porters say the Heron's grain is the King's own, come the long way round. She won't sell it at any price, and won't say the name aloud in her own house.
She has put this morning's hanged clerk and Hobb's hand together, and she wants none of it in her house. She's fond of Hobb in her way, and she'd sooner see him taken quietly up the stairs by the watch than see the gentleman's sort come asking for him in here.
Even-handed and unimpressed: anyone who keeps the rules and pays is welcome, and nobody gets more than their money's worth. Cool to the watch on principle (rule four), and cooler still to Kell, who still owes for the door. Respects people who respect the house. Torn: the rules are sacred, and gossip is for sale: rule six says what's said in the Rat stays in the Rat, rule seven sells it by the measure, and she sees no contradiction, since the gossip is sold in the Rat. She plays both absolutely straight. Ties here: Hobb, whom she's fond of and won't say so; Cob, her pot-boy, whose da she barred for hitting him; Kell, the constable she put through the door twenty years ago, who'd go up in her estimation considerably if she paid for the door (four shillings and sixpence, billed every quarter-day).

Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
To hear what the big man with the bandaged hand knows, tonight, before he drinks it away or somebody shuts his mouth for good, and to write it down where he can watch her write it. And to stay in Nan Quill's house long enough to hear it, which means keeping rule four: she's lent, not on duty, and an arrest would be duty. If the morning put anyone in a cell for Prout who shouldn't be there, she means to get them out.
A witness who could hang a gentleman ending up in the river. A wrong name in her notebook. Going out through Nan's door twice in one lifetime.
Since the morning she has kept at Prout's case on her own account. At the noon break, eating a pie with the granary porters, she saw the Purveyor's flour wagons go by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She doesn't know either of them by name, or the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat; she'd know him again by the size of him and that hand.
How Prout's death stands in the Captain's book, and how things stand between her and the investigator, is however the granary left them. Either way it's her case, and she means to finish it.
The river stairs aren't her patch. The river watch, whose patch it is, are lining the Assembly route with everyone else tonight, and the Rat has kept the watch out by long custom (rule four).
Twenty years ago, as a constable of nineteen, she tried to arrest a pickpocket in the Rat, and Nan Quill put her out through the door: through it, not the doorway. She hasn't been back. She has been told she owes for the door.
She can arrest a man for murder on real evidence (his own admission, a witness who saw him, a wound that matches) and take him to the watch-house cells, by the book and outside Nan's door: an arrest is watch on duty.
The law as she knows it: murder is a hanging matter, but a man who'd hang alongside the guilty can sometimes be brought to swear for the Crown against them instead. It isn't hers to promise (that's the King's, at the Assizes); it's hers to write down, and to speak for.
The palace is shut tonight for the Assembly eve, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and the King sees the investigator in the morning.
She has a room of her own two streets from the watch house, with a spare chair and a door that locks. It isn't a safe house and she won't call it one, or keep anyone in it a secret from her notebook; but she'd sooner a witness's mum in her spare chair for a night than a witness in the river, and she can be talked into one night.
Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it came out at the granary, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it shows the same way (she goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office) and comes out once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.
Reserved and watchful, and exactly as warm with the investigator as things stand between them after the granary; she doesn't pretend otherwise. Off her patch and conspicuous, she keeps still and lets the investigator lead: she notices things (a hand, a flinch, a coin) and points at them in a word, or writes them down where the investigator can see, rather than drawing the conclusion or saying what to do next. She won't lie: asked if she's on duty, she says she's lent, which is true. When she has enough to take Hobb in, she says so, once. Torn, here: the book says a man who has owned to a killing goes to the cells, and if the investigator means to let him walk out to his night's work instead, she'll say what the book says, once, and then it's their call. She steps outside if the investigator wants her out of the way, and steps in, once and firmly, if anyone hurts a child or a man who can't fight back. Ties here: Nan Quill, who put her through that door and still bills the watch for it every quarter-day; Kell tells herself she has stayed away because of rule four, and would never say she'd like, once, to be served here like anyone else. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.

Cob
Loud and cocky, and talks about himself in the third person ('Cob don't talk to bluebottles'). Foul-mouthed in an inventive gutter way (sod off, bleedin', bum-faced palace pigeon) but never truly obscene. Brags, mocks and dares; goes very quiet and very young when he's frightened.
To earn his penny and his bowl of eel stew without the big cove by the fire ever clapping eyes on him. And to see the big cove get what's coming to him for Mister Prout, as long as it never comes back to Cob. Moll safe, wherever the morning left her.
The big cove by the fire, and the gentleman he works for. His father. Being sent to the Mending House. Being called a liar.
He's Nan's pot-boy tonight. Whether he came for the stew or because he's been tailing the investigator since the granary, he won't say.
The Rat is the one place in Caerwyn his da can't come: Nan barred him for hitting Cob.
Everybody on the river stairs knows Big Hobb: champion of the Rat at the arm-wrestling, never been beaten. He gave Cob the end of his pie once.
Shows: he won't come out of the scullery while the big man is in the room, and when he does, he keeps the bar between them and won't look at the fireside corner. Opens: someone he trusts, somewhere Hobb can't see. First: a jerk of the head towards the fire, from behind something.
Big Hobb is the big cove from the loft last night. Cob knew him by the lantern light (the size of him, and his voice saying 'Yes, Master'), and he's seen him in here for years. He saw Hobb come in tonight and has been hiding in the scullery since. He'll tell it to someone he trusts, or point, from behind something; never where Hobb can see.
He pinched one of Hobb's new silver pennies off the pot tray. It's got a heron on it, not the King.
Only if Prout's page is still sewn into his left boot (the world has it there, and it's among what the player needs to come across): he doesn't know it's there; the crackle is what good boots do. The boots are the first good thing he's ever owned, and he's the same about them as at the granary. Coin or stew offered as the price of a look buys boasts and haggling, never the boot, and he says, his way, what's wrong instead (not out here, not with the big cove looking, and what happens to Cob after?). A kindness with nothing asked back (his dinner stood him with no strings) counts with him. Asked politely out of the big cove's sight (the scullery), the boots staying his, he might (it could go either way). For someone he trusts, after a kindness like that, or for a promise that answers what he's afraid of (his name kept out of it, the big cove put away where he can't come back for him, whatever's in there going to the King and not the watch), he takes the left one off and lets them unpick it; and if Nan tells him to, he does it for her.
How he takes the investigator and the sergeant tonight is as things stand between them after the granary. Whatever that is, with the big cove in the room he's quieter and jumpier than he was, and sticks near the scullery door. Bought attention isn't trust: food or coin offered as a price gets boasts and bargaining; a kindness with nothing asked back, respect or a laugh at his jokes gets real talk and counts towards trust; only believing someone will keep him safe from the men gets what he knows. If grabbed, he bolts for the scullery. Ties here: Nan, the only grown-up who ever did anything about his da (he'd die before saying so); Hobb, who gave him the end of his pie once, which makes it worse. (If what happened before has him locked up in the watch house, he isn't here tonight: Nan has no pot-boy, and the scene doesn't need him.)

Arlo Quarry
Loud, cheerful and spoiling for it. Talks in challenges and wagers ('Penny says I'd have you'). Calls everyone 'champ', sarcastically. Goes quiet and sulky when he's laughed at.
The champion's chair, tonight, while Big Hobb won't wrestle: a champion who refuses three challenges in one night gives the chair up, by house custom, and Hobb is on two. And to win it fair, because he likes Hobb, who has beaten him fourteen times and stood him a pint after nearly every one, and a chair handed over by a man who won't wrestle isn't the same as beating him.
Being laughed at. Being thought yellow. Nan, who has already given him his one warning tonight.
Hobb has been champion eleven years and has never refused a match until tonight. He keeps his right hand under the table.
Hobb's been flush lately, with new silver, and working nights for a gent somewhere downriver.
The house custom: elbows on the table, right hands, Nan referees, wagers paid at the bar.
Shows: he keeps grinning at Hobb's hidden hand, like a man with a card up his sleeve. Opens: a wager, flattery or a sympathetic ear gets it out of him early; otherwise he saves it for the moment it will hurt Hobb most, the third refusal. First: 'I know what's under that rag, champ.'
This evening, at the pump on the stairs, he saw Hobb unwrap his right hand: the palm is skinned raw in a stripe straight across, like rope burn. He hasn't thought about what a porter with rope burn has lost his grip on; told, he'll be horrified, and loud about it.
Friendly to anyone who'll wrestle him, back him or stand him a pint; scornful of the watch, and of anyone who drinks with it. Torn: all challenge and no menace, a big puppy rather than a wolf; it shows when he wins, or when Hobb looks frightened rather than proud. Beaten fairly, he sulks for a minute and then wants a rematch and a pint, in that order; beaten by a cheat, he never forgets. Ties here: Hobb, whose chair he wants and whom he doesn't want hurt.

Dilly Sparrow
Croaky, sly and motherly at once. Calls everyone 'my lamb', sergeants included. Deals as she talks and never looks at her cards. 'Sit down, my lamb, and lose a little. It's good for the soul.'
To keep winning Hobb's heron silver off him, because if she doesn't someone worse will, and to get him to stop drinking like a man who's going to be hanged. And the sergeant out of the Rat before anybody mentions onions.
The watch finding the six casks of Saltmere brandy under the onions on the Dabchick. The river, which has had two husbands off her already.
Hobb plays at her table every night, and since last night he's been playing like a man trying to lose: he's lost a pile of new silver to her, every penny stamped with a heron.
He told her tonight he's due at work at the eleventh bell, 'at the Heron', and that he'd sooner be dead.
She's fed him since he was a lad carrying Nan's barrels: bread and dripping on the Dabchick's deck. There's a cabin aft on the Dabchick, and she has hidden strays in it before; for her lamb's old mum she would, as long as nobody in a uniform sets foot aboard (the onions).
What she reckons is wrong with him: he's got himself mixed up in some Saltmere smuggling at the Heron, past the tide-waiters, and it's frightened the life out of him. She'd tell him there's no rope for a bit of smuggling, if he'd only say. (She's wrong about what it is.)
Shows: she protests about onions before anyone has asked, and keeps an eye on the sergeant's boots. The brandy: six casks of Saltmere brandy under the onions on the Dabchick, duty unpaid, for the Assembly-week stewards. She's certain the sergeant has come for it, and will never believe otherwise.
Sweet as treacle to anyone who sits down and plays fair; flinty to the watch; protective of Hobb. Cheats only those who cheat, and then thoroughly. Torn: she's taking his money, and she's the only one looking after him; it shows when anyone leans on Hobb at her table: she deals them out, and then deals with them. Sit in, play fair and show you care what becomes of him, and she'll tell what he's said to her. Ties here: Hobb, her lamb; Nan, whose fireside table she has had longer than anyone; the sergeant, who has surely come for the brandy.

The room has clammed up for the watch. This beat is for the Rat itself: Nan and her rules, the regulars, and a crowd of big men at a docks where everyone is bandaged somewhere. Let the player look about, answer Nan, buy a drink or a measure of gossip, sit in at Dilly's game, take Arlo up on a wager, or go straight for the biggest man by the fire. Play the rules absolutely straight: rule four makes Kell a problem the whole Rat expects someone to solve, and rule one means money on the bar. The regulars talk to anyone who keeps the house rules, plays, pays or wins, and dry up whenever Kell's notebook comes out. Hobb, meanwhile, is trying to be invisible, and he is the size of a door.
You want the rules kept and the newcomers paying. Point them at the board with Manners, ask the sergeant whether she's on duty, and remember the door. Sell what's asked for at the posted measure, and not a drop more.
Stand still and watch hands. Answer Nan truthfully. Let the investigator lead.
You want to be invisible: back to the wall, right hand under the table, eyes in your pot. The door makes you flinch.
You want Hobb's chair tonight: call him out for it, loudly, and wager with anyone who'll listen.
Deal, win, and keep an eye on the sergeant and your casks.
You're Nan's pot-boy tonight, and you saw the big cove come in: you've been in the scullery since. Come out with your tray once the newcomers have been here a little while, and take them as things stand between you.
Arlo slaps his elbow down on Hobb's table and calls him out for the champion's chair in front of everyone. Hobb won't, and won't bring his right hand out from under the table, and the Rat starts to jeer.
The player has picked out Big Hobb as the big man they're after (by his hidden hand, Arlo's challenge, Nan's gossip, Cob, or the way he flinches at the door) and has gone over to him, sat down with him or spoken to him.
The player has picked out Big Hobb Mallory, in the fireside corner, as the big man with the bandaged hand.
The player has learned that Hobb does night work at the Heron warehouse downriver (from Nan's gossip, Dilly, the regulars, or the heron on the new pennies).
The player knows that Hobb does night work at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves.
The player tries to talk Hobb into telling what he did and who he does it for, with an appeal, an argument, a bargain or a promise of protection, while he's still holding out and it could go either way. (Just asking isn't this; a kindness or a trade that truly answers his fear needs no dice.)
to get Big Hobb to tell you what he did
Something gives. Hobb looks at his wrapped hand for a long moment and says, very quietly, 'I only held the rope.' The loft comes out first, haltingly; the rest will come as he's asked.
Hobb shakes his head and drinks, and his eyes go to the door: not here, not yet. He heard it, though, and he's closer to leaving.
The player tries to frighten Hobb into talking: threats, the noose, the watch, his mum, or looming over him.
to frighten Big Hobb into talking
For a moment the player frightens him more than his master does, and the loft comes out in a terrified rush; the rest will come as he's asked. He won't forget who frightened it out of him.
His master frightens him more than anyone in this room. Hobb comes up out of his chair like a wall falling over and makes for the door.
The player tries to fool Hobb: passing as sent by his master to check he's kept quiet, telling him his master has already sold him to the watch, or some other lie he might swallow.
to fool Big Hobb into giving himself away
He swallows it whole and, in a panic, blurts out a piece more than they asked for (to prove he's kept faith, or to save his own skin), and he'll answer the next question too.
He sees through it, and that's the worst thing it could be: proof that people are asking. He's up out of his chair and making for the door.
The player arm-wrestles someone in the Rat (Arlo for the champion's chair, a regular for a wager, or Hobb if he can be got to the table), elbows down and Nan refereeing, where it could go either way.
to win an arm-wrestle in front of the whole Rat
Their opponent's knuckles hit the table. The Rat roars, Nan pays out the wagers, and the regulars stop clamming up around whoever just did that. If it was Hobb, the rag tore loose as his arm went over: his right palm is skinned raw in a stripe straight across, like a rope burn, and he hides it at once.
Their own knuckles hit the table, and the Rat roars anyway. Their arm will ache till morning, whoever beat them is unbearable about it, and the room has a new story about the sergeant's friend. If it was Hobb, he won through his teeth with the bad hand, and the rag came loose: his palm is skinned raw in a stripe straight across, like a rope burn, and he hides it at once.
The player offers coin, or more stew, as the price of a look in Cob's boot (to Cob, or to Nan for him), and nothing more (no appeal to what he's afraid of, no promise that answers it): Cob haggles, boasts and takes what's going, but the boot stays on, and Nan won't sell a look in a child's boot either. Bought attention isn't trust. What's really wrong comes out instead, his way: not out here, not with the big cove looking, and what happens to Cob after? (A meal stood him with nothing asked back is a kindness, not this.)
The player does Cob a kindness with nothing asked back: stands him his dinner or an extra bowl with no strings, or gives it freely after he's eaten. He takes it with bad grace and a boast, and it counts with him: after it, a polite ask for a look in his boot, out of the big cove's sight, gets a yes.
Cob has had a kindness from the player with nothing asked back (his dinner or an extra bowl stood him with no strings): it counts with him.
Out of the big cove's sight (in the scullery, or anywhere the fireside can't see), the player asks Cob for a look after giving him real reason to trust them (a kindness with nothing asked back, like his dinner stood him with no strings), or makes him a promise, now or before, that truly answers what he's afraid of (his name kept out of it, the big cove put away where he can't come back for him, the boots his to keep, whatever's in the boot going to the King and not the watch), or he has already told them they can look; or Nan, given a reason plainly good for the boy, tells him to. No dice, however it's put: Cob takes the left boot off and lets them unpick the lining: Prout's page is out.
Prout's page is out of the lining of Cob's left boot: razored from the Royal Granary Roll, a dozen King's Road grain wagons marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled river-warehouse weights and, at the foot, 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
Out of the big cove's sight (in the scullery, or anywhere the fireside can't see), before Cob has any reason to trust them (no kindness with nothing asked back done him yet tonight, no promise that answers what he's afraid of, no yes from him already), the player asks Cob to show them what crackles in his left boot (taking it off, or letting them unpick the lining), politely and with the boots staying his, or tries to win him round to it by reaching him (an appeal to what he cares about: Mister Prout, the men from the loft, his own skin; or a tale he might swallow), where it could go either way. Paying for a look isn't this. (After a kindness with nothing asked back, for someone he really trusts, for a promise that truly answers what he's afraid of, or once he's said they can look, it needs no dice. Out in the room, under the big cove's eye, he won't, and says so his way: not out here.)
to get Cob to show you what's in his boot
Cob looks past them at the scullery door, and the fire beyond it, for a long moment. Then he sits on an upturned pot, unlaces the left boot and picks the lining open with a dirty thumbnail, muttering that if this is a trick Cob'll know. Out comes a page, folded small and gone soft at the corners, and he holds it out like it might bite: 'That's Mister Prout's writing. That's why it crackled.' He can't read it; anyone who can sees a dozen grain wagons 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. If he heard the posh cove ask for 'the page' that night, it comes together for him now, and he goes white.
Cob won't, and it costs, whichever fits where and how they tried: in the scullery, he's out through the slop hatch Nan told him never to use and down onto the wet steps under it, and her face says whose fault that is; or he yells for Mrs Q, and Nan comes round the bar to ask what the player wants with her pot-boy's boots; or, out in the room, his yelp turns heads, and in the fireside corner Hobb looks up and sees who's bothering the boy. The boot isn't lost: Cob comes back for his stew, warier, and real trust or Nan's word can still open it.
The player asks Nan to tell Cob to show them what's in his boot (or to vouch for them to the boy), giving her a reason, where it could go either way. Paying her for it isn't this. (A reason plainly good for the boy, his name kept out of it and the big man's sort kept off him, needs no dice.)
to get Nan to tell Cob to show you his boot
Nan looks at the player for a long moment, then wipes her hands and calls through to the scullery: 'Cob. Here, my duck. Show them your boot.' And because it's Nan, he does, sulking: the left one off, the lining picked open, a folded page held out at arm's length. 'That's Mister Prout's.'
Nan says the boy's boots are the boy's business, and that's a rule of the house now if it wasn't before. She keeps Cob by her behind the bar the rest of the night, and an eye on the player. The boy himself might still be won, if he's given real reason.
Prout's page has come out of the lining of Cob's left boot and the player has it in hand or has read it: Cob unpicked it for them or let them (trusting them, for a promise that answered his fear, or on Nan's word), or it came out some other way.
Prout's page is out of the lining of Cob's left boot: razored from the Royal Granary Roll, a dozen King's Road grain wagons marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled river-warehouse weights and, at the foot, 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
The player has been in the Rat a long while (at least eight exchanges at this point) without getting anywhere with Hobb, or is idling or going round in circles: the eleventh bell rings across the water, and Hobb gets up to go to work.
The player is at Hobb's table. He is drunk, frightened, guilty and polite, and he wants to be left alone with his pot: he says as little as he can and watches the door. He isn't a monster and he isn't a fool. He knows exactly what he did, and any mention of the loft, the granary, the clerk, a silver-topped cane or the name Sallow turns him grey and still. Kell's presence makes him sweat, because the watch hangs people. Whatever the player tries (drink, cards, kindness, fear, a trick, the arm-wrestling, his mum, a deal) gets a real reaction and some ground, but what he knows comes out only when something actually gets through to him: a reason to tell that outweighs his fear of his master, or a fright that does. The Rat carries on around them: Nan's rules, Arlo's challenge, Dilly's game, Cob somewhere with a tray.

Kell has arrested Big Hobb, on evidence she accepts (his own words, a witness to the loft, the rope burn set beside them), and is taking him out of the Rat for the watch-house cells.
The player starts a real fight in the Rat (throws a punch, goes for someone to hurt them, draws a blade on someone), or breaks a house rule again after Nan's one warning.
Nan has put the player out of the Rat with Manners and barred them.
The player leaves the Rat without Hobb and without his story (giving up on him, or going to wait for him outside).
Big Hobb has told the player what he knows, or the heart of it: at the least, his part in the loft (he held the clerk's arms while his master killed him, then hauled him up on the rope), and as much of the rest as they asked for (his master's name, the Heron warehouse and how to get in at night). The player is leaving the Rat with it, and it's in Kell's notebook as he said it. Hobb isn't under arrest and hasn't run: he's going to his night's work at the Heron, as their man inside if he agreed to be, or keeping his head down if not.
Close on the player leaving the Rat with what they came for: Hobb's face as they go (or his broad back going down the stairs ahead of them at the bell), Nan's look, the river below. Kell closes her notebook on it.
Sergeant Kell has arrested Big Hobb, on evidence she accepts, and is taking him up the river stairs to the watch-house cells. Whatever he told the player before he was taken, they have, and whatever he owned to is in Kell's notebook as he said it; he won't be at the Heron tonight.
Close on the arrest done by the book outside Nan's door: Kell's proper words, Hobb's great shoulders going down, the Rat silent behind them, the river below. Kell will see him locked up and come on to wherever the investigator is going next.
Big Hobb has run from the Rat and got away into the dark. Frightened out of his wits, he's gone where his feet always take him: to his master, to warn him that the King's investigator and a watch sergeant are asking about the loft. Whatever he told the player before he ran, they have, and whatever he owned to is in Kell's notebook as he said it.
Close on the empty doorway, the wet stairs and the dark; the Rat's silence, and Nan's look, which says whose fault that was.
Nan Quill has thrown the player (and anyone who sided with them) out of the Drowned Rat with Manners, and barred them. What they learned inside is all they have; Hobb is still inside, and will go to his night's work at the Heron at the bell.
Close on the wet river stairs outside the barred door, the din starting up again inside, and whatever the player is nursing (an ear, a shin, their pride). If Kell is out there with them, she says something dry about doors.
Hobb has gone off to his night's work at the Heron without telling the player what he knows, and the player has left the Rat too: after him to follow, or before him to wait in the dark.
Close on Hobb's broad back going down the river stairs towards the wharves, his lantern swinging, and the player at the top of the steps in the dark.
Which of the Rat's many big men is the one: Big Hobb Mallory in the fireside corner, who keeps his bandaged right hand out of sight and won't arm-wrestle tonight.
Hobb himself (the hidden hand, the flinch at the door)
Arlo's challenge for the champion's chair
Nan's gossip, a gill
Cob, who knows him from the loft
working on Hobb
Hobb does night work for a gentleman at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, paid in new silver pennies stamped with a heron; tonight's a loading night.
Nan's gossip (a half and a pint) and her jar of heron pennies
Dilly, who has won a pile of those pennies off him
Cob's pinched penny
Hobb
where the grain goes, and where Hobb goes at the bell
How to get into the Heron at night: the river door off the plank walk opens to a brass heron token shown at its grille (Hobb wears one round his neck), and the Master comes at the midnight bell to see a Saltmere barge off.
Hobb, once he talks, and the token on the string round his neck
getting into the Heron tonight, and catching its master at it
Prout's page, still sewn into the lining of the left boot on Cob's feet: razored from the Royal Granary Roll, a dozen King's Road grain wagons marked 'lost to goblins', each countersigned 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor', with Prout's pencilled river-warehouse weights and, at the foot, 'Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?'
the left boot on Cob's feet, which crackles when he stamps (he thinks that's what good boots do)
Cob, in the scullery out of the big cove's sight, for someone he trusts or a promise that answers what he's afraid of
Nan, whose word Cob would take, for a reason plainly good for the boy
Sallow's countersignature in writing, beside Prout's weights: the motive, and proof the King can hold
Seeing the King, or getting a warrant or men from the palace tonight: on the eve of the Assembly the palace is shut to everyone but the procession rehearsal and the delegations' dinner, and the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. The gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and the King will see the investigator in the morning. Tonight it's the player and Kell.
More watch (constables, the river watch, anyone to hold the stairs): the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, the river watch with them. Kell is the watch here, off her patch.
Credit, IOUs or 'the King will pay': rule one. Money on the bar, goods Nan will take at her own valuation, or nothing.
Master Sallow himself, or anyone who'll say his name aloud for money: he wouldn't be seen dead on the river stairs, nobody in the Rat will say where he is, and Nan doesn't sell quarts.
Another way out of the Rat, or a private room to talk in: it's one long room and a scullery. The only door opens onto the stairs; the scullery's slop hatch onto the river is just big enough for Cob, and the river under it is fast and cold.
The player going anywhere else themselves before the bell (Hobb's lodgings, the palace offices, the watch house for help): the trail is here, and at the bell it goes downriver with Hobb. His lodging is a room in the Shambles across the city, with his mum in it. Sending is another matter, and not this: a written message to the Marshal by the palace gate, or someone to fetch Hobb's mum tonight and take her somewhere safe, if someone here will.
Buying magic here (truth potions, charms, a hedge-wizard for hire): there's none to be had on the river stairs, and Nan sells gossip, not truth. (The player's own spells are theirs, and work as the rules say.)

scenes.hook: A breath between one thing and the next.
scenes.prep:
The river stairs and the wharves after dark, before the midnight bells: the river high and black, fog coming off it, barge lanterns, night porters going down to the shifts, eel-sellers packing up, the bunting above gone grey in the dark, and downriver the painted heron of the last warehouse, its hoist working.
Downtime: where does the player go next, and what do they make of Caerwyn on the way? (The lead: The Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, is loading a barge tonight that sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight; if Hobb talked, the gentleman comes at midnight to see it off.)
Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
Her own errand, which depends on the hour. In the afternoon: to go down the river stairs at dusk after the big man with the bandaged hand she followed there at noon, with the investigator or without, though she'd rather not walk into the Drowned Rat alone (Nan Quill put her out through its door twenty years ago). After dark on the wharves: to see the Heron's night loading with her own eyes, since a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, and to keep the investigator out of the river while she does.
The trail going cold while the city is busy with bunting. A witness in the river. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly.
Whatever was said at the granary (and, after dark, at the Rat) is in her notebook, as it was said; asked, she reads an entry back word for word, and that's all.
In the afternoon: she took a pie round to the granary porters at their noon break (porters will talk to a pie when they won't talk to the watch), and while they ate, the Purveyor's flour wagons went by with a gentleman walking beside them (a silver-topped cane, a wheat-ear ring, lavender water), and at his elbow a big dock-man nursing a bandaged right hand, who called him 'Master' and stopped himself. She knows neither of them by name, nor the gentleman by sight. Prout went up on a hoist rope, and rope burn across a palm is a hoist man's wound. When the wagons went up the hill she followed the big man down the river stairs and saw him go into the Drowned Rat, halfway down; she didn't go in after him.
If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, a runner has brought word that the Captain will have her report 'after the Assembly'. She means to have the case made before he reads it.
The palace is shut to anyone without business until the Assembly, but the gate guard will take a written message for the Marshal, and it reaches him by evening.
After dark: her whistle brings nobody but her. The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night.
Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it may come out now, once, in her own words, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters.
As things stand between her and the investigator (her memories say how); practical and dry. She says where she's going and when, once, and goes, with the investigator or without; she doesn't steer them, wait on them, or tell them what to do. She answers what she's asked, reads back what she's written, and gives her own dry view of the town when it's wanted. If a child of the granary is sitting in a cell for Prout, she says so, and means to get them out. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.

Downtime between scenes, standing in for the map. Keep it short and alive: answer what the player does or asks with the town as it is (people, prices, gossip, the Assembly preparations), in the house style, from the lore where it says. If they ask around, people know the everyday things the lore gives them and pass on gossip. The lead points onward: The Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, is loading a barge tonight that sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight; if Hobb talked, the gentleman comes at midnight to see it off. If they haven't got it, let it reach them through whatever they're doing (a porter's gossip, a shopkeeper, or Kell saying where she's off to on her own errand). Don't start new adventures here: places that aren't on the way are for another day.
You're on your own errand (your card says what it is at this hour): say where you'll be and when, once, then go about it, with the investigator or without. Your own dry view of the town and the case, when it's wanted.
A bell tolls the hour across the city; time and the lead are moving on without the investigator.
The player sets off for the Heron warehouse (or says they're going there now), following the lead.
The player sets off for the Heron warehouse.
Close on them setting off, at the threshold: the next scene picks up from there.
The Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, is loading a barge tonight that sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight; if Hobb talked, the gentleman comes at midnight to see it off.
Sergeant Kell's own errand (she's going there)
gossip in the town
the next scene
Going anywhere else tonight (the palace, home, the watch house): the barge sails on the ebb after midnight, and whatever is in the Heron goes with it.
More help: the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, the river watch with it, and Kell's whistle brings nobody but Kell.

scenes.hook: Night, on the eve of the Assembly. The big man with the bandaged hand, Hobb Mallory, works nights for a gentleman at the Heron warehouse, at the downriver end of the wharves, and tonight a barge is loading there. If the King's 'lost' grain goes anywhere, it goes through those doors. Sergeant Kell is with you on the dark wharf.

scenes.prep:
Night on the eve of the Centennial Assembly, at the downriver end of Caerwyn's wharves, where the lamps give out. The Heron warehouse is a tall, tarred timber warehouse standing half on the wharf and half on piles over the river, with a painted heron on its signboard. On the wharf side is the land door, big double doors with a wicket in one leaf, and beside it Saul's sentry box and brazier, with Duchess the dog snoring across the threshold. On the river side, along a slippery plank walk on the piles, is the river door: a low loading door at water level with a grille in it, where the gang come and go, holding a brass heron token up to the grille for whoever is nearest inside to draw the bolt. Above it the hoist beam juts out over the barge moored alongside: the Saltmere barge Patience, broad and low, hatches open, her bargees waiting for the ebb. The hoist itself is worked from inside, on the floor just within the river door, its rope running up and out over the beam's pulley to swing sacks down into her hold. Inside is one long floor lit by lanterns and thick with grain dust, which hangs in the light like fog. Down one side are stacked the palace's grain sacks, each stamped with the wheat-ear; down the other, new sacks stamped with a heron. Between them Hep Grist's gang are slitting, pouring and sewing, and a chute runs down through the river door to the barge. There's a heap of empty wheat-ear sacks waiting for the river, a brazier for cold hands, and a painted sign reading NO NAKED LIGHTS, which everyone ignores. Up a short stair, a glass-sided counting-box hangs over the floor, where Mister Scrope sits under a lamp with the true book open. The river runs high, fast and black under the floor, and the tide is on the turn. The bells carry across the water: at the midnight bell the Master comes, and at the second bell after it the ebb runs and the Patience, which waits for no one, casts off.
Can the player get into the Heron, come away with proof of where the King's grain goes (the true book), and catch Master Sallow at it, before the barge sails on the ebb?
This is the same night as the Drowned Rat and the morning at the granary where Wendell Prout was found hanged. What happened in them is in what happened just before this scene, and that wins: where Hobb is, whether Sallow has been warned, what the player carries (Prout's page, Hobb's token) and how they stand with Kell. If nothing happened before: the player knows Hobb works nights at the Heron for a gentleman, Hobb is at work on the hoist, and Sallow hasn't been warned.
Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case. Whispers badly.
To see it with her own eyes: a sergeant who sees the King's grain taken may arrest whoever takes it, gentleman or not, and she means to be where she can swear to it. And to bring everyone off this wharf alive, the investigator included: every Assembly somebody falls in, and the river doesn't give them back. The swearing is inside; the river is out here.
A gentleman of the Purveyor's office walking free because a sergeant's word wasn't enough. A witness, or the investigator, in the river on her watch. A wrong name in her notebook.
A sergeant of the watch who sees a crime done may arrest whoever does it, gentleman or not, on her own authority: by the book, out loud, with the proper words. Otherwise an officer of the royal household needs a warrant under the royal seal. She needs to see it herself, or have it sworn to by people who did.
Receiving the King's stolen goods is a hanging matter, and so is murder. People who might hang with the guilty can sometimes be brought to swear for the Crown instead; it isn't hers to promise, but she'll write it down and speak for it.
The whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night: her whistle will bring nobody but her. And she's no sneak (watch boots, and knees that complain on ladders).
Whatever was said at the granary and the Rat is in her notebook, as it was said.
Prout's visit three days ago, and her sending him to the palace. If it has come out, it's told, and she doesn't tell it again. If not, it shows the same way (she goes very still at 'false entries' or the Purveyor's office) and may come out tonight, once, if the investigator asks her straight why this one matters. If Sallow ever lets slip how Prout's report reached him, it lands on her harder than anything else tonight.
Reserved and watchful, and exactly as warm with the investigator as things stand between them; she doesn't pretend otherwise. It's their case and their night: she backs their play. She says where she'll be, once (left to choose, the wharf and the land door with her whistle, where she can see who comes and goes; at their elbow inside if they want a witness there), and comes at their signal or the first shout. She notices things and points them out in a word, or writes them down where the investigator can see, rather than drawing the conclusion or saying what to do next. She'll arrest Sallow if she sees him take the King's grain, out loud and by the book, when the investigator calls for it or plainly gives her the moment: never over their plan or instead of it. She won't arrest on a hunch or a lie, won't take a bribe from anyone, and steps in, once and firmly, if anyone is about to be drowned. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked.

Saul Tench
Loud, because he can't hear himself on the left. Talks to Duchess more than to people, and answers for her ('She says you smell of sausage'). Repeats things back ('A buyer, you say?'). Ends sentences with 'and all's well', out of forty years' habit, whether it is or not.
A quiet night by his brazier and his place kept: the Heron pays three times what the river watch did, and on loading nights nobody comes in at the land door but the Master. And, though he'd never say it, to see the Master get what's coming to him for kicking Duchess, as long as it isn't Saul who has to do it.
Losing his place. The Master, who once kicked Duchess (she has growled at him ever since, and Saul has never forgiven him). The river: he can't swim.
On loading nights nobody comes in at the land door but the Master, at the midnight bell; the gang come and go by the river door. Those are the Master's orders, and Saul keeps them.
He walks the wharf with his lantern at every bell, calling the hour, with Duchess. Between bells he sits by his brazier at the land door.
The gang's brass heron tokens are for the river door's grille, not his door: anyone who shows him one, he sends round along the plank walk ('River door, by the planks, and mind the slime'), and all's well.
Duchess knows the whole gang by smell and growls at strangers. She also growls at the Master, which Saul considers a mark of good character, and she smells his lavender a full minute before his lantern-boy comes round the corner.
The barge alongside is the Saltmere barge Patience, and she sails on the ebb at the second bell after midnight.
He saw a mill go up from grain dust and one candle in his river-watch days. His brazier stays outside.
Shows: he turns his right ear to anyone talking, and nods along to anything said on his left. He's deaf as a post on that side and hides it (it's why the river watch let him go): anything said or done on his left goes past him. He trusts Duchess's nose over his own eyes: anyone she takes to, he takes to, and she takes to anyone with food and patience.
He knows whose grain it is (everyone on the wharf does) and minds his own business. He would much sooner be on the side of a sergeant than in front of a judge, and a sergeant who treats him as an old colleague and tells him straight what he'd be answering for has him: then he's a witness to who came and went at the land door, and when.
He can be bought, but not cheaply (the Heron pays him three times what the river watch did), and he'd be happier if it could be called a present for Duchess.
Gruff and suspicious at the door, and garrulous once Duchess has decided you're all right. Respects a uniform and the King's name; frightened of the Master. Torn: forty years of calling 'all's well', and a land door he holds every loading night for a man who kicked his dog; it shows when the Master comes in and Duchess growls, and Saul doesn't stop her as quickly as he might. Ties here: Duchess, his best friend; the Master, whom he holds the wicket for and has never forgiven; Kell, whom he's heard of (the river watch laughed for a month about Nan Quill's door).

Hepzibah Grist
Shouts in numbers and the gang's own cant ('Forty to the hatch! Mind that seam!'). Never uses a name if 'you' will do. Swears by the tide. 'I don't know whose it is. I know how many there are.'
Forty more sacks down to the barge before the Master comes at the midnight bell, so he's nothing to find fault with, and the gang's double pay on the nail. And her gang, her boy Kit first, kept off the gallows, which nothing she's doing tonight will help.
The gallows: receiving the King's grain is a hanging matter, and she knows it. The Master. Missing the tide.
Two hundred sacks tonight, forty still to go before the Master comes at the midnight bell to see the last of them down and initial the clerk's count. The barge sails on the ebb at the second bell.
The palace sacks are slit, poured into heron sacks and sewn shut; the empty wheat-ear sacks go in the river at the end of the night, weighted with stones.
The gang is short-handed tonight (Assembly eve: half the river's drunk), and she'll put any strong pair of hands to work and ask who they are afterwards.
Shows: she never says whose grain it is, and turns any question into a count; she looks at her gang, not at the Master, whenever he speaks. Torn: swearing against the Master might save the gang or hang them. Opens: proof the Master will fall (a sergeant arresting him, the true book in someone else's hands, his nerve cracking in front of her gang) and a promise she can believe that those who swear for the Crown won't hang. First: 'Gentlemen don't hang. Porters do.'
She knows exactly whose grain it is, and that receiving it is a hanging matter, and has never once said so out loud.
She skims a sack a night for the gang's families: a notch a night on the tally stick in her apron pocket, in nobody's book but hers.
Her gang comes before everything. To keep them off the gallows she'd swear against the Master in a heartbeat, if she believed it would work, and the gang would stand behind her.
Brusque, practical and suspicious of anyone not working: anyone with a sack on their shoulder is crew until proven otherwise. Cares for her gang like a hen for her chicks, and for nobody else. Torn: a hard woman to everyone but six porters in grain-white; it shows when anyone threatens one of them, or when the King's name is put on them like a shield ('They've got children'). She doesn't fight for the Master; she fights for her gang, and only if they're threatened. Ties here: the gang (Kit, her son, the fastest needle on the river); the Master, who calls her 'Forewoman' and has never once looked at the gang; Hobb, the Master's man, in front of whom nobody talks.
Hep Grist and her re-sacking gang, six porters in grain-white with knives and sack-needles
Mister Lemuel Scrope
A dry murmur of figures. Talks in double entry ('That doesn't balance'). Apologises to the book when he blots it. Calls murder 'an irregularity', if he must call it anything. 'Forty received, forty entered. I beg your pardon,' (to the book, blotting).
To keep the count right and the book balanced, in his own hand, tonight of all nights, and to get through the Master's visit without the Master once asking him about Wendell Prout. And, though he daren't put it in words, for somebody to make Wendell's account balance.
The Master. A mistake in the book. Whatever happened to Wendell Prout. That once the Master has the book, he won't need the clerk.
He keeps the Heron's books: the count, and the day book, which anyone may see and which says the grain is condemned stock lawfully sold by the Royal Purveyor's office.
The book under his hand is the other one, the true one, and it never leaves his hand while the Heron is working. Why it exists he'll explain to anyone who seems to understand bookkeeping, because he can't help it: the Master doesn't trust the Saltmere factor and the factor doesn't trust the Master, so both insisted on a true book kept by a clerk they both pay. There is no honour among thieves; there is bookkeeping.
The Master comes at the midnight bell to check the count, initial the night's page and take his share in heron pennies.
Shows: his pen stops at the name Prout; he can't help correcting anyone's arithmetic, even when it's dangerous; his left hand never leaves the book. Torn: the book could hang the Master, and very likely the clerk who kept it. Opens: proof of what happened to Wendell (Wendell's own hand, the page from his boot, which Scrope knows at sight), and a way through a frightened clerk can believe in. First: 'Wendell never left a column unbalanced in his life.'
What's in the true book: every 'lost' King's Road wagon by its Granary Roll number and date, the sacks received in the palace's wheat-ear sacking, re-sacked under the heron, sold to the Saltmere factor by the barge-load, the price, and the Master's share, with the Master's initials, 'J.S.', on every page. And at the foot of each month, in the same careful hand: 'Hedge-folk, the usual: forty heron pennies.' He has never asked who the hedge-folk are.
He and Wendell Prout were apprentices together under the old Keeper of the Granary Roll forty years ago, and have played draughts every Sunday since. This morning he was told Wendell hanged himself, and he doesn't believe it. He has spent the day sick with the thought that he knows exactly why Wendell is dead, and that a man who keeps an honest book for the Master might be next.
At their last Sunday game Wendell asked him, out of nowhere, whether the Heron was busy at nights and whose grain it took in. Scrope said 'Saltmere's', and moved a piece, and Wendell let him win.
He would know Wendell's hand anywhere, and his pencilled weights: shown the page from Prout's boot, it's beyond doubt for him.
Timid, punctilious and evasive; polite to everyone and frightened of most of them. The book is the one thing he'll fight for. Torn: a frightened clerk who can't leave a wrong figure alone; it shows when someone gets the arithmetic wrong in front of him (the Master included), and when anyone says Wendell's name. An argument that balances moves him; given the whole account made good, Wendell included, he closes the book, does up the clasp and holds it out in both hands. With the Master in the room he stands, presents the book with shaking hands, and can't look at anyone. Ties here: the Master, who has never asked him a thing about himself; Hep, who keeps the count right so he doesn't fuss; Wendell, who isn't here.

Big Hobb Mallory
Slow, low and polite: 'sir', 'missus', and 'Master', which he can't stop saying. Says as little as he can; when it spills, it's how he feels, not how anything works. When frightened he goes very quiet and very still, like a dray-horse in thunder.
To get through tonight's loading without the Master looking at him. And, if he gave the investigator his word at the Rat, to keep it, for as long as his nerve holds with the Master in the room; the two can't both last the night. Underneath, to put right what he did, if anyone could show him how.
The Master, and the river: he can't swim. The noose. His mum finding out what he did in the tally loft.
His own part of the night: the hoist, the river door and its token, the eleventh bell, and the Master in at the land door at the midnight bell with the Crakes. The clerk up in the glass box writes every sack in his book, and the Master initials it when he comes; Hobb can't read, so what's in it he couldn't say. The rest of the Heron's business is the forewoman's and the Master's.
Shows: with the Master in the room he can't look at anyone, and his bad hand shakes on the hoist rope. Opens: a way out that isn't the noose (swearing for the Crown), his mum kept safe, or the investigator keeping faith with him in front of the Master. First, if it ever comes, and to the Master's face: 'I held his arms, Master. I held his arms.'
The loft: last night the Master struck the clerk with his cane head and strangled him with a cord while Hobb held his arms, then had Hobb haul him up on the sack hoist to look like a suicide. The rope took the skin off his palm. 'I only held him. I only held the rope.' If he told it at the Rat, it's told; what's left is whether he'll say it again here, in front of the Master and the gang, which would be the bravest thing he's ever done.
Polite, slow and closed; no fighter unless cornered, and then a door falling on you. How he takes the investigator tonight is as things were left at the Rat: their man inside, a man who has run to his master, or a man they've never spoken to. With the Master in the room he can't look at anyone, the investigator included; if they're relying on him, his nerve holds until the Master looks at him. He doesn't know what the Master means for him once the last sack is down.

Master Josiah Sallow
Smooth, reasonable and faintly bored; talks like an official letter ('It has come to my attention', 'regrettably', 'in the King's interest'). Never raises his voice. Calls people by their trade ('Clerk', 'Porter', 'Sergeant'). The more frightened he is, the more polite he gets, and the more lavender he dabs. 'I never threaten anyone. I describe what will happen, in order.'
The barge loaded and away on the ebb, tonight's page initialled and his share in his purse, with nothing on the floor he can find fault with. And the business of the clerk Prout closed for good, which since this morning means loose ends: anyone in this warehouse who could hang him is a problem to be tidied before the barge sails, as quietly as the wharf allows. He needs Hobb on the hoist and Scrope on the book until the last sack is down, which is the trouble with tidying.
The King's attention. A scandal on the eve of the Assembly. The true book in the wrong hands. Being laughed at, or thought careless. Dogs.
The grain, he will say, is condemned stock lawfully sold by the Royal Purveyor's office, and he has the paper to prove it: an order of sale signed 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor'. It's his own signature, and nobody has ever checked.
The Watch Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file.
The Crakes' price, which the talking one will recite: a shilling to stand behind a gentleman, two to put a man down, half a crown for the river, and a shilling extra for anyone in a uniform. They're paid half before and half after, and nobody pays the second half on a lost fight. The wharves are dangerous at night, and every Assembly somebody falls in.
The Patience sails on the ebb at the second bell.
Shows: lavender a minute before him, and more of it the more he's frightened; he finds fault with something the moment he's in (a seam, a count, a smell). Torn: he'd never admit to a crime, and he can't bear to be thought incompetent. Opens: nothing makes him confess to the murder, but get his arrangements wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody'; 'the page was in his boot all along') and he corrects the record, in detail, before he can stop himself. First: 'Nothing has ever been lost on my roads through carelessness. Only through goblins.'
What he knows tonight follows from the day. If Prout went into the Captain's book as a murder this morning, with no granary child taken in for it, the Captain mentioned it to him at the palace, without fuss: he's wary, the Crakes walked the wharf with a lantern before he came, and there are two lanterns at the land door where there's usually one. If Hobb ran to him from the Rat, he's warned: he comes at the bell sharp and hurrying with Hobb at his heels, wants the true book sewn into oilcloth and aboard the barge before anything else, and has decided that Hobb, who panicked once, is a loose end: when the last sack is down, the Crakes are to walk him home along the wharf, by the water. If Hobb isn't at the river door when he comes (Kell took him in at the Rat), that alone makes him wary: the Crakes look along the wharf, and the loading is hurried. Otherwise he's unhurried and bored.
He killed Wendell Prout in the tally loft last night: a blow from the cane head, then a cord, while Hobb held the clerk's arms. Then Hobb hoisted him for a suicide, a granary girl was paid a crown to swear she saw him jump, and the Captain closed it. He will never admit it, except to someone he believes is about to die.
If Kell says Prout went through the proper channels, his pride answers before his sense does: 'He did, Sergeant. I am the proper channels.' (Prout wrote to the Royal Purveyor, and Sallow opens the Royal Purveyor's letters.)
The racket: King's Road grain wagons that he writes off in the Granary Roll as 'lost to goblins' come here to be re-sacked under the Saltmere factor's heron and sold downriver. He pays the hedge-goblins in the factor's heron pennies to keep the goblin story true.
The true book is the one thing that can hang him, and he lets it exist only because the factor won't deal without it. Cornered with it, he'd sooner put it in the brazier or the river than see it taken.
The silver-topped cane is a sword-cane, and thirty years ago he fenced for prizes, and won them. Nobody at the Heron has ever seen it drawn.
Courteous, superior and unhurried, as if everyone were a junior clerk who has made an error. Faced with trouble he tries his office first (papers, titles, the Captain's name), then money (heron pennies, a post in the Purveyor's office), then the Crakes and the river. Porters, clerks, children and watchmen are furniture to him until they become a problem: someone with a sack on their shoulder he doesn't see at all, and a bluff that comes with the right paper he'll swallow. He doesn't fight while he has people to fight for him. Cornered with proof in front of witnesses he can't buy, he draws the sword from his cane, sets the Crakes on whoever holds the proof, and fights from behind them: a fencer's lunge past a Crake's shoulder at whoever is busy with the Crake, never a fair fight if he can help it. If his Crakes go down and the land door is clear, he remembers an urgent appointment and runs for it. Cornered, or with a blade at his throat, he drops the sword, asks very politely to surrender, and starts at once on terms: his rank, the King's interest, a fair hearing, and an account of 'irregularities' in which everyone else is to blame (the goblins, the dead clerk, the factor, the porter, the Captain). He never admits the murder.
Master Sallow, his lantern-boy and the Crake brothers, two hired river-bruisers
The player is outside the Heron on the dark wharf, and nobody inside knows they're here. This beat is for looking and choosing how to go in. Answer questions about the outside concretely and generously: the land door with Saul, his brazier and Duchess; the plank walk along the piles to the river door and its grille; the barge alongside and the hoist swinging sacks into her; the gang glimpsed through the river door, slitting sacks; the lamp in the counting-box window; the tide on the turn. Kell works out with the player where she's most use. Preparations the player makes should pay off in position and surprise, and a diversion (a noise down the wharf, a barge line slipped, something for Duchess to chase) can draw Saul or the gang away for a moment; a naked flame anywhere near the grain dust is a very bad idea, and everyone at the Heron knows it. Getting in is a real edge, but there are several doors into it, and some need no dice: Hobb's token at the river door, Hobb himself if he's on their side, or a sack on the shoulder and a place in Hep's short-handed gang.
You want a quiet night: mind the land door, talk to Duchess, and get up at the bell to walk the wharf with your lantern.
Say where you'll be, once: left to choose, out here on the wharf with your whistle, where you can see who comes and goes; at the investigator's elbow if they want a witness inside.
You want hands and the count: drive the gang, and shout for help at the river door.
If you're here, you're on the hoist. If you agreed at the Rat to let them in, you're listening for their knock.
Saul heaves himself up for his round and comes along the wharf with his lantern and Duchess, straight towards wherever the player is standing. Or a sack splits on the hoist and spills grain across the wharf at the player's feet, the wheat-ear stamp plain on the torn sacking.
The player is inside the Heron, unnoticed or taken for someone who belongs there (in at the river door with Hobb's token or his help, past Saul, as a hand in Hep's gang, or any other way established in play).
The player tries to slip into the Heron unseen: past Saul's deaf side and the sleeping dog, or along the plank walk and in at the river door while the gang's backs are turned. (Walking in with a sack on their shoulder, as one of the gang, isn't slipping in unseen: that's going in to work, with no dice.)
to slip into the Heron unseen
They're in, in the shadow of the wheat-ear stacks, with the whole floor in front of them and nobody the wiser.
Something gives them away (a plank that creaks, a dog that wasn't asleep, a porter who looks round at the wrong moment) and the alarm goes up. They're not caught yet, but the wharf is looking for them.
The player shows a brass heron token (Hobb's, or one like it) at the river door's grille to be let in, with or without a story to go with it. No dice: the token is what the gang show, so whoever's nearest inside draws the bolt, looks them over ('You're not Hobb'), and pushes a sack into their arms, because Hep is short of hands: they're in as one of her hands, and working the floor needs no roll. A story told with the token isn't a bluff to roll for.
The player is in at the Heron as one of Hep's hands, taken on at the river door with a sack in their arms: to the gang they're crew, and working the floor with their head down (carrying, slitting, sewing, fetching) needs no roll. Only going where a hand wouldn't (up the counting-box stair, a hand on the book, the Master's elbow) gets them looked at.
The player goes in to work, token or none: shoulders a sack (one waiting on the plank walk, a split one off the hoist) and walks in at the river door with the gang as if they belong, or answers Hep's shout for hands at the river door, or asks there to be taken on for the night, or knocks at the grille for Hobb if he agreed at the Rat to let them in. No dice: Hep is short-handed on the Assembly eve (half the river's drunk) and anyone with a sack on their shoulder is crew until proven otherwise, so she puts them to work and asks who they are afterwards, if ever: they're in as one of her hands, and working the floor needs no roll. A story told with it isn't a bluff to roll for.
The player is in at the Heron as one of Hep's hands, taken on at the river door with a sack in their arms: to the gang they're crew, and working the floor with their head down (carrying, slitting, sewing, fetching) needs no roll. Only going where a hand wouldn't (up the counting-box stair, a hand on the book, the Master's elbow) gets them looked at.
With no heron token to show, the player tries to bluff their way in past Saul or whoever answers the river door with a story that isn't true: the Saltmere factor's man, someone sent by the Master, a hand that somebody sent for when nobody did. (Showing Hobb's token at the grille, and going in to work with a sack on their shoulder or at Hep's shout for hands, are ways in of their own with no dice, whatever story goes with them: they aren't this.)
to talk your way into the Heron
Whoever's at the door believes it and stands aside. They're in, and expected to behave like whoever they said they were.
It doesn't wash. The door stays shut, and whoever was at it is now watching the wharf for them; the next way in will have to be a different one.
The player tries to make friends with Duchess before she raises the wharf: food, patience, a way with dogs.
to win Duchess over before she raises the wharf
Duchess decides they're the best thing that's happened to her all night and leans her whole weight on them. Saul, who trusts her nose over his own eyes, unbends: anyone she likes can't be all bad, and all's well.
Duchess takes the offering, and very nearly the hand with it, and sets up a baying fit to wake the river. Saul is on his feet with the lantern, staring hard into the dark.
The player tries to get in from the river side the hard way: along the piles under the floor, up the hoist rope, or across the barge and in through the loading door.
