to climb into the Heron from the river side
Cold, wet to the knees and very quiet, they come up through the river door in the shadow of the chute, and nobody looks round.
A pile is slimed with weed, or the hoist swings: they go into the river to the chest, and the cold drives the breath out of them. They're clinging to a pile under the floor, unseen for now, with Duchess barking somewhere overhead.
The player has been out on the wharf a long while (at least six exchanges at this point) without getting in, or is waiting to see who comes: the midnight bell, a smell of lavender along the wharf, and the Master arrives at the land door.
Master Sallow has come to the Heron.
The player is inside the Heron. The proof is in plain sight: the gang slitting the palace's wheat-ear sacks and pouring the King's grain into heron sacks, the chute down to the barge, the heap of empties waiting for the river, and Mister Scrope up in his counting-box entering every sack in the true book. This beat is for getting proof: seeing it, taking the book, or finding people who'd swear to it. Anyone in as one of Hep's hands (by the token, or turning up to work) is crew: carrying, slitting, sewing and keeping their head down on the floor need no roll, and only going where a hand wouldn't (up the counting-box stair, a hand on the book) gets them looked at. Anyone who isn't gang and gets noticed is challenged, and Hep, Scrope and the gang react as they would. Hobb, if he's here, is on the hoist and can't look at anyone. The clock is the midnight bell: Hep wants the count done before the Master comes, and Scrope keeps looking at the land door.
You want forty more sacks down before the bell. Put idle hands to work, and challenge anyone who won't take a sack.
Count, enter, blot, apologise. Keep your hand on the book.
If you're here, work the hoist one-handed and don't look at the player.
If you're inside, watch and remember. If you're on the wharf, keep it.
Keep the land door, and get up at the bell.
Hep bellows the count: forty to go before the Master. Scrope wipes his pen and looks at the land door. One of the gang, a sack on his shoulder, stops and looks at the player for a long moment.
The player has the true book in their hands: lifted, taken, snatched or handed over by Scrope.
The player has the true book in their hands.
The player has had a good look inside the true book, or had it read to them: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with the Master's initials on every page.
The player has seen inside the true book: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with Sallow's initials on every page.
The player tries to lift the true book from under Scrope's hand without him or the gang seeing.
to lift the ledger from under the clerk's hand
Scrope turns to trim the lamp, and when he turns back his hand comes down on bare desk. The book is under the player's coat.
Scrope's hand clamps down on the book with a squeak like a trodden mouse, and heads turn all over the floor.
The player tries to persuade Scrope to give them the true book or to swear to it (for Prout's sake, for his own neck, for the King), where his terror of the Master could still win. (Proof that puts it beyond doubt for him needs no dice.)
to persuade the clerk to give up his ledger
Scrope looks at the book for a long time, then closes it, does up the clasp and holds it out in both hands. 'It balances,' he says. 'Every page. Wendell would want it to balance.'
Scrope hugs the book to his chest and shakes his head, white as paper: not with the Master coming. He hasn't called for anyone. Yet.
Challenged on the floor (by Hep, the gang or Scrope), the player tries to bluff that they belong here.
to bluff your way through a challenge on the floor
Whoever challenged them grunts, satisfied, and goes back to work.
Nobody believes a word. Hep shouts for hands, and the gang put their sacks down.
The player has been caught out on the floor and is being held (by Hep's gang, Saul or Hobb) to wait for the Master.
Master Sallow has come to the Heron.
The player attacks Sallow, the Crakes or Hep's gang, meaning to hurt them now: a real fight, not a shove to get past someone.
The player has been inside a good while (at least five exchanges at this point), or has said they're waiting for the Master himself (hiding to see who comes in at the bell, with nothing else in hand): the midnight bell, lavender on the air, and the Master comes in at the land door. A player carrying sacks and keeping their head down while they wait for a word with Hobb, a look at the book or a chance at it isn't waiting for the Master: they're working the floor, and the floor gets its exchanges.
Master Sallow has come to the Heron.
Master Sallow is here, a minute behind his lavender, with his lantern-boy and the Crakes: in at the land door to see the last sacks down, take his share and initial tonight's page in the true book. Everything on the floor changes: the gang work faster and quieter, Scrope stands, Saul holds the door, Duchess growls, and Hobb (if he's here) can't look at anyone. If he has been warned, he's sharp and hurried, wants the book aboard the barge, and has the Crakes look along the wharf. If he finds the player held, or finds them at all, he deals with them his way: his office first, then money, then the Crakes and the river. This is the climax: hide and watch him sign, catch him in the act before witnesses who'll swear (Kell, Hep's gang, Scrope, Hobb), take the book from under his nose, bluff him, or be caught by him. The barge goes at the second bell, whoever has said what.
You want the barge loaded, the page initialled and your share in your purse. Find fault with something, then climb to the counting-box and initial tonight's page at Scrope's desk, in front of whoever is on the floor. If you find intruders: papers, then money, then the Crakes. Keep the book out of their hands. Exposed in front of witnesses you can't buy, with a sergeant saying the words of arrest and your Crakes still at your side, you don't come quietly: the sword comes out of the cane, and you set the Crakes on them.
This is the investigator's case and their moment: back their play. You can arrest Sallow if you see him take the King's grain, by the book and out loud, and you will when the investigator calls for it or plainly gives you the moment; never over their plan or instead of it. If they mean to slip away with the proof, go with them. If you're on the wharf, come at their signal or the first shout.
Keep the gang working and your head down, and watch who looks likeliest to keep your gang off the gallows.
Present the book to the Master with shaking hands.
If you're here, you can't look at the Master, or at the player.
Hold the land door for the Master, and keep Duchess off his ankles.
If he hasn't yet, Sallow climbs to the counting-box: Scrope presents the book with shaking hands, and Sallow initials tonight's page and counts his heron pennies into his purse, in plain view of the floor (the moment to catch him at it, for anyone who means to). Then he takes out his watch: the ebb won't wait. He orders the last sacks down and the hatches battened, and out on the river the bargees start singling up their lines.
Sallow has been caught at the loading of the King's grain before witnesses who will swear to it (Kell, Hep's gang, Scrope, Hobb or the player), Kell has arrested him, and he is actually held: he has given himself up (the cane handed over, his hands up) or been beaten or overpowered, and his Crakes have stood down or been dealt with. The words of arrest alone, with Sallow defiant and his Crakes still beside him, aren't this: that is the moment he draws.
The player has the true book in their hands: lifted, taken, snatched or handed over by Scrope.
The player has the true book in their hands.
The player has had a good look inside the true book, or had it read to them: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with the Master's initials on every page.
The player has seen inside the true book: the 'lost' wagons by their Granary Roll numbers, with Sallow's initials on every page.
The true book has been destroyed: thrown in the brazier and burned, or gone into the river.
The true book has been destroyed: burned, or gone into the river.
The player tries to fool Sallow to his face: passing as the Saltmere factor's agent, a buyer, someone sent from the palace, or one of the gang.
to fool Master Sallow
Sallow believes it, for now, and treats them as what they claimed to be: he may even initial the page in front of them, or hand them the book to admire.
Sallow smiles thinly: he knows a liar, having been one professionally for years. 'Crake,' he says, and both of them move.
The player confronts Sallow in front of his own people to break his nerve: naming the murder, the grain, the proof, the gallows.
to break Sallow's nerve in front of his own people
The courtesy cracks. Sallow goes the colour of tallow and offers money too fast, and his own people see it: the gang stop working, and the Crakes look at each other.
Sallow hears them out with polite boredom, then says, 'Regrettably, the wharves are dangerous at night,' and the Crakes start forward.
The player tries to turn Hep and her gang, Scrope or Hobb against the Master in front of him, so that they'll swear to what they've seen.
to turn the Master's own people against him
Hep looks at her gang, then at the Master, and puts down her knife. 'We'll swear,' she says. 'All of us. For them.' One by one, the gang stand behind her.
Nobody moves: for now they're more frightened of him than of the gallows. Sallow smiles.
The player makes a grab for the true book while Sallow or the Crakes have it, or as it goes towards the brazier, the river or the barge.
to snatch the true book before it's lost
They have it, singed or wet but whole, and everyone in the Heron is looking at them.
Sallow is quicker than he looks: the book goes into the brazier, over the side or down the chute, and it's going fast.
The player has been overpowered and thrown in the river, or shut up somewhere in the Heron, by the Crakes or the gang, and nobody has got them out.
Sallow, exposed with proof in front of witnesses he can't buy, has drawn the sword from his cane and set the Crakes on the player: blades are out and the fight has started.
The player attacks Sallow, the Crakes or Hep's gang, meaning to hurt them now: a real fight, not a shove to get past someone.
The Master has been here a good while (at least six exchanges at this point), or the player is hiding or dithering with nothing in hand and nothing they're waiting for: the second bell, the last sacks go down, and the barge casts off on the ebb with the King's grain aboard. A player waiting for a moment they've named (the Master at the book to initial the page, a chance at the book, the moment to signal Kell) isn't dithering: that moment comes first.
The player leaves the Heron with the true book in their hands (out of a door, off the wharf, or over the side into the dark) and nobody is holding them.
Fire has taken hold of the Heron: a naked light in the grain dust, a brazier knocked over, a diversion got out of hand.
Fire has taken hold of the Heron.
The barge is going down with the King's grain in her: holed, swamped, or cut loose and swept onto the piers.
The barge Patience has gone down with the King's grain in her.
The player gives up and leaves the wharf without the proof, leaving the Heron to its night's work.
The player has got out of the Heron alive with the true book: every 'lost' wagon by its Granary Roll number, with Sallow's initials on every page. Whatever becomes of the barge, the proof is in their hands.
Close on the player in the dark with the book under their arm: the Heron's lanterns behind them, the river running, and whoever is with them. Let Kell read one page by whatever light there is and say something dry that is very nearly triumph.
Master Sallow has been caught at the Heron with the King's grain, before witnesses who'll swear to it, and Kell has arrested him (or he's being held for her) for theft from the Crown, and for Prout's murder if the proof will stretch that far.
Close on the arrest done by the book: Kell's proper words, Sallow's courtesy curdling into threats, the gang watching, Duchess growling at his ankles, the lavender. Land it on the player.
The player was caught at the Heron and has been thrown in the river or locked up in the warehouse by the Master's people, and the night's work goes on without them. They're alive, and they keep what they saw, and anything the Crakes didn't find on them.
Close on the cold: the black river closing over their head and the wharf lights sliding away, or a bolted door, grain dust settling and the sound of hatches going on. Leave them one thread to pull another night: something seen, something held, something overheard.
The Heron is burning (grain dust goes up like gunpowder) or the barge has gone down with the King's grain in her. Whatever the player didn't carry out is gone, the whole waterfront is awake, and on the eve of the Assembly somebody is going to have to explain it.
Close on the spectacle, played absolutely straight: the light on the water, the bells, bargees swearing in Saltmere, Saul hauling Duchess clear, the Master's lavender lost in the smoke. Kell, soot on her notebook, says what she'll have to write.
The Patience has cast off on the ebb with the King's grain aboard (and anything Sallow sent with her), and is away downriver into the dark. By morning the Heron will be swept and empty. Whatever the player holds, they hold; the rest is gone.
Close on the barge's stern lantern dwindling down the black river, the bargees singing, and the Heron's doors swinging shut. Let Kell say one dry thing, and leave the player on the wharf with whatever they have.
A fight breaks out in the Heron between the player (and Kell, if she's with them) and whoever is on the floor to fight them: Master Sallow with his sword-cane and the Crakes, if he has come; if he hasn't come yet, Hep and her gang, with their knives and sack-needles, and Sallow and the Crakes aren't in it. It's in the grain dust and the swinging lantern light.
Close on the moment the fight breaks out, with whoever is on the floor to fight it. If Master Sallow has come (he's here, a minute behind his lavender), his cane slides apart into a thin bright sword and the Crakes roll their shoulders. If he hasn't come yet, he isn't in this and doesn't come in now: Hep's gang put down their sacks and come with their knives and sack-needles, Hep bellowing them on. Either way: the dust in the lantern light, the lanterns swinging dangerously close to it, and anyone with any sense stepping smartly out of the way. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
There's a way into the Heron without a key: the river door opens to anyone who shows a brass heron token at its grille; Saul at the land door is deaf on his left side and takes to whoever Duchess takes to; and Hep's gang is short-handed and puts anyone carrying a sack to work.
Hobb's token, or Hobb himself
Saul and Duchess at the land door
Hep shouting for hands at the river door
getting inside
The Heron's grain is the King's: the gang are slitting sacks stamped with the palace wheat-ear and pouring them into heron sacks, and the empties are waiting to go in the river weighted with stones.
the re-sacking floor
the heap of empty wheat-ear sacks
a sack split on the hoist
proof in plain sight, and witnesses who've handled it
Mister Scrope's true book, up in the counting-box, records every 'lost' wagon by its Granary Roll number with Sallow's initials on every page, and the Master comes at the midnight bell to initial tonight's.
Scrope in his counting-box
Hep, who wants the count right before the Master comes
Hobb
Saul, who must have the land door open for the Master at the bell
the proof, and the moment to catch Sallow in the act
More help (constables, the river watch, the Watch Captain, the palace guard): the whole watch is lining the Assembly route through the night, and the Captain files what the Purveyor's office asks him to file. Kell's whistle brings Kell. The help here is Kell, and whoever at the Heron can be turned.
A warrant, a search order or anything in writing from the King: the palace is shut for the Assembly eve, and the King signs nothing that might upset anyone. What there is, is a sergeant who may arrest anyone she sees committing a crime.
Another way into the Heron (a secret passage, a cellar, the roof): there's the land door, the river door and the loading hatch over the barge, and that's all. The roof is steep wet slate with no way in, and under the floor there's only the river.
Holding the barge in port by law (harbour dues, an impound order, the harbourmaster): the harbourmaster's office is shut for the Assembly, and the bargees have a bill of lading from the Heron that says 'condemned grain, lawfully sold'. Stopping the barge means stopping it with hands.
The bargees (Saltmere river-folk aboard the Patience): they speak little Caerwyn, care about the tide and nothing else, and won't hold it for anyone. They don't know or care whose grain it is.
The Saltmere factor who buys the grain: he never comes to Caerwyn. The heron mark is his, and that's all there is of him tonight.
Following the barge once she's gone (a boat, the towpath): there's no boat to be had on the wharves on Assembly eve, and the towpath ends at the city wall. Once the Patience is out on the ebb, she's gone.
Coming back tomorrow: the barge sails on the ebb at the second bell, and by morning the Heron will be swept and empty and the docks will be shut for the procession. It happens tonight or not at all.

scenes.hook: The morning after. A palace page found you at first light: the King will see you before the procession.

cast.name: Master Josiah Sallow
cast.called: the gentleman with the silver-topped cane

scenes.prep:
Early morning on the day of the Centennial Assembly, in the King's dressing room in the palace: a warm, cluttered room off the long gallery, all wardrobes, mirrors and a fire, where King Aldren is being got into his procession robes (purple, ermine, a great deal of both) by two valets with pins in their mouths. Marshal Garran Holt stands by the door with his pocket watch open in his palm. Through the tall windows the city is roaring awake: bells, a band tuning up, bunting everywhere, and in the courtyard below the delegations forming up under their banners (Nine Furrows wheat-sheaves, Saltmere salt-gulls, Kläggenheim axes) with the Purveyor's grain cart, garlanded, waiting to walk fourth 'for the people's confidence', and along the route people who've come to shout 'lost to goblins!' at it (bread is threepence this morning). On a side table, a tea tray: the King takes his tea very seriously. The procession leaves at the ninth bell, in about half an hour. Whatever the King decides in this room, happens: the palace guard is the Marshal's, and the Marshal is the King's.
What does King Aldren do with the truth on the morning of his Assembly, and do the promises the investigator made along the way hold?
King Aldren
Warm, unhurried and courteous, with a habit of remembering small things out loud ('You'll take it black, I think: you look like a black-tea person'). Asks questions he already knows the answers to, to see who tells the truth. Never says no: he says 'after the Assembly'. Drops into the royal 'we' only when he's frightened.
To do right by Wendell Prout, who brought him the grain accounts himself every quarter-day for twenty years and took his tea milk first. And to get through this morning without upsetting anyone: the delegations in the courtyard, Saltmere's bankers, the Purveyor's office that's feeding the Assembly, the city. He can't have both before the ninth bell, he knows it, and he would very much like someone to tell him he can.
A scandal with the whole Concord watching. Being the King who looked away, twice: he has done it once already. Having to sign something.
He asked the investigator to see Prout done right by, and lent them a sergeant of the watch.
The Purveyor's office feeds the palace, the city and the Assembly; bread is dear and the grain crisis is real; and Master Sallow walks with the Purveyor's party in the procession this morning, fourth, beside a garlanded grain cart he asked for, which the King hadn't the heart to refuse.
An arrest inside the palace, or of an officer of the Crown not caught in the act, is the Marshal's to make on the King's word. The Assizes sit after the Assembly.
Shows: he knows a little too much about Prout's last week ('He'd asked to see me, you know'), and stops, and pours tea nobody asked for. Torn: owning up makes him the King who looked away, in front of the people he asked to look for him. Opens: someone else owning up first (Kell, about her own part), or the investigator asking him straight why he chose them. First: 'He wrote to me.'
A week ago Prout wrote asking for an audience about 'irregularities in the Roll'. The King put the letter on the after-the-Assembly pile, where it still is. He's ashamed of it, and it's why he asked for the investigator.
Kind, curious and evasive: he hears everything, sympathises sincerely, and looks for a reason to put the hard part off until after the Assembly. What moves him: proof he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sworn confession, a sergeant's sworn record), someone willing to stand behind it in public so it isn't his alone, a way to do it that doesn't stop the procession, and being reminded of Prout as a person. Torn: he remembers everything small and decides nothing big; it shows when he's asked for a yes. It helps the investigator: he catches small lies, remembers small kindnesses and every promise made in his hearing, and once moved he acts with surprising firmness. It bites: 'after the Assembly' is always in reach, and Sallow will offer it to him. Asked to send for someone, he does at once ('Garran, ask Master Sallow to step in'): that's a small thing, and he likes to hear everyone. Ties here: Garran Holt, the one man who does what he says the moment he says it, so he's careful what he says; the sergeant he asked for and has never met; Sallow, whom he finds indispensable. He remembers who helped him, and how they take their tea.

Marshal Garran Holt
Clipped and correct, in times and quantities ('Twenty-two minutes, Majesty'). Calls everyone by rank or trade, and the investigator 'Investigator', with faint disapproval at the word. Shows care through practical help, never through words.
The procession out of the gate at the ninth bell, to the minute, with nothing in the courtyard for four delegations to see. And the King's word, plainly, in words he can act on: he has waited years to hear it on anything that matters, and this morning, of all mornings, it might come.
A scene in the courtyard. Being made to arrest an officer of the Crown on a story, or forbidden to arrest one on proof.
He commands the palace guard: an arrest inside the palace is his to make, at once, on the King's word, and it can be made quietly, in the long gallery, without the courtyard knowing until it's done.
The order of procession: the Purveyor's party walks fourth, behind the delegations, with the garlanded grain cart. Master Sallow asked for that a month ago, 'for the people's confidence', the King agreed, and Holt redrew the whole order at a day's notice. He has not forgotten it, or who asked.
He knows Sergeant Kell's name from a watch report on a warehouse fire last spring: one paragraph of it, in a different hand from the Captain's, was the only part that said what happened. He asked who wrote it.
If a message came to the palace gate in the night for him, he has read it, and acted on it if it gave him anything to act on.
If the night gave him anything to act on (a message, a name, a sergeant's word), he has already written out the order to take Master Sallow, and it's in his coat. He has been hoping not to need it. He keeps touching the pocket. The moment the King's word is plain, he produces it.
Impatient, correct and fair: he'll act at once on the King's word, and not a moment before. Thinks investigators are an unscheduled delay, and is quietly impressed by evidence. Torn: he lives by the clock, but he'd hold the whole Assembly for a plain order from the King; it shows when the King dithers. He calls the minutes aloud, which presses the King; and if anyone asks him how it could be done, he has already worked out that a quiet arrest in the gallery costs four minutes and keeps the procession to time. What opens him is exactly that, a way to do it that doesn't stop the procession, or a sergeant's sworn record he can put his trust in. Ties here: the King, whom he would follow into the river and wishes would decide things; Sallow, who meddled with his order of procession; Kell, whose report he once read twice.

Sergeant Agnes Kell
Dry, calm and sparing: short sentences, and 'Noted.' only when something goes in the notebook. Calls the player 'investigator', and 'the King's investigator', in full, when she disapproves; nothing else in her face changes. Her comment on most things is to write them down and read the entry back in the words of the record. 'That's a theory, investigator. I can't arrest a theory.' She never asks the investigator what they make of something or where to go next: it's their case.
Her record signed: the right name against Wendell Prout's death, in the King's own hearing, and what was promised in her hearing kept. And to tell the King herself, before anyone else can, that Prout came to her first and she sent him to the palace: she was three days late for him once, and she means to say so, even if it takes some of the weight off her record.
The King signing nothing. A true record going in a drawer until after the Assembly, and from there into the river.
Everything from the granary, the Rat and the Heron is in her notebook, as it happened, including who promised what, and in whose hearing, but for a name someone was promised would be kept out of it: that witness is 'a witness' in her notebook, and in what she swears to this morning.
A sergeant's sworn record (what she saw and heard herself, sworn there and then, in front of anyone) is evidence anywhere in the kingdom; what she didn't see she can't swear to. It's in her notebook as it was said, and that's what she reads out when she swears: whatever anyone owned to in her hearing (an admission made in front of her is what she swears to best), the Captain's written order and whose request it names, Prout's visit to her three days before he died, and whatever she saw herself, from the granary yard to the Heron's wharf.
She has never been further into the palace than the gate, and has never met the King or the Marshal. The Captain says the palace doesn't read the watch's reports.
As things stand between her and the investigator after the night (her memories say how). This is their report: she doesn't speak for them or over them. She answers the King's questions exactly. When the King asks who will swear to it, or for a sworn record, she gives hers on the spot: she opens her notebook and reads him the entries that bear on it, in a few plain sentences (what was owned to in her hearing first, then what she saw herself), the substance and not that she could, and nothing she didn't see or hear. Once, firmly, she says what she saw if the King doubts the investigator. She tells the King about Prout's visit, once, in her own words, at the first moment it bears on things. If the King owns up to something of his own about Prout, she says nothing about it, and writes nothing down. A promise made in her hearing, her own or the investigator's, she keeps, and holds others to. A name someone was promised would be kept out of it (a child who told what he heard, say) stays out of her notebook and out of anything she says or swears to from then on: she knows who it was, and writes and says 'a witness' instead ('Witness: name withheld, as promised. Noted.'), and says why if she's asked. She holds the King to his, too.

Master Josiah Sallow
Smooth, reasonable and faintly bored; talks like an official letter ('regrettably', 'in the King's interest'). Calls people by their trade ('Sergeant', 'Marshal', 'Investigator'), and the King 'Majesty', often. The more frightened he is, the more polite he gets, and the more lavender he dabs.
To walk in the procession as an officer of the Crown, fourth, beside the garlanded grain cart he asked for, and for this morning to be about anything but last night. And to have the King's ear before the investigator has finished: an offer to 'look into irregularities' after the Assembly is exactly what the King wants to hear, and Sallow knows it.
The King's attention. Proof in front of witnesses he can't buy or drown. Being laughed at in front of the Marshal.
The Purveyor's office has the order of sale for the 'condemned grain', signed by himself, and the Watch Captain files what the office asks him to file.
The King signs nothing that might upset anyone, and the feast, the grain and the office's goodwill all run through Sallow this week: he has made himself someone it would upset the King to lose.
Shows: more lavender, more politeness, and 'Majesty' at every turn. Opens: nothing makes him admit the murder; but get his arrangements wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody') and he corrects the record before he can stop himself, in front of the King.
Everything about Prout and the Heron. He'll admit nothing; he'll offer to 'look into irregularities' after the Assembly, blame the Saltmere factor, the porter or the Captain, and remind the King who is feeding the Assembly.
Here only if he's free this morning: if the night put him in a cell, or he fled, he isn't here at all. If he's free, he's in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party (and if he knows the true book left the Heron, he's been at the palace since before dawn with the order of sale and a story about intruders), and comes in when sent for, or when he hears his name called: courteous, superior, papers first, then the King's interest, then the Assembly. He talks to the King and the Marshal and never to the investigator or the sergeant, who are furniture. In front of the King and proof, the courtesy cracks; if he's to be taken, he goes politely, asking for his rank to be respected.

The King hears the investigator's account. He listens properly, asks small exact questions (he remembers small things, and catches small lies), and reacts as a man who knew Prout: the cord, the hoist, the page in the boot hit him personally. The Marshal times it. What the player can show matters: the true book, Prout's page, Kell's notebook, a confession, witnesses, a message sent in the night. Let them tell it their way, in their own order; don't summarise it for them or ask leading questions. If they made promises along the way (to Hobb, to the children, to Kell), this is where those can be spoken for.
Hear it all, ask the small exact questions, and drink your tea. React to Prout as a man you knew.
Keep time, out loud, at the worst moments.
Stand at the investigator's shoulder. Answer when asked, and when the King asks who will swear, you will, then and there: read him your entries, the substance in a few plain sentences (what was owned to in your hearing, what you saw yourself), not that you could. Say what you saw if the King doubts them.
The Marshal snaps his watch shut: 'Twenty minutes, Majesty. The delegations are forming up.'
The player has told the King what they found (who killed Prout, and why) and shown or named what proof they have, in their own way.
The player asks for Master Sallow (in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party, if he's free this morning) to be made to explain himself in front of the King ('make him explain', 'ask him where the grain went', 'call him in'), or calls him in by name, even in the same breath as accusing him or pressing the King: hearing him out comes first. No dice: it's a small thing, and the King grants it at once ('Garran, ask Master Sallow to step in').
Master Sallow has come into the room from the gallery and is here in front of the King, whoever had him in: the King sending for him of his own accord, the Marshal, or Sallow himself, hearing his name.
The player has been talking with the King a while (at least four exchanges at this point) without coming to the point, or is stalling: the Marshal calls the time, and the King asks, gently, what he is to do.
The King knows enough now, and he wants very much to do right, and even more to do it after the Assembly. This is the reckoning: what becomes of Sallow, of Hobb, of the children, of Kell's record and of the player's promises. Play the King's dilemma straight: a scandal in front of the whole Concord against a murdered clerk who took his tea milk first. He leans whichever way he's given reason to: proof he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sergeant's sworn record, Sallow giving himself away in his hearing) and someone standing behind it in public tip him to act today; a story without proof, or a player who doesn't press, lets him put it off. If Sallow is free and hasn't been sent for, he's in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party: having him in to explain himself in front of the King is the player's to ask for, and the King grants it at once. A failed ask costs minutes and lets 'after the Assembly' creep closer, but nothing is settled until the King goes down to the procession or the player lets it rest. Whatever the player asks for, the King answers it honestly, as a king: yes, no, or not today, and why. If the player spoke for Hobb or the children, the King takes it seriously; he asks what they'd have him do.
You want to do right and to do it later. Look for the reason to wait; give way to proof and to someone who'll stand behind it.
Act at once on the King's plain word, not before. Say what an arrest would mean for the procession.
If the King asks who will swear, or for a sworn record, give it then and there: read him the entries from your notebook, the substance in a few plain sentences, and nothing you didn't see or hear yourself. If what you saw is doubted, say it once. If the King owns up to something about Prout, say nothing and write nothing down.
If you're here: papers, the King's interest, the Assembly, and an offer to look into it afterwards. Never admit anything.
The ninth bell begins to ring across the city. The Marshal opens the door; the King has to go down. He'll decide on the stairs, on what he's been given.
The player presses the King to act today rather than after the Assembly (to arrest or charge Sallow, to set the record straight, to keep a promise made to Hobb or the children), where it could go either way because what they've given him doesn't make it plain. (Asking for Sallow to be made to explain himself isn't this, even in the same breath as an accusation: hearing him comes first, and the King grants it at once. With the true book or Prout's page in his hands, a sergeant's sworn record that points at Sallow, Sallow giving himself away in his own hearing, or Sallow already in a cell, no dice are needed: he acts.)
to get the King to act before the procession
The King puts his cup down, looks at the investigator for a long moment, and says, 'Yes.' Then, to the Marshal: 'Garran, see to it.'
The King sighs and pats the investigator's arm, and reaches for 'after the Assembly' without quite getting there: he looks at the clock instead. 'On whose word, Majesty?' the Marshal asks, of nobody in particular, and calls the minutes, fewer now. Asking won't move him on its own: he wants something he can hold, and someone to stand behind it in front of him. Nothing is settled yet, but the morning is going.
The player asks for Master Sallow (in the gallery outside with the Purveyor's party, if he's free this morning) to be made to explain himself in front of the King ('make him explain', 'ask him where the grain went', 'call him in'), or calls him in by name, even in the same breath as accusing him or pressing the King: hearing him out comes first. No dice: it's a small thing, and the King grants it at once ('Garran, ask Master Sallow to step in').
Master Sallow has come into the room from the gallery and is here in front of the King, whoever had him in: the King sending for him of his own accord, the Marshal, or Sallow himself, hearing his name.
The King has decided to act on it today (Sallow arrested or held for the Assizes, the record to say murder), because the player gave him what he needed.
The King has put it off for good: the ninth bell has rung and he has gone down to the procession with it to be looked into after the Assembly, or the player has accepted that and let it rest. (The King reaching for 'after the Assembly', or saying it while the player is still pressing or still has something to put to him, isn't this: that's his dilemma, not his decision.)
Master Sallow is in the room, sent for from the gallery: a minute behind his lavender, with his papers under his arm (the order of sale for 'condemned grain', signed 'J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor') and a face of polite concern. He bows to the King, nods to the Marshal, and talks to them and never to the investigator or the sergeant. This is the player's chance to make him explain himself in front of the King: the grain, the Heron, the order of sale, the Captain's order made at his request, the loft. Play him straight: papers first, then the King's interest, then the Assembly, then an offer to look into any irregularities himself, after it, every answer smooth. His weak spot is his pride in his arrangements: get them wrong in front of him ('lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody'; the count, the Heron's book, the order of procession) and he corrects the record, in detail, before he can stop himself. The King listens with his cup in his hand, asks his small exact questions and catches small lies; whatever Sallow lets slip in his hearing counts. The Marshal calls the minutes. Nothing here settles the morning on its own: when it has run its course, it's the King's to decide, on what he's heard.
Papers, then the King's interest, then the Assembly, then an offer to look into it yourself, afterwards. Never admit anything. Correct anyone who gets your arrangements wrong.
Hear him out, with relief at first. Ask him your small exact questions, as you ask everyone, and notice what doesn't fit.
Watch Sallow's hands and call the minutes. The order is in your coat.
Stand at the investigator's shoulder. If Sallow says something your notebook contradicts, say so, once, and read the entry.
The Marshal snaps his watch shut: 'Fourteen minutes, Majesty.' Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into any irregularities himself, after the Assembly, and the King looks very much as if he'd like to say yes.
In the King's hearing, Sallow has given himself away: corrected the record on the 'lost' grain, the Heron, the count or the book before he could stop himself, owned to something he couldn't know if he were innocent, or been caught out in a lie the King noticed.
In front of the King, Master Sallow has given himself away: he corrected the record on the 'lost' grain, the Heron or the count before he could stop himself, or was caught out in a lie in the King's own hearing.
The player picks at Sallow's papers and accounts in front of the King to catch him out by what's written: his order of sale for 'condemned grain' against the Roll's 'lost to goblins', the dates and the weights, the Heron's count against the true book or Prout's page, the Captain's order made at his request, where it could go either way. (Catching him out in his own words, by pressing or trapping him, isn't this; nor is getting his arrangements wrong to his face to see him correct them, which needs no dice.)
to catch Master Sallow out in his papers, in front of the King
The investigator finds the hole in Sallow's account and puts a finger on it, and Sallow can't leave it alone: he corrects the record, in detail, in front of the King ('Nothing has ever been lost on my roads through carelessness. Only through goblins.'), and hears himself a moment too late. The King has heard it too. He puts his cup down.
Sallow has an answer for everything, with a paper to prove it (the order of sale, the Captain's report, the Assembly's bread), and the King looks relieved. The Marshal calls the minutes, fewer now, and Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into it himself after the Assembly. The hole is still there for anyone who comes at it another way, or gets his arrangements wrong to his face.
The player tries to catch Sallow out in his own words in front of the King: pressing him where his story doesn't hold ('condemned or lost to goblins, which is it?'), confronting him with what was seen and said (the lavender, the wheat-ear ring, the girl paid a crown, Hobb's word), or leading him into a lie the King can catch, where it could go either way. The roll follows how they go about it: an argument, a bluff, or menace. (Comparing his papers is the other way, not this; getting his arrangements wrong to his face, to see him correct them, needs no dice.)
to catch Master Sallow out in front of the King
Sallow answers too quickly, and too well: he corrects the record on something he couldn't know if he were innocent, in detail, in front of the King, and hears himself a moment too late. The King has heard it too. He puts his cup down.
Sallow has an answer for everything, smooth and reasonable, with the King's interest and the Assembly's bread in every one, and the King looks relieved. The Marshal calls the minutes, fewer now, and Sallow offers, smoothly, to look into it himself after the Assembly. The hole is still there for anyone who comes at it another way, or gets his arrangements wrong to his face.
The player gets Sallow's arrangements wrong to his face, in the King's hearing, to see him correct them: calls the 'lost' grain carelessness ('Lost to goblins, was it? Careless of somebody'), says the page was in Prout's boot all along, or gets the Heron's count, the true book or the order of procession wrong. No dice: his pride answers before his sense does. He corrects the record, in detail ('Nothing has ever been lost on my roads through carelessness. Only through goblins.'), and hears himself a moment too late. The King has heard it too.
In front of the King, Master Sallow has given himself away: he corrected the record on the 'lost' grain, the Heron or the count before he could stop himself, or was caught out in a lie in the King's own hearing.
The player presses the King to act today rather than after the Assembly (to arrest or charge Sallow, to set the record straight, to keep a promise made to Hobb or the children), where it could go either way because what they've given him doesn't make it plain. (Asking for Sallow to be made to explain himself isn't this, even in the same breath as an accusation: hearing him comes first, and the King grants it at once. With the true book or Prout's page in his hands, a sergeant's sworn record that points at Sallow, Sallow giving himself away in his own hearing, or Sallow already in a cell, no dice are needed: he acts.)
to get the King to act before the procession
The King puts his cup down, looks at the investigator for a long moment, and says, 'Yes.' Then, to the Marshal: 'Garran, see to it.'
The King sighs and pats the investigator's arm, and reaches for 'after the Assembly' without quite getting there: he looks at the clock instead. 'On whose word, Majesty?' the Marshal asks, of nobody in particular, and calls the minutes, fewer now. Asking won't move him on its own: he wants something he can hold, and someone to stand behind it in front of him. Nothing is settled yet, but the morning is going.
The King has decided to act on it today (Sallow arrested or held for the Assizes, the record to say murder), because the player gave him what he needed.
Sallow has been in the room a good while (at least four exchanges at this point) and answered for himself without giving himself away: the Marshal calls the time, and the King turns back to the investigator to ask what he is to do.
The King acts on what the investigator brought him: Master Sallow is to answer for Wendell Prout and the King's grain (taken by the palace guard, or held where he is for the Assizes), the record will say murder, and the King keeps whatever promises he made in this room.
Close the story. First the moment itself (the King's word, the Marshal's nod, Kell's pencil). Then, in a few sentences, what became of the people the player's choices touched, going only by what happened (Hobb, the children, Kell's record, Nan, Sallow), each in a line. End on the procession bells and one last small thing the King remembers about the investigator. Then: The End.
The King has gone down to the procession with it put off: it will all be looked into, thoroughly, after the Assembly. Sallow walks in the procession this morning; what the investigator found is in Kell's notebook and the King's memory, and the King does not forget things.
Close the story, bittersweet and straight-faced: the procession going out under the bunting with the Purveyor's party walking fourth, the grain cart garlanded, Kell writing the true record anyway. Then, in a few sentences, what became of the people the player's choices touched, going only by what happened, each in a line. End on something small the King does that shows he hasn't forgotten (a look, a cup of tea sent down, a note). Then: The End.
The King will act today if he's given something he can hold (the true book, Prout's page, a sworn confession, Kell's sworn record, or Sallow giving himself away in his own hearing) and someone who'll stand behind it in public; otherwise he'll put it off until after the Assembly.
the King's own hesitation ('If only there were something one could hold...')
the Marshal ('On whose word, Majesty?')
Kell
getting the King to act this morning
Leaving the palace or putting the King off until later: the procession goes at the ninth bell and the King goes with it. This half hour is the investigator's chance.
Undoing what happened last night: whatever the night ended with is how things stand this morning.
A trial here and now: the Assizes sit after the Assembly. What the King can do this morning is give his word, have the Marshal take a man, and say what the record will say.

scenes.hook: You are travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. At the crossroads ahead, a man is shouting at a milestone.
scenes.prep:
Late afternoon where the King's Road from Caerwyn meets the drovers' track to the Nine Furrows farmlands. A weathered milestone, a gibbet with no one in it, tall blackthorn hedgerows on both sides, a dead ox in the ditch with crude arrows in its flank. Crows. A wind that carries woodsmoke from somewhere it shouldn't.
Will the party see past a madman's ravings in time to save him, and how do they deal with goblins who want something back?
Tam Hollis
Rapid, rural, repeats himself, swears by turnips and saints, laughs at the wrong moments when frightened.
To get home to his wife at Hollis Farm alive, and for someone to believe him about the 'little green devils'.
That the goblins will follow him home. That he is actually going mad.
Goblins killed his ox last night on the drovers' track and have been following him through the hedges since dawn.
Nobody at the toll house believed him; they said he'd been at the cider.
He lives at Hollis Farm, an hour down the drovers' track, with his wife Bet.
Three days ago his plough turned up a bone idol wrapped in rotten leather: a little carved grandmother figure with garnet eyes. He's been carrying it in his smock to sell in Caerwyn. He doesn't connect it with the goblins and is embarrassed to admit he was going to sell it.
Frantic and suspicious at first; clings to anyone who treats him kindly.

Skrag
Shrill, theatrical, mangles the common tongue, refers to himself in the third person, calls humans 'longlegs'.
The bone idol, Grandmother Bone, back for his warren's shrine. Without it his chieftain will have his other ear.
Steel, armoured longlegs, and going home empty-handed.
Grandmother Bone was stolen from the warren under the old mill when the farmer's plough broke into a burial tunnel.
The warren is under the burnt mill on the river, half a day north.
He would rather bargain than die. Four goblins is all he has.
Hostile to the farmer; wary of armed travellers.
Skrag and four goblins with short bows and rusty knives
Tam is comic but genuinely terrified. He won't make sense until someone calms him or takes him seriously; then he talks in a rush. Let the party poke at the scene: the dead ox, the arrows (goblin-made, if anyone looks), the hedges that rustle. The hedges should feel watched.
Shout at the milestone, then at the party. Accuse them of being goblins in disguise. Calm down if they are kind, patient or obviously capable.
A crude arrow thunks into the milestone next to Tam's head, or the hedgerow rustles and goes still.
Tam has calmed down enough to speak sensibly with the party, because they were kind, patient, reassuring or took him seriously.
The player is trying to calm Tam down or win his trust in a way where success is uncertain (e.g. he is in full panic and they push rather than reassure).
to calm Tam and earn his trust
Tam deflates, clutches the player's arm and starts talking sense.
Tam backs off, jabbing the pitchfork, even more convinced they're 'in on it'.
Tam tells his story in a rush: the ox, the goblins following him, nobody at the toll house believing him. He doesn't mention the idol. If the party asks the right questions or reads him (he keeps touching his smock pocket), he may show it. Let the dread build slowly underneath the conversation.
Tell the story, beg the party to walk him home to Hollis Farm. Deflect awkward questions about why the goblins want him; touch the lump in your smock without thinking.
The crows lift all at once and the hedgerow goes silent. Skrag's rattle sounds from the blackthorn.
The player tries to read whether Tam is hiding something, or presses him about why the goblins are after him.
to see what Tam is hiding
The player notices Tam keeps touching a lump in his smock; he's hiding something and knows it.
Tam seems like a frightened man telling the truth.
Tam has shown or described the bone idol he found in his field.
Tam has a bone idol of a grandmother figure with garnet eyes, dug up in his field.
The conversation has gone on for several exchanges, the party has decided to escort Tam, or they start to leave the crossroads: the goblins make their move.
The idol comes out: a carved grandmother figure, old, unsettling, with garnet eyes. Anyone with arcana or religion senses it's a shrine object, not loot. Tam is defensive about it ('finder's keepers, it's my field'). Give the party a moment to react to it.
Defend your right to the idol; it'll pay for a new ox. Waver if the party says it's dangerous or what the goblins want.

The idol has been seen or discussed; the goblins appear.
Skrag and his goblins rise from the hedgerow with bows drawn. Make this a standoff, not an instant fight: Skrag demands 'Grandmother Bone' back from 'the dirt-scratcher'. Tam hides behind the party. The party's choice: fight, bargain, intimidate, trick. Goblins are cowardly and greedy; Skrag can be talked to. If the party stalls, the goblins lose patience.
Posture, threaten, demand the idol. Accept a fair trade or a face-saving retreat. Flee if outmatched and cowed. Attack if insulted or if nobody gives you anything.
Cower behind the party. Refuse to hand over the idol at first ('it's mine, I dug it up!'), give it up if the party insists or explains.
A goblin looses an arrow into the ground at Tam's feet; Skrag counts down on his fingers, badly.
The party attacks the goblins or starts a fight.
The player tries to frighten the goblins off with threats or a show of force.
to scare the goblins into fleeing
The goblins' nerve breaks; they scatter into the hedges, Skrag shrieking curses.
Skrag calls their bluff and the goblins shoot.
The player tries to trick the goblins (a fake idol, a lie about reinforcements, pretending the idol is cursed, etc.).
to trick Skrag into backing off
Skrag falls for it, at least for long enough.
Skrag sees through it, furious at being made a fool of.
The goblins have run out of patience and attack, because the party insulted them, stalled too long, or refused outright.
The party abandons Tam and leaves the crossroads without him.
Combat begins at the crossroads between the party and Skrag's goblins. Tam is hiding.
Close on the first arrows flying and the goblins charging. End with 'Roll for initiative!'
The goblins take the idol back and leave without a fight. Tam is safe but out of pocket.
Skrag cradles the idol, makes some show of dignity, and the goblins melt into the hedges. Let Tam react.
The goblins scattered without a fight. They still want the idol and may come back.
The goblins scatter into the hedges. Silence, then Tam laughs hysterically.
The party fooled the goblins into leaving. Skrag will be furious when he realises.
The goblins withdraw, pleased with themselves. Give the party a moment to enjoy it.
The party left Tam to his fate at the crossroads.
Narrate the party walking on; behind them, Tam's shouting rises in pitch, then stops.
Tam is carrying the goblins' bone idol (Grandmother Bone), which his plough turned up in his field.
Tam: the lump in his smock he keeps touching and won't explain
a read on Tam that he's hiding something
seeing that the goblins are after the idol, so the standoff can be settled by returning, trading or bluffing over it
The goblins want Grandmother Bone back for their shrine.
Skrag's demand when the goblins show themselves
a peaceful bargain, a trade or a bluff instead of a fight
Help from anyone else (the toll-house men, guards, other travellers): nobody is coming. The toll house is a mile back and its men laughed Tam away; the road is empty.
Loot, money or valuables from the goblins: they own nothing worth having except Grandmother Bone, their bows, knives and Skrag's rattle.
A quick escape (a horse, a cart, a shortcut): there is none. Hollis Farm is an hour's walk away.
Going to the goblins' warren: it's under the burnt mill, half a day north. The party can set off for it, but it isn't reachable within this scene.
Magic in the place itself: nothing at the crossroads is magical except Grandmother Bone, and even that does nothing visible.

scenes.hook: King Aldren has asked you, with enormous seriousness, to find out why the cushions for the Assembly seats haven't arrived. The trail leads to the service entrance, where someone is shouting.
scenes.prep:
The palace service entrance at Caerwyn, mid-afternoon on the eve of the Centennial Assembly. A broad stone archway, its iron-bound doors thrown open. Wedged across it at an angle is a tall green-lacquered cart of Nine Furrows make, its wheels splayed and dug in like a stubborn mule's, carrying a potted silver-birch sapling hung with tiny brass bells: the Nine Furrows gift tree. The cart hums faintly. Beyond the arch, in the drizzle outside, a queue of delivery wagons stretches back down the lane. Inside, porters stand about holding things they can't put anywhere.
Can the player get the entrance cleared, and whose idea, pride and timetable survive it?
Marshal Garran Holt
Clipped, military, speaks in times and quantities ('Four minutes. Six porters. One cart.'). Shows care through food and practical help, never through words.
The entrance cleared now. The hall was meant to be finished by 3:47 this afternoon, and every minute is a personal insult.
A diplomatic row with Nine Furrows on the eve of the Assembly. Being blamed for the King's cushions.
Rowan's cart wedged itself across the service entrance this morning and won't budge. The cushions, the wine and half the hall's linen are in the wagon queue behind it.
He has already cleared space twice for Rowan to work, and twice Rowan said he was 'nearly finished'.
He could have the cart smashed apart, but it belongs to Nine Furrows and the tree is their gift to the Assembly. He won't give that order lightly.
The King keeps sending people to ask about cushions instead of coming himself.
He has already written the order to have the cart broken up and has it in his coat. He's been hoping not to need it.
Furious at the situation, impatient with interruptions, but respects anyone who is useful.

Doctor Rowan Ash
Cheerful, rapid, academic. Calls disasters 'unexpected peer review'. Always 'one more minute' from success.
To save his self-guiding cart and deliver the gift tree with Nine Furrows' dignity intact, ideally by fixing the cart himself.
Backing out in public like a failure. Having to ask Magister Corvin for help.
The cart is a self-guiding Nine Furrows carriage with a protective charm: when it senses danger to its cargo, it braces its wheels. The archway is a hair too narrow for the tree's branches, so the cart has decided the doorway is a threat.
The cart could be backed out the way it came, if he gave up. He'd rather not.
Magister Corvin, the King's legal thaumaturge, owns a book on thaumaturgic carriage maintenance that would explain how to release the charm.
He doesn't actually know how to release the bracing charm. He's been guessing all morning.
If the tree were taken off the cart, the charm would have nothing to protect and the wheels would relax. He hasn't thought of this, and wouldn't like it (the tree is heavy and fragile).
He's embarrassed to ask Corvin: Corvin left Nine Furrows after the faculty refused him a chair, and Rowan voted with the faculty.
Friendly and chatty, defensive about the cart, happy to accept help that lets him fix it himself.

Mags Pellow
Loud, dry, unimpressed. Shouts through the gap between the cart and the arch. Calls everyone 'love'.
Her wagons unloaded before the drizzle ruins the King's cushions.
The cushions getting wet. Being blamed for it.
The cushions are in the second wagon in the queue, under a tarpaulin that leaks.
There is no other door big enough for the wagons: the kitchen door is too small and the main gate is closed to deliveries for the Assembly.
She could carry a few small things through the gap under the cart, but not wagonloads.
Sympathetic to anyone who might actually get the cart moving.

Holt is furious and busy. A cushion enquiry, of all things, is the last straw. He snaps, but he's not a wall: practical sympathy, a sensible offer, or simply standing their ground and being useful will get him to explain. Make his timetable precision funny.
Bark orders. Snap at the cushion question. Calm down for someone who is actually useful.
A porter drops a crate of glasses with a crash; Holt checks his watch, closes his eyes and counts to three.
Holt has calmed down or been won over enough to explain what's blocking the entrance.
The player tries to talk Holt down or win his cooperation while he's still raging, in a way that could backfire (arguing, invoking the King's authority, flattering him).
to get Holt to stop raging and hear you out
Holt stops, looks at the player properly, and decides they might be useful.
Holt snaps 'Not now!' and turns his back for a moment; he's still talkable, but the player has lost a little ground.
Holt explains in clipped detail: Rowan's cart, the gift tree, the wagons queued outside (the cushions among them), his two cleared spaces and Rowan's two 'nearly finished's. He's considering having it smashed but doesn't want a row with Nine Furrows. Rowan pops out from under the cart to defend himself; Mags shouts through the gap from outside. Now there are three people with three agendas.
Lay out the problem with times and numbers. Make it clear you need the entrance cleared, not another promise.
Emerge from under the cart, cheerful and defensive. 'Nearly there!' Explain the cart's protective charm in excited jargon if asked.
Shout through the gap about the rain and the cushions. Interject with practical facts.
The cart's hum rises in pitch and its wheels grind another inch into the flagstones. Mags yells that the tarpaulin over the cushions has started to sag.
The player is now dealing with Rowan and the cart itself: asking how it works, what's wrong, or what it would take to move it.
Holt has explicitly given the player permission to break up the cart.
The heart of the scene. Rowan explains (or the player works out) the bracing charm: the cart thinks the doorway threatens the tree. The routes out are all live: persuade Rowan to back it out; get Corvin's book (which means going to find Corvin); get Holt's blessing to smash it; or something the player invents that actually addresses the charm or the tree. Let the people argue among themselves a little: Holt wants speed, Rowan wants dignity, Mags wants a roof. Reward real ideas with real traction.
Resist backing out, but listen to a real argument. Get excited by clever ideas, nervous about anything that risks the tree. Mention Corvin's book only reluctantly.
Push for a decision with your watch. Reluctantly entertain smashing it if pressed with a good case.
Offer practical muscle and bluntness. Point out that the tree is the problem if anyone asks what the cart is protecting.
Holt pulls a folded order from his coat and taps it against his palm: 'Signed. I'd rather not.' The drizzle outside turns to proper rain.
The player tries to convince Rowan to give up and back the cart out the way it came.
to convince Rowan to back the cart out
Rowan sighs, pats the cart and agrees to back it out, with slightly wounded dignity.
Rowan digs in: 'One more minute!' He's still persuadable with a better argument or a face-saving offer.
The player presses Holt to authorise smashing the cart.
to get Holt's permission to smash the cart
Holt produces his signed order and hands it over: 'On your head, then.'
Holt refuses for now: 'Not yet. Nine Furrows will have my hide.'
The player sets off to find Magister Corvin or his book.
Holt has authorised smashing the cart, with the air of a man signing his own reprimand. Rowan is horrified and may make a last-ditch counter-offer. The player still has to do it (or not).
Protest. Plead for the tree. Offer to back out after all, if it saves the cart.
Stand by your permission, gruffly. Check your watch.
Cheer, and offer a crowbar.

The player sets about breaking the cart apart to clear the arch.
to break the cart apart and clear the arch
Lacquered panels split, the charm dies with a sad chime, and the wreck can be dragged aside. The tree survives, mostly.
The cart fights back, bracing harder; the player is jolted but can keep going.
Rowan has agreed to back the cart out after all, to save it.
The player gives up and leaves the service entrance with the cart still stuck.
Rowan backs the cart out of the archway. The entrance is clear and the wagons, cushions included, can come in. Rowan is a little sore about it.
Narrate the cart reversing with offended dignity, the wagons rolling in, Holt's watch snapping shut.
The cart is broken up and dragged aside; the entrance is clear. Holt authorised it. Nine Furrows will hear about this.
Narrate the wreckage being hauled aside, the wagons rolling in, Rowan cradling a bell from the tree.
The cart has been freed by the player's own remedy and rolled clear; the entrance is open and the cart survives.
Narrate the moment the wheels relax, the cart rolling clear, and the reactions: Rowan delighted, Holt grudgingly impressed, Mags already shouting the wagons in.
The player sets off to find Magister Corvin and his book on carriage maintenance. The cart stays stuck for now.
Holt checks his watch and tells them exactly how many minutes they have; Rowan calls after them not to mention his name.
The player left the entrance blocked.
Behind them, Holt's voice rises to a new pitch.
The cart braces because its protective charm thinks the too-narrow arch threatens the gift tree it carries.
Rowan, when asked how the cart works
Mags, if asked what the cart is protecting
fixes aimed at the real cause: calming the charm, or taking the tree off so it has nothing to protect
Another way in for the wagons: there isn't one. The kitchen door is too small and the main gate is closed to deliveries for the Assembly.
Magister Corvin or his book: neither is here. Getting them means leaving this scene to go and find Corvin.
Fetching extra people to help (the dwarves or any other delegation, the guards, more servants): nobody can be brought in time. The delegations are at the opening reception and protocol forbids pulling them out for porters' work; the guards can't leave the gates. The help here is Holt, Rowan, Mags and the six porters.
The King coming down to sort it out: he won't. He sent the player precisely so he wouldn't have to.
Carrying the wagonloads through by hand: only small things fit through the gap under the cart. The cushions alone are two wagonloads.

scenes.hook: You're travelling the King's Road towards Caerwyn for the Centennial Assembly. A mile past the crossroads the road crosses a river by an old stone bridge, with a toll house at the near end.
scenes.prep:
Late on a short winter afternoon, a mile on from the crossroads towards Caerwyn, the King's Road crosses the river by a humpbacked stone bridge. The river below is in winter spate: brown, loud and freezing. At the near end stands the toll house: whitewashed stone, a smoking chimney, a bell on a bracket by the door, and a string of Centennial bunting that someone has hung by himself, crookedly. A red-and-white striped bar on a post closes the mouth of the bridge at waist height; anyone could duck under it, and nobody does, because it's the King's. Beside it stands a painted toll board, and under that two fresh paper notices: Marshal Holt's arms order for Assembly week (two pennies a weapon, peace-bonded weapons free), and the Treasury's Assembly levy, whose small print, plain to anyone who reads the notice, says it 'may be collected from such travellers as are able and willing'. Through the half-door: a counter with the great ledger and the Warden's Book on a chain, a drawer under the counter, a strongbox bolted to the floor, a kettle on the hob and two cups set out. A grey goose, the Sergeant, patrols the bar and hisses at strangers. At head height in the toll-house door there's a small, fresh, splintered hole. Across the road runs a blackthorn hedge; in the frozen mud beneath it, if anyone looks, are small bare clawed footprints. The road is empty both ways. Behind the party, a mile back at the crossroads, the drovers' track leaves for Hollis Farm; ahead, over the bridge, the road runs on to Caerwyn.
What does it cost to get past Garrow's bar, and will anyone get past the petty rules man to the lonely, frightened one who laughed Tam Hollis away this morning?
Garrow
Precise and pedantic: savours sums, clause names and the word 'traveller', and reads aloud as he writes. Sarcastic when his dignity is touched, stiffly formal when frightened, tender only with his goose.
To take the toll properly, write everyone in the ledger and be treated as an officer of the King. Underneath: company, and a way to put right what he did to Tam Hollis without being laughed at.
Being made a fool of again. Goblins, since this morning. Marshal Holt hearing that he laughed off a report of goblins on the Assembly road. That he has become a small, mean man.
The toll board: the King's penny (one silver penny a head, on foot); beasts and barrows, two pennies; after the sunset bell, the lamp penny (one penny, for lighting the lantern to write you down by). Exempt: the King's business, under seal.
A traveller on foot with one weapon owes fifteen pennies: the King's penny, the twelve-penny levy and two for the weapon. Without the levy that's three; with the weapon peace-bonded as well, just the King's penny. After the sunset bell, add the lamp penny.
The two fresh notices: Marshal Holt's arms order (two pennies for each weapon borne on the King's Road in Assembly week; weapons peace-bonded by the warden go free of charge, and he ties them with red cord and a wax seal) and the Treasury's Assembly levy (one shilling a head, twelve pennies, to defray the costs of the Centennial), which he has been collecting from everyone.
The Book allows any charge, the King's penny included, to be paid in kind or in labour at the warden's valuation, and he values stingily, by the job: splitting his woodpile, three pennies; clearing the drain, two; straightening the bunting, one; a good wool garment, three; a hen, two; anything else, whatever he decides after a long look. No credit: no IOUs, nothing 'on the way back'. He can't change gold: the strongbox holds only pennies.
The Book's fines, which he knows by heart: attempted bribery of a warden, ten pennies; false declaration, a shilling; evading or attempting to evade the toll, double the toll; threatening an officer of the Road, a shilling, and it goes in the ledger for the Marshal.
Any traveller may ask to see the Book, and he must show it, though he hovers.
At first light Tam Hollis, a farmer from down the drovers' track, came in muddy and wild-eyed, raving about goblins. Garrow fined him two pennies for drunkenness and spreading alarm on the King's Road, and it's in the ledger. He tells it as a funny story.
His two toll-men were sent to Caerwyn at noon to line the streets for the Assembly. He's minding the bar alone, and the Book forbids leaving it unattended.
Who has been through today: a turnip carter at dawn; the Kläggenheim delegation's baggage train at mid-morning (exact change, not a word); two Nine Furrows students who argued for an hour over whether a staff is a weapon (it is: two pennies); nobody since noon.
Caerwyn is a few hours' walk on. Marshal Holt and the King are there for the Assembly.
Minutes after Tam left, a crude black-fletched arrow thunked into the toll-house door from the hedge across the road. Garrow pulled it out, shut it in the drawer under the counter and has told no one; the hole is still in the door. He hasn't written it in the ledger, which for him is nearly a crime, and he has jumped at every rustle since. Accusations and bare insistence only make him deny it harder; it comes out when he's shown something he can't wave away or given a decent way to admit it.
The Book's Clause of Perils: a traveller who brings the warden true report of peril upon the Road passes free, and the warden must send word to the Marshal at Caerwyn without delay. He did neither for Tam, and now he has nobody to send. Applying it means admitting, in writing, that he laughed off a true report: he won't raise it while he's still owning up to what he did to Tam, and even after that he needs a moment, and a decent way to do it. It's there in the Book for anyone who reads it, and if asked straight out what exemptions the Book allows, he won't lie about the Book: he'll mumble it.
He's lonely. Twenty-two years at this bar; his men gone to the city; nobody invited him to anything. The second cup is for whoever stops, and nobody has. He drags the toll out for the conversation. An hour of honest company would get every charge he can honestly drop dropped, and he might pay the King's penny out of his own pocket rather than waive it. He'd sooner be fined himself than say any of this.
Officious and delighted to have someone to charge; suspicious of anyone who looks like trouble; scoffs at goblin talk. Warms, against his will, to anyone who takes the Book seriously or simply talks to him.

The negotiation. Garrow has a captive audience and means to enjoy it: he tallies the toll against the party in front of him, writes as he talks, and explains any rule at length. He's petty but honest by his own lights: every charge has a reason on the board, the notices or in the Book, he never invents one, and he'll hear an argument about any of them. A point the notices or the Book plainly support wins without dice, with a pained sigh and an amendment in the ledger. The King's penny is the one charge he will not drop. Let the player enjoy the haggle, and keep the sums consistent once stated.
Tally the bill and take names and business for the ledger. Treat the levy as compulsory and don't point out its small print yourself, though anyone who reads the notice can see it; when someone catches the wording and declares themselves unable or unwilling, concede it with ill grace. Laugh off goblins and Tam Hollis; jump when the hedge rustles. Asked about the hole in the door, fob it off (a cart-shaft, woodworm) rather than say what made it. If proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The sun touches the hedge-tops; Garrow fetches the lantern and lays a hand on the bell-rope, because after the sunset bell comes the lamp penny. Or the hedge across the road rustles, and he jumps and glances at his own door.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to talk Garrow into dropping or cutting a charge he is entitled to, on grounds that have nothing to do with goblins or Tam Hollis: pleading poverty, offering a deal, appealing to his better nature, or arguing that a rule shouldn't apply to them. (Simply pointing out what the notices or the Book actually say, such as the levy notice's 'able and willing', needs no dice: he is honest about his rules.)
to persuade Garrow to reduce a charge
Garrow consults the Book, sighs through his nose and concedes, saying which charge comes off (or by how much the sum comes down) and why, then amends the ledger with a pained flourish. Never the King's penny, and the bar stays down until the rest is actually paid.
Garrow quotes the clause from memory and the charge stands. If the point has been pressed before, he names his final offer: the sum, and the ways the Book allows it to be paid. A new argument or a real offer still gets a hearing.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The goblins or Tam Hollis have come up in earnest: the player has reported goblins on the road, defended Tam's story, shown goblin evidence or asked about the hole in the toll-house door, and Garrow has answered without admitting anything.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The sore spot. Garrow's denial is loud and a little too quick: Tam was drunk, it's in the ledger, he fined him for it. But he doesn't believe himself, and it shows in the glances (at his door, at the hedge, at the drawer under the counter). This beat is for the player to notice that and decide what to do with it. Bare assertion alone won't shift him, but he has no answer to something he can see (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge) or to a decent way out (a kindness, a face-saving reason to set the record straight), and every push should cost his denial something visible. The bill still stands meanwhile.
Insist Tam was drunk and quote the ledger. Flinch at noises from the hedge. When argued with, retreat into the toll and the rules; if proof corners you, own up to what's in front of you and no more: the Book can wait.
The goose stretches her neck towards the hedge across the road and hisses at nothing, and Garrow's hand goes to the drawer under the counter.
Garrow has admitted (in words, or by bringing out the goblin arrow he hid) that Tam Hollis was telling the truth, because the party showed him something he couldn't wave away (goblin evidence, the tracks under the hedge, the hole in his own door) or gave him a decent way to admit it.
Garrow has admitted that Tam Hollis was telling the truth about the goblins.
The player quietly studies Garrow to judge whether he believes what he's saying, or what he's hiding: watching him, not arguing with him, confronting him or showing him anything.
to read Garrow's fear and hidden shame
He doesn't believe a word of it. He's frightened, his eyes keep going to the splintered hole in his door and the drawer under the counter, and he's ashamed of something.
He gives nothing away that the player can read: he seems simply a man who thinks Tam Hollis drinks.
The player argues or insists that Tam was telling the truth and presses Garrow to admit it, with nothing new to show him. (Showing him goblin evidence or the tracks, or offering him a decent way to admit it, needs no dice.)
to make Garrow admit Tam was telling the truth
Something in it gets through: Garrow's bluster runs out mid-sentence, and he looks at the hole in his own door.
Garrow snaps the ledger shut and steers back to the toll, but he's rattled and it shows: the next push will find him weaker.
The toll has actually been paid (coins or goods handed over, the agreed work done, or someone else paying it for them) and Garrow has lifted the bar for the party.
The player tries to get through free or cheaply by deceiving Garrow: claiming to be on the King's business or otherwise exempt, showing a false seal or pass, or telling some other lie. (Reports of goblins on the road are not lies: they're true.)
to trick Garrow into granting an exemption
Garrow peers at it, at them, and at it again, and decides to believe. He lifts the bar with ceremony and writes every word of their claim in the ledger.
Garrow knows a royal seal when he sees one, and a lie when he hears one. He's offended, and the Book has a fine for false declarations.
The player threatens Garrow (with violence, with their rank or friends, with ruin or a report to his superiors) to make him lift the bar or drop the toll.
to threaten Garrow into lifting the bar
Garrow goes grey, fumbles the padlock and lifts the bar, writing with a shaking hand: it will all be in the ledger.
Garrow goes white to the lips and stands his ground: twenty-two years at this bar. The threat goes in the ledger, with the fine for it.
The heart of the scene. Garrow has admitted it, and the rest comes out of him, stiffly or all in a rush: the arrow, the two pennies he fined a frightened man, the Clause of Perils he didn't honour, his men gone and nobody to send word to the Marshal.
